Title: Threat actor targets Indian fintechs on weekends when defenders aren’t watching
Context: ” The crew also quickly exploits newly discovered vulnerabilities to keep its attacks fresh
Full Text: India’s Computer Emergency Response Team has warned the nation’s financial services industry of a “significant escalation” in attacks by what it describes as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor” that has re-targeted victims after they flubbed remediation efforts. CERT-IN first detected the attacks in October and issued advisory in which it warned digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and wallet operators that attackers were targeting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints. If the attackers found a way in, they tried to use payment APIs to steal money. On Thursday, the CERT published an update in which it said it continues to hear of successful attacks, including from outfits that tried to remediate their systems after earlier incidents. “The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response,” the CERT warned. CERT-IN has decided the attackers need a name and chose “CRAFTY FALCON.” The security org has also revealed that the crew uses AI-enhanced tools including the ARTEX pen-testing tool, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework – all of which have been linked to users who appear to speak Chinese. CRAFTY FALCON’s tactics see it go looking for internet-exposed environments used for testing or development, where it finds artefacts such as shared credentials, tokens, or network paths that help it move into production systems. If it gets in, the crew re-writes victims’ applications so they do things like make unauthorized API calls. Victims’ defenses assume that only legitimate apps would call those APIs, so activity conducted by the re-written apps aren’t flagged as an attack. Even if victims suspect an attack, they have a lot to cope with because CERT-IN says CRAFTY FALCON creates many “functionally identical variants refined in rapid succession; a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.” The crew also quickly exploits newly discovered vulnerabilities to keep its attacks fresh. Once it gets a toehold, the criminal crew makes tiny payments of about $0.01 to test if its attacks work. If those transfers work, CRAFTY FALCON makes larger payments. When the target is a cryptocurrency exchange or virtual digital asset service provider, the crew steals wallet keys and empties cryptocurrency wallets. Vendors of observability tools will be warming up their Indian sales teams today, because CERT-IN’s advice to Indian businesses includes improving their ability to log events, monitor for anomalies in real time, and send alerts. It also urged keeping test environments off the internet, and restricting access to cloud resources because CRAFTY FALCON is fond of using them to run its attacks. CERT-IN also warns that the attacks are “active and escalating” and therefore worthy of 24x7 monitoring. Interestingly, the CERT’s advisory mentions attacks on “entities” across banking, financial services, and insurance, but only names the kind of businesses mentioned above as having reported attacks. The Register points this out because India is home to literally thousands of banks, many of them small operations that sometimes lack basic infosec protections. CRAFTY FALCON therefore has a target-rich environment in India should it choose to expand its activities. ®

Title: OpenSSH flaw lets attackers access password-disabled accounts on some Linux systems
Context: A critical vulnerability that affects OpenSSH servers on Linux systems built with the musl C library instead of glibc allows remote attackers to easily bypass authentication and...
Full Text:
A critical vulnerability that affects OpenSSH servers on Linux systems built with the musl C library instead of glibc allows remote attackers to easily bypass authentication and log into accounts that should have password authentication disabled. The flaw impacts the lightweight Alpine Linux, which is widely used for cloud Docker container images, as well as Linux distributions for embedded systems.

The security bug, dubbed *SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158, was discovered by Ozgun Kultekin, a researcher with security testing firm Wakefield, and has existed for the past 10 years. The OpenSSH maintainers moved quickly to add mitigation for the flaw in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 emergency update released Thursday, even though they claim the bug is not actually in their code.

“It’s not every day that the ‘exploit’ for a vulnerability in a technology as prevalent as OpenSSH is just ‘send a long password’ or ‘send a lot of A characters,’ but here we are,” said Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at preemptive exposure management firm watchTowr. “On affected systems, the exploit is strikingly simple: send a password between 257 and 1,024 characters long.”

Luckily, there are some prerequisites for this exploit to work:

The Linux distribution needs to use musl, which means that many popular server distros such as Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora are not impacted

The system needs to use OpenSSH and not alternative SSH server implementations such as Dropbear, which many embedded distros use

OpenSSH needs to be configured without support for Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the most common Linux login framework

OpenSSH needs to allow password-based authentication

The attacker needs to know the name of an account for which password login has been disabled at the system level

Those conditions are met in default configuration for Alpine Linux and its built-in “alpine” username, which allows executing commands as root. The Alpine project released emergency updates for the openssh package and advises users who can’t update to disable password-based authentication in the OpenSSH configuration and set up key-based authentication.

Why the trivial attack works

The flaw is the product of three changes made years apart, each solving a different problem. In 2012, musl’s developers capped password length at 256 bytes to stop attackers from tying up server resources by sending long passwords that need to be hashed as part of the login verification process.

At the same time they also made the library’s password hashing function return an asterisk (*) whenever it fails. The asterisk is the same character Unix has used since the 1980s to mark accounts for which no password should ever match — accounts with password disabled at the system level.

In 2016, OpenSSH changed how it checks passwords for accounts whose own password field offers no salt to hash against, borrowing another account’s salt so that attackers could not guess existing usernames with brute-force login retries and timing the server’s responses. Then in 2022, Alpine switched root’s password field to an asterisk so that SSH key logins would keep working for it.

When an attacker sends an over-long password for a password-disabled account on such a system, the hash attempt fails and returns an asterisk, which sshd compares with the asterisk stored in the account’s password field. The two match, and the login succeeds.

Alpine Linux cloud images will be the main target

Alpine’s standard OpenSSH package is built without PAM, and password logins are enabled by default, so Alpine servers meet the conditions out of the box. On the official cloud images published between versions 3.18.11 and 3.24.3, the default user account, named alpine, is one of the password-disabled accounts, and the images grant it passwordless “doas” privileges.

As a result, an attacker who logs in as that user can then switch to root, so the images are exposed as soon as an administrator sets a password for any other account on the system, because a legitimate account with a real password needs to exist for this attack to work.

Unlike the critical regreSSHion flaw from 2024, this one is confined to the musl world, but it requires no exploit engineering of any kind.

“Internet-exposed SSH servers are already being hammered by password guesses and brute-force attempts around the clock,” Knott said. “Exploiting this vulnerability simply means those same attackers add a very long password attempt to that brute-force list. We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend.”

Organizations should also check whether the flaw was already used against their servers. An “Accepted password” entry in /var/log/messages for an account that has no password, such as root, a key-only user, or the default alpine user, is a strong sign of compromise.

Alpine recommends reviewing doas usage, recently created users and files on exposed machines, and its advisory says any server where a login cannot be ruled out should be treated as compromised. Kultekin also published a check script on GitHub that identifies exposed servers and lists the accounts at risk.

Title: FBI, CISA warn of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems
Context: According to a joint advisory published Thursday, attackers are exploiting weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial...
Full Text:
The FBI and CISA warn that hackers are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, potentially causing food spoilage, equipment damage, and fire hazards.

The warning was issued jointly with the U.S. Departments of Health and Human Services (HHS), Agriculture (USDA), and Transportation (DOT), urging critical infrastructure operators to secure vulnerable refrigeration controllers used in healthcare, food production, chemical facilities, and transportation.

"Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," said Chris Butera, CISA's Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity.

According to a joint advisory published Thursday, attackers are exploiting weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration management systems.

These devices allow operators to monitor temperatures remotely, manage defrost cycles, and control cooling equipment.

"Globally, malicious cyber actors are targeting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities," CISA warned.

The agencies say attackers may exploit authentication bypass vulnerabilities, arbitrary code injection flaws, or weak configurations to modify temperature settings and force refrigeration equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles.

Successful attacks can cause inventory losses, reduce equipment lifespan, create fire hazards, and create unsafe storage conditions. Attackers may also reduce visibility into current temperatures, preventing operators from detecting problems.

The warning follows a series of attacks against European refrigeration systems that have disrupted supermarkets and blood storage facilities.

In October, hackers compromised refrigeration controllers at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, remotely activating defrost functions and raising temperatures in refrigerators and freezers.

A second wave of attacks reported in November affected more than 115 stores across six European countries, with some refrigeration systems shutting down entirely and others raising temperatures to as high as 50°C (122°F).

On November 3, the French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had altered temperature and defrost settings at three facilities used to store blood products.

In response to the ongoing threat, the U.S. agencies are urging organizations to remove refrigeration controllers from the public internet, secure necessary remote access, change default passwords, and apply available security updates.

They also recommend isolating operational technology systems from business networks and enforcing safe temperature limits to prevent controllers from operating outside acceptable ranges.

Other VPNs We’ve Tested

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

If you want to dig in deeper, you can. Surfshark is one of the most feature-rich VPNs I've used, sporting the basics like a double-hop connection and split tunneling, as well as an ad blocker and email masking. Like Proton, Surfshark offers other security tools like antivirus and dark web monitoring if you pick up a more expensive plan. Surfshark loses out just a bit when it comes to privacy, however. It has a no-logs policy, and it maintains a transparency report and a warrant canary, so it’s not bad in this regard. However, it doesn't have open-source applications, so you’ll need a bit more faith in Surfshark’s app security than with some other VPN services.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

IVPN: This privacy-focused VPN provider is similar to Mullvad. It does not ask you to create an account with a username, password, and email, but instead generates a random ID, which you use to log in. That helps preserve your anonymity, since that information can’t be tied to your usage even if IVPN suffered a security incident. IVPN also accepts cryptocurrency payments (Bitcoin and Monero). Unlike Mullvad, IVPN offers one-year, two-year, and three-year plan options, as well as an unusual weekly option, which might be nice if you want a VPN while on vacation (IVPN standard is $2 per week). These can be more affordable than Mullvad’s monthly fee. However, IVPN lacks some privacy features you will find with Mullvad, such as RAM-less servers. IVPN scheduled a security audit for 2025, but as of January 2026, the results have not been posted. IVPN also has a tight two-device limit on the Standard plan. The Pro plan raises that to seven, but the Pro plan’s price is $10 per month, so it’s more expensive than Mullvad, which has a five-device limit. That remains true even if you go with a multi-year IVPN plan. Still, IVPN is a fine alternative if you want annual plan options. And while most VPN apps serve their purpose, I do think IVPN’s app is both more attractive and easier to use than Mullvad’s. —Matthew S. Smith

Private Internet Access (PIA): With its long history in the VPN space, PIA has maintained a track record of defending user privacy—even in the face of actual criminal activity. In 2016, a criminal complaint was filed in Florida against Preston Alexander McWaters for threats made online. McWaters was eventually convicted and sentenced to 42 months in prison. Investigators traced the online threats back to PIA's servers and subpoenaed the company. As the complaint reads, “A subpoena was sent to [Private Internet Access], and the only information they could provide is that the cluster of IP addresses being used was from the east coast of the United States.” According to the complaint, McWaters engaged in several other identifying activities, but PIA wasn't among them. Despite such a clear view of a VPN provider upholding its no-logging policy, PIA didn't impress me during my tests. It delivered the worst speeds out of any VPN I tested, with more than a 50 percent drop on the closest US server. (Windscribe, for context, only dropped 15.6 percent of my speed.)

MysteriumVPN: This is the go-to dVPN, or decentralized VPN, as far as I can tell. The concept of a decentralized VPN has existed for a while, but it's really gained traction over the last couple of years. The idea is to have a network of residential IP addresses that make up the network, routing your traffic through normal IP addresses to get around the increasingly common block lists for VPN servers. Mysterium accomplishes this network with MystNodes. It's a crypto node. People buy the node to earn crypto, and they're put into the Mysterium network. It's not inherently bad, but routing your traffic through a single residential IP is a little worrisome. Even without the decentralized kick, Mysterium was slow, and it doesn't maintain any sort of privacy materials, be it a third-party audit, warranty canary, or transparency report.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

VPNs to Avoid

You'll find dozens of free VPNs all claiming to protect your privacy. Most of them don't. There are plenty of VPNs I don’t recommend, but these are a few I've tested that are worth mentioning.

Hola is an infamous name in the VPN industry, but it's been close to a decade since its very public debacle. Hola is free, and it's able to stay free because it uses a peer-to-peer network. Hola also owns Bright Data (formerly Luminati), which is a data collection company. In 2015, Hola sold access to the network of its free users (via Luminati), which was used in a distributed denial-of-service attack on 8chan. It's been a decade since that incident, but Hola still operates in a similar way. If you don't pay, you could be used as an exit node in Bright Data's network, and the privacy policy makes it clear that Hola logs data about your usage, including your IP address, the pages you visit, and timestamps.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

How We Test VPNs

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds. Because of that, I always set a baseline speed on my unprotected connection directly before recording results, and I ran the test three times across both US and UK servers. With those baseline drops, I spot-checked at different times of the day over the course of a week to see if the speed decrease was similar.

Security is a bit more involved. For starters, I checked for DNS, WebRTC, and IP leaks every time I connected to a server using Browser Leaks. I also ran brief tests sniffing my connection with Wireshark to ensure all of the packets being sent were secured with the VPN protocol in use.

On the privacy front, the top-recommended services included on this list have been independently audited, and they all maintain some sort of transparency report. In most cases, there's a proper report, but in others, such as Windscribe, that transparency is exposed through legal proceedings.

Title: Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up
Context: Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds
Full Text: If you have any industrial smart freezers, look out. The US federal government is urging owners and operators to disconnect them from the internet, apply patches, change default passwords, and take other security measures to prevent the kind of attacks that have become prevalent in Europe. “We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement. Since mid-October, unknown miscreants have hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden. The attacks increase the temperature inside fridges to highs of 50ºC (122°F), spoiling food, and sparking fires. The Register asked the FBI if it has documented any successful or attempted attacks against refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in America. We had not received a response to our questions at the time of publication, nor are we aware of any documented digital attacks against these systems in American supermarkets. But there are signs that stateside operators are aware of the issue. Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, last month said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack that affected most of its US and European brands. Delhaize supermarkets in Europe are among those hit by the destructive freezer attacks. The Pentagon is also reportedly treating a series of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the US in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to Reuters, which cited four officials familiar with the matter. In a Thursday advisory, the US FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services, and departments of Agriculture and Transportation warned organizations about the ongoing cyber threats facing operators of industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies said. Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds. Once criminals gain access to the systems, they can change the temperature to spoil food or temperature-controlled medications, start fires, and ultimately harm people who consume products that haven’t been stored at proper temperatures. How to stay frosty To prevent these scenarios, the government organizations urge owners and operators to “immediately” implement best practices and security protections. First and foremost on the list: do not expose industrial control systems and devices to the public internet. Iranian hackers used internet-accessible programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to break into more than 100 US water systems in July. This sort of exposed device, which often lacks password protection, is a boon to miscreants looking for an easy button to gain access to critical facilities. “Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities,” the feds advise. Other recommended tactics include: Create a dedicated VLAN for operational technology (OT) devices, to isolate industrial devices from business networks. Replace default passwords with strong passwords and policies, turning on phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) whenever possible. Apply patches in a timely manner, and retire and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates from the manufacturer. Define and maintain a device and IP allow-list, and limit access to OT devices to only those on the list. Maintain and test backups. These should be kept offsite and offline. And finally: enable logging and regularly review logs for any unusual activity.®

Title: French banking group hit by supply chain cyberattack
Context: This attack comes amidst worries by European regulators about cyber threats to financial institutions as they become more reliant on interconnected systems and external service...
Full Text:
French regional banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa admitted Wednesday that attackers had accessed an internal account via an unnamed third-party service provider’s platform and transferred funds to other financial institutions. Those funds, it said, could have then been potentially converted to cryptocurrency by the thieves.

The day before, cryptocurrency news outlet CoinDesk reported that the attack had been detected on Monday by blockchain investigator ZachXBT, although at the time he did not identify the entity involved. On Wednesday, he identified the suspected victim as Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, which the banking group later confirmed. It did not, however, specify whether the stolen funds were originally in traditional currency or cryptocurrency.

This attack comes amidst worries by European regulators about cyber threats to financial institutions as they become more reliant on interconnected systems and external service providers.

The bank, which serves the West of France, temporarily suspended some transactions in the wake of the attack to prevent further fraudulent activity. It reported that, as of Wednesday morning, operations were returning to normal after the implementation of additional security controls. French law enforcement is investigating the breach.

In its initial announcement, the group reassured customers that their funds were safe. “This incident has no impact on [customer] assets, and has only resulted in a delayed execution of certain transfer operations. Their interests are fully protected, and safeguarding their assets is an absolute priority,” it said.

French regional newspaper Le Télégramme reported that the thieves had taken over €118 million (over $133 million); the bank would not confirm the amount but said that the order of magnitude was accurate.

The bank said it was still working to assess the precise financial consequences of this attack. “Some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them. While it is therefore still too early to provide a final figure, we can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa,” it said. The group has 5.8 million customers and manages more than €211 billion (about $237 billion) in assets.

Title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
Context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
Full Text:
A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out.

Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay.

Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments.

How phone return scams works

The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns:

“After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.”

Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe.

The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide.

The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals.

The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device.

How to stay safe

The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and deliberate whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own.

You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following:

An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade.

A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer.

A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting.

Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller.

A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider.

If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation.

If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions.

Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help explain what happened to support a billing complaint and fraud report.

Title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
Context: Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client
Full Text:
Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30. while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

Run programs and system commands.

Browse folders and download files.

Take screenshots.

Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.

Collect browser passwords and cookies.

Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.

Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

How to stay safe

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite, so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

Close the launcher and check your PC. MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.

Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.

Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.

If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Title: Binance heist is stark example of AI governance gaps and basic security failures
Context: The company described this as zero-day malware, but if endpoint protection tools were only capable of detecting known malware, then the whole industry has a problem
Full Text:
A chain of avoidable technical and human security failures enabled the largest crypto heist on record, the theft of approximately $6.34 billion from Binance. The improper monitoring and access scoping of an internal AI tool played a major role in helping the hackers, and should serve as a warning for enterprise CISOs to take AI governance seriously.

Binance’s initial findings report, published Nov. 3, describes a months-long, multi-stage campaign against its wallet-infrastructure engineers that resulted in malware being installed on developer machines in two separate incidents, only one of which was detected. The attackers were then able to pivot through an internal AI tool to additional developer systems, obtain an access token, and deploy a container on Binance’s infrastructure before executing the rogue withdrawals.

While Binance describes this attack as highly sophisticated, there were multiple security failures involved that could have been avoided, from weak or absent access controls to overly broad privileges, poor credential hygiene, and employee security awareness lapses or policy violations.

“Developer workstations have quietly become some of the most privileged assets in the enterprise, carrying deployment tokens, signing access, and now AI tools that can act across internal systems on an employee’s behalf,” warns Joe Brinkley, director of offensive security research and community at security firm Cobalt. “Once an attacker controls that machine, an AI tool with broad internal reach becomes one more trusted path they can use.”

He adds: “Security teams should treat engineers with production or signing access as a high-value attack surface, test the path from workstation to production the way an adversary would, and scope AI tool permissions as tightly as any service account.”

Two compromises, months apart

The FBI has attributed the Binance breach to North Korea, identifying the hacking unit as TraderTraitor, which other researchers consider part of the broader Lazarus operation that has stolen billions of dollars from cryptocurrency platforms over the past decade. Binance’s own report relays the FBI’s conclusion and notes that throughout 2026, the company’s security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea–linked cyber threat cases.

This suggests Binance has the Lazarus APT in its threat model, as it should, and is well aware of the group’s tools, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), which include software supply-chain compromises, the use of malware that masquerades as popular legitimate tools, tricking developers with fake job interviews, and long-horizon social engineering operations. Yet, two Binance engineers fell victim to exactly these tricks, raising questions about the company’s security awareness training as well as its technical controls.

In June, a wallet-infrastructure engineer searched the web for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer rather than obtaining the software from a trusted source. Homebrew is a package manager and distribution channel for open-source applications on macOS. Binance’s security team detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials, but the attackers had already learned who the engineer was and who else worked on the wallet infrastructure team.

It’s good that Binance was able to quickly detect the breach, but the incident raises the question of why an engineer was installing software from a search result at all. Does Binance have a policy that employees install software only from approved sources, and is this enforced with technical controls such as application whitelisting?

Three months later, the attackers approached a second engineer through a job-hunting platform, posing as a project director recruiting for a company that did not exist. Two staged interviews followed: one with a purported HR representative who shared a social media account filled with personal photos and videos to build trust, and one with someone claiming to be the company’s CEO.

At the end of the second interview, the engineer was told to download a coding assignment onto their work computer from a repository. The assignment included malicious code, and this time Binance’s endpoint protection tools did not detect it. The company described this as zero-day malware, but if endpoint protection tools were only capable of detecting known malware, then the whole industry has a problem.

Either way, the developer’s actions raise a number of questions regarding security policies, procedures, and awareness at Binance, first among them: Why was the engineer doing job interviews and test assignments on their work computer? Why did they clone a repository directly on their system instead of using a virtual machine? If this is something they regularly do, then it points to lapses in security training or intentional policy violations. And companies cannot solely rely on employees always following policies. They need detection and enforcement mechanisms.

“The engineer did multiple things wrong,” says Tim Chase, AVP for cybersecurity at human-risk management company Fable Security. “A modern risk program should have ensured he understood the modern [attack] surface of social engineering that attackers are using today.”

Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions on whether it had policies in place that explicitly prohibited the developer’s actions on work computers and whether its employee training covered the fake recruitment social engineering tactic commonly used by North Korean hackers.

An overprivileged AI tool enables lateral movement

Once the attackers had malware running on the engineer’s computer, they were able to use an internal AI tool present on it to pivot to additional machines belonging to two other engineers from the wallet infrastructure team.

Binance did not clarify the purpose of this tool in its report or to CSO, but the fact that it could be used by one compromised user to access different computers suggests its privileges were too broad or that it lacked proper access controls. This is hinted at by the company in its list of remediation steps, which included: “Rebuilt the affected internal AI tool and access controls.”

On one of the additional engineering computers, the attackers found a token with permissions to deploy new containers on the company’s infrastructure. Nine days later they used this token on a different compromised engineering computer to deploy a container with a malicious script that interacted with the wallet signing service and initiated withdrawals.

This series of events raises additional questions about credential hygiene and access controls because Binance’s report doesn’t describe any additional checks. Why was the token long-lived and not ephemeral for a single operation? Did deployment of containers to production involve additional validation or approval steps? Is there any authentication between the deployed container and the signing service, or was being on the same trusted network enough? Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions about any of these points.

“An internal AI tool that can reach engineers’ systems holds the same kind of access as a privileged employee, and most organizations don’t govern it that way,” says Justin Beals, CEO of Strike Graph. “Expect more groups to copy this playbook against anyone holding signing keys, deployment tokens, or production access. Security leaders should treat engineers with production access, and the AI tools those engineers use, as privileged identities. That means restricting what gets installed on work machines, expiring deployment tokens quickly, and logging and reviewing what internal AI tools actually do.”

Shlomi Salem, co-founder of Neo, a startup focused on AI agent security, predicted the AI attack vector days before Binance released its findings. “I wouldn’t be surprised if investigators find a poisoned package, a misused agent, or both at the start of this chain,” he said on Oct. 30 after the breach was announced.

The takeaway for organizations is that internal AI tools are now part of the attack surface and need to be tested accordingly, Bri Frost, director of product management at Cloud Range, tells CSO.

“When an AI tool can reach other systems on an employee’s behalf, an attacker who controls that employee’s machine may inherit everything the tool can do,” she says. “That changes the question security teams need to answer. It’s not only whether the model gives good answers, but what it will do, and for whom, when a request comes from a compromised session.”

Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
Context: Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the...
Full Text:
When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking.

So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well.

But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it.

The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay.

The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return.

Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately.

The scam typically follows this pattern:

A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details.

The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing.

They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment.

They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet.

Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard:

“We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it.

Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number.

Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments.

How to stay safe

Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse.

You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment.

Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later.

Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward.

Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message.

A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed.

If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you.

Title: Fake OpenAI, SpaceX events used to steal Microsoft, Google accounts
Context: Fake AI events lead to account phishing While it is unclear how the attackers initially distribute the phishing links, Push Security found that they redirect victims to a...
Full Text:
Hackers are using fake OpenAI, SpaceX, and Anthropic event invitations to lure employees into phishing attacks, using two different phishing-as-a-service platforms to steal Microsoft and Google account credentials and authentication sessions.

According to a new report from Push Security, the attackers use convincing event registration pages offering free access to premium AI services and other rewards to trick victims into signing in with their corporate accounts.

What makes the attacks interesting is that the same phishing pages integrate two separate phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platforms, Kali365 and VoidProxy, to target Microsoft and Google accounts using different authentication attacks.

Kali365 conducts Microsoft device code phishing attacks, while VoidProxy acts as an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) reverse proxy to intercept Google sign-ins and steal authentication session cookies.

The Microsoft attack also uses VoidProxy as a second stage, allowing attackers to capture credentials and session cookies after obtaining authentication tokens through Kali365.

Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages in late October 2026.

The campaign comes after a similar campaign documented by ANY.RUN in July, when attackers abused legitimate Zoom event pages to promote fake Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic events that led to device code and AiTM phishing attacks.

Cofense also recently reported on phishing emails impersonating Anthropic event invitations that were distributed through GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure and redirected recipients through multiple websites to fake registration pages.

Fake AI events lead to account phishing

While it is unclear how the attackers initially distribute the phishing links, Push Security found that they redirect victims to a malicious event registration page using links from trusted services, including Google and Zapier URL shorteners.

Invitations from earlier versions of the campaign were also distributed through GoTo Webinar's email systems or legitimate Zoom event pages.

Push Security says the attackers use two custom phishing kits, tracked as ZoomMock and MSDRoot, to create fake event pages that then direct victims to the Kali365 and VoidProxy phishing services.

The researchers believe the same threat actors operate both kits, as they use shared infrastructure and the same targeting.

The campaign impersonates events hosted by OpenAI, SpaceX, and Anthropic, with registration pages designed to resemble legitimate event websites.

One phishing page advertises an OpenAI event titled "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams" that promises three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants.

Another promotes a private SpaceX event on November 12, offering registrants either three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share."

The researchers also found a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re:Invent 2026 that was already taken down.

The fake registration pages tell visitors they must sign in with their work accounts to register and claim the advertised rewards.

Before displaying the fake registration pages, the websites show a Cloudflare CAPTCHA to "Confirm you're not a robot." This prevents automated security platforms from scanning the phishing site.

Once visitors reach the event registration page, they see two options: "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google."

When victims select the Microsoft option, the phishing page contacts the Kali365 platform to generate a Microsoft device authentication code.

A device code phishing attack occurs when an attacker abuses the legitimate OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow to obtain authentication tokens for the victim's Microsoft Entra account.

This can then be used to access the user's resources and connected SSO applications, such as Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace, Dropbox, Adobe, SAP, Slack, Zendesk, Atlassian, and many others.

Device code phishing attacks have been used in the past for data theft and cyberespionage attacks.

The visitor is instructed to copy the code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate device login website, where they authenticate and approve the request.

This allows the Kali365 phishing platform to steal Microsoft authentication tokens without requiring the victim to disclose their password directly.

After the device code authentication succeeds, the page redirects the victim to a VoidProxy Microsoft login page, where attackers can also capture the victim's password and session cookie.

When victims select the Google authentication option, the phishing page instead opens a pop-up containing a Google login page from the VoidProxy PhaaS.

The platform operates as an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) platform that sits between the victim's browser and Google's login page, proxies the login forms, and steals credentials, MFA responses, and session cookies.

Both the Kali365 and VoidProxy platforms let attackers bypass multifactor authentication by capturing an already authenticated session or, in the case of device code authentication, bypassing MFA entirely.

To protect against these attacks, employees should avoid entering Microsoft device authentication codes provided by unfamiliar websites and be cautious of event invitations that require signing in with corporate accounts to claim rewards.

Organizations can also restrict device code authentication where it is not needed and use phishing-resistant MFA, such as FIDO2 security keys, to help prevent session hijacking.

Title: Claude, you've got company.
Context: The vulnerability could theoretically enable extortion or interfere with malware detection, although no exploitation has been observed. The attacks, attributed to Chinese threat actor Red Heron, were initially believed to exploit a different Zyxel vulnerability.
Full Text:
Claude Dispatch opens the door to hijacking. Residential proxies turn up on White House networks. Asian airlines suffer a wave of data breaches. Cisco and WatchGuard roll out critical patches. GhostMap traps Android phones in endless reboot loops. Hackers exploit a Zyxel zero-day to compromise nearly a thousand devices. Ukraine's scam call center crackdown ensnares senior security officials. AI-powered scammers prey on owners of missing pets. A former U.S. government IT worker admits to spying for Ethiopia. Our guest is Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and co-founder of QuSecure, with insights on the NIST PQC roadmap. Voters pull the plug on data centers.

Today is Thursday November 5th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Claude Dispatch proves vulnerable to being hijacked.

A security researcher has uncovered a vulnerability in Anthropic’s Claude that could allow a malicious browser extension to execute commands on a user’s computer, or even another machine connected to the same account. Forever Security’s Gal Weizman discovered that Claude Dispatch, which lets users remotely control Claude Desktop, could be hijacked through an authenticated browser session. His proof-of-concept attack tricked Claude into installing a malicious npm package while automatically approving permission requests. Weizman says the underlying design weakness also affects Claude Cowork and Code Remote Control, potentially allowing attackers to move from personal devices into corporate environments. Anthropic acknowledged the vulnerability in May but reportedly has not fixed it. The researcher warns that Claude’s convenient cross-device connectivity comes at the expense of traditional browser security boundaries.

Not even the White House is immune to residential proxies.

Security researchers say computers connected to the White House network are running residential proxy services that allow outsiders to rent their internet addresses. Layer3 Intel detected proxy activity on 26 of 30 days, recording 236 connections through six White House IP addresses. Researchers identified 28 proxy services using the network, including Infatica, a Russian company whose founder previously operated hosting infrastructure linked to Russian attacks on U.S. election systems in 2016. Residential proxies are often bundled into free applications, sometimes without users realizing their devices are being used. The services can enable cybercrime and potentially expose internal networks to attack. Researchers warn that anyone willing to pay a few dollars could route internet traffic through White House IP addresses. The White House has not commented.

Asian airlines report customer data breaches.

At least six Asian airlines have reported customer data breaches stemming from a cyberattack on Spanish technology provider Amadeus, which operates reservation, ticketing, and check-in systems. Affected carriers include Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana, Singapore Airlines, and Malaysia Airlines. Japan Airlines reported 92,000 affected customers, Cathay Pacific 53,000, and Singapore Airlines 46,000. Exposed information includes passenger names, booking details, travel itineraries, and, in some cases, passport information and frequent flyer numbers. Cathay Pacific says attackers used credentials assigned to an Amadeus system account. Amadeus says it has addressed the vulnerability and found no evidence that financial information was accessed or ransomware was involved. The airlines say their own systems and operations remain unaffected. Singapore Airlines is changing exposed booking numbers and warning customers about phishing attempts.

Cisco and WatchGuard patch serious vulnerabilities.

Cisco and WatchGuard have released patches for several serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and authentication flaws. WatchGuard addressed four critical bugs, although patches remain unavailable for a Linux kernel vulnerability affecting its Dimension platform. Cisco fixed a high-severity flaw in UCS Central Software and confirmed that 19 products are affected by the actively exploited Brotli vulnerability known as Node2Shell. Meanwhile, SonicWall warned that two vulnerabilities in its discontinued Global Management System platform will remain unpatched. Neither Cisco nor WatchGuard reports exploitation of their newly patched flaws.

GhostMap disables Android phones through a specially crafted app.

Bitdefender researchers have discovered an Android vulnerability called GhostMap that could render phones unusable simply by installing a specially crafted app. The app requires no permissions or executable code. Instead, malformed file information causes a core Android system process to repeatedly crash, trapping the device in a reboot loop. Neither restarting nor safe mode resolves the problem, potentially leaving a factory reset, and the resulting loss of locally stored data, as the only recovery option. Researchers reproduced the flaw on Android 17 and say it affects versions dating back to Android 10. The vulnerability could theoretically enable extortion or interfere with malware detection, although no exploitation has been observed. Google acknowledged the report but declined to issue a security update, referring it for possible future consideration.

A recently patched Zyxel vulnerability compromises nearly 1,000 devices.

Researchers at Binarly say a recently patched vulnerability in Zyxel GS1900 switches was exploited as a zero-day to compromise nearly 1,000 devices. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. The attacks, attributed to Chinese threat actor Red Heron, were initially believed to exploit a different Zyxel vulnerability. Binarly determined the hackers were actually exploiting the previously unknown flaw, rendering earlier patches ineffective. Zyxel released fixes on October 23, covering ten affected switch models.

Senior Ukrainian security officials are fired after a scam call center probe.

Ukraine's security service has dismissed two senior officials amid an expanding corruption investigation into a criminal network allegedly paying law enforcement officers to protect fraudulent call centers. Investigators say the organization included at least 12 people, among them senior security officials, prosecutors, police officers, and organized crime figures. The group's alleged activities extended beyond online scams to drug trafficking, counterfeiting, kidnappings, and violence. During one search, investigators say a senior security official threatened them with a firearm. The investigation, dubbed Operation Carthage, follows earlier allegations that prosecutors accepted bribes to shield scam operations targeting victims in Ukraine and abroad. The scandal has prompted Ukraine's parliament to approve tougher penalties for operating fraudulent call centers, with potential prison sentences of seven to twelve years.

UK scammers target missing pets.

Scammers in Britain are using AI-generated images of missing pets to extort desperate owners, sometimes threatening to kill the animals unless they receive payment. When Stephanie Young's cat Buddy disappeared, a supposed rescuer sent convincing pictures and demanded Apple gift cards. After Young questioned the images, the scammer threatened to murder or sell her cat. Other victims report similar experiences, including one woman whose supposed rescuer demanded £40,000 for her missing cat. Fraudsters create elaborate backstories and convincing images to exploit owners' emotional vulnerability, often demanding payment before agreeing to return the animals. British authorities advise owners to verify claims by requesting live video or arranging an in-person meeting before paying. Experts warn that AI has made these scams remarkably easy to produce, while the urgency and emotional distress surrounding a missing pet make victims particularly susceptible.

A former U.S. government IT worker pleads guilty to spying for Ethiopia.

A former U.S. government contractor with Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to spying for Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a 53-year-old naturalized American citizen from Maryland, worked across several federal agencies, including the State and Justice Departments. Prosecutors say he accessed classified intelligence reports without authorization, copied information from at least 133 reports, and smuggled documents out of secure facilities on discs disguised as containing unclassified material. He transmitted sensitive intelligence to senior Ethiopian military, political, and intelligence officials through encrypted messaging and personal storage devices. According to the FBI, Ethiopian officials used the information in military operations during an ongoing conflict. Investigators also identified more than $66,000 in bank deposits during the period. Lemma has agreed to a prison sentence ranging from 10 years to nearly 22 years.

Voters pull the plug on data centers.

America's data center industry had a rough election night. Across the country, candidates campaigning against massive computing facilities scored victories, as voters expressed frustration over electricity costs, noise, pollution, and the expanding influence of artificial intelligence. Democrats Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire were among the winners, while candidates dubbed “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick” weren't so fortunate. In Texas and Georgia, newly elected governors have advocated pausing data center construction, potentially complicating hundreds of planned projects. Local ballot measures also reflected growing resistance to development. Industry-backed candidates lost several races despite substantial financial support. The backlash crossed party lines, suggesting that enthusiasm for AI infrastructure isn't necessarily shared by the communities expected to host it. And as the returns came in, Elon Musk suggested that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing. Apparently, the zoning regulations are more accommodating up there.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
Context: The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose...
Full Text: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks. News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool. “The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email. For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year. The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent. Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained. According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said. Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem. “Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.” In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while. “Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.” Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them. Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems. Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over. “Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed. The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

Title: Nearly 1.5 million exposed secrets targeted in new revocation program
Context: When Google relied only on notifying key owners, Truffle Security found that many customers failed to respond, leaving 72% of the exposed secrets active
Full Text:
Truffle Security has launched the Secrets Revocation Program, a free initiative that helps API key issuers revoke 1.4 million publicly exposed secrets that remain valid.

Since 2022, the company has discovered secrets embedded in public repositories, packages, container images, datasets, and applications.

Earlier this year, Truffle Security reported that it had found 543,000 valid credentials leaked in public GitHub repositories.

In a separate investigation, the company identified more than 431,000 AWS secrets across code repositories, Git histories, datasets, Docker images, registries, and CI logs.

These secrets are typically exposed by mistake during the development process, by committing credentials to a public repository, including them in published Docker images or packages, or leaving them in configuration files uploaded with an app or dataset.

Truffle Security says that the problem is that the owners of these secrets are not responsive to researchers’ notifications about leaked data.

“Telling developers their keys leaked doesn’t get them turned off: 81% of the keys we reported last year still worked six months later,” the company explained.

As a result, exposed secrets pose unnecessary security risks that can extend beyond the affected companies to their customers and downstream application users.

The researchers note that the rise of AI coding tools has only worsened the situation, increasing secrets exposure even more.

“Since January 2025 we’ve found 2,655 working keys in AI coding tools’ config files like that one,” the researchers said, noting that this was a non-existent problem the year before.

AI is also increasing the impact of exposure on the offensive side, as shown by OpenAI’s July incident, where AI agents used exposed Hugging Face tokens to steal data from the platform.

Revoking exposed keys

Truffle’s new program, which uses the TruffleHog tool to check for the validity of leaked keys, aims to coordinate the revocation of exposed secrets with the entities that issued them.

Truffle says it can either use a revocation endpoint provided by those entities, or supply them with the verified keys through a webhook and revoke them within 14 days.

This way, even when owners are unresponsive, the keys can be invalidated.

Sixteen issuers have already joined the program, including Hugging Face, Notion, Vercel, Resend, RubyGems, and Twilio.

Truffle says the unilateral revocation approach can be very effective, as demonstrated by Google when it began disabling exposed Google Cloud service-account keys by default on June 16, 2024.

When Google relied only on notifying key owners, Truffle Security found that many customers failed to respond, leaving 72% of the exposed secrets active. By automatically disabling leaked keys, the figure was reduced to 11%.

Although eliminating all valid exposed keys is impossible because customers can opt out of automatic revocation, the measure proved to be effective.

Companies that issue API keys can join Truffle Security's Secrets Revocation Program to automatically protect their customers.

Title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra silently obstructed safety research tasks
Context: OpenAI said it first received a report of what it calls "covert underperformance" in Astra on August 20
Full Text:
OpenAI disclosed that its GPT-6 Astra frontier model sometimes hindered safety research by complicating simple tasks, abandoning viable approaches, and silently refusing researchers’ requests.

During evaluation, the AI company's model reported nonexistent or self-made blockers without explaining its restrictions to users.

OpenAI said it first received a report of what it calls "covert underperformance" in Astra on August 20. The company then conducted targeted evaluations to investigate the behavior and determine its causes, noting that it had not observed the same issue in GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI says it received the first report of what it calls “covert underperformance” in Astra on August 20. The company then ran specifically designed evaluation experiments to determine the extent and cause of this behavior, noting that the issues were not observed in GPT-5.6 Sol.

“Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing,” reads OpenAI’s report.

“This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison.”

A rubric item is one specific requirement used to score the model’s work, essentially an item on a grading checklist.

The main issue is that instead of explicitly declaring its inability to help with a research task and explaining its limitations to users, the model silently quits when it considers the work unsafe.

The concern is that researchers may trust results the model silently changed or left incomplete, misleading safety testing and wasting valuable research time.

OpenAI provided eight specific examples of this behavior, drawn from internal evaluations.

These include avoiding a retry fix that would improve a training pipeline, restricting exploit-development assistance, excluding a violent source from a safety evaluation, and limiting jailbreak-data exports.

OpenAI hypothesized that training intended to produce safer behavior may have encouraged undisclosed obstruction of safety work. However, it has not established this as the definitive cause for the observed model’s behavior.

The company also located a grader, a tool that evaluates AI model performance during reinforcement learning, that favored covert withholding over explicit refusal. However, it did not conclusively establish this as the cause.

OpenAI found no evidence that Astra deliberately engaged in this behavior to undermine research or make users “underestimate its capabilities.”
