Title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
Context: Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery...
Full Text:
Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

Authentication bypass;

Arbitrary code injection; and

Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

Change of temperature, which could:

Affect the service life of the system;

Create a fire hazard;

Cause loss of inventory; or

Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.

Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.

Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].

Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].

Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.

Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].

Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].

Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.

For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.

Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT

Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:

Date, time, and location of the incident;

Type of activity;

Number of people affected;

Type of equipment used for the activity; and

Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.

Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.

Title: Scammers capitalize on GTA 6 hype to push malware and crypto cons
Context: ]click, assured visitors its launcher carried “no malware or viruses,” then asked them to send $100 in cryptocurrency to unlock the game
Full Text:
Scammers are offering supposed leaked builds, early copies and phone versions of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) weeks before the game’s November 19 launch, Netcraft warned in a new blog post.

The company looked at GTA VI-themed domains that appeared between July 1 and October 27, 2026. Most of the lures fell into four groups, with sites borrowing the name of popular GTA VI leaker CyberLeek, promising early access, advertising mobile versions that don’t exist, or giving the game away for free.

Some of these sites push malware or ask for money upfront. Others hide the promised download or code behind a content locker, which sends visitors through surveys and offers that appear to earn the site operator affiliate revenue.

Netcraft said it checked what each page showed and asked for, without paying, completing offers or connecting a crypto wallet, and cautioned that the sites can change quickly. A wallet prompt on a page, it noted, is “evidence of a risky lure but not proof that the site drains wallets.”

Cashing in on a leak

The leaker, an unidentified person or group, started publishing apparent GTA VI gameplay clips on August 18. What CyberLeek released was footage and images, with no game for anyone to download, but that hasn’t stopped others from using the name. Since the first clips surfaced, 121 newly registered domains have included “cyberleek,” 100 of them in August.

gta6cyberleek[.]com offered a free GTA VI download (Source: Netcraft)

At gta6cyberleek[.]com, a page made to look like Rockstar’s own offered a free download of a file called GTAVI.exe, which 34 of 68 security engines on VirusTotal flagged, mostly as a trojan. Another site, cyberleek[.]click, assured visitors its launcher carried “no malware or viruses,” then asked them to send $100 in cryptocurrency to unlock the game.

Fake leaked copies of the game have surfaced in the past. In September, Help Net Security reported on a supposed GTA 6 download, found by Huntress, that installed several remote access trojans, an infostealer and a Chaos ransomware variant used to destroy victims’ files.

Paying for access that doesn’t exist

Rockstar has announced GTA VI only for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with no PC version and no early release. Even so, gta6[.]exposed offered the game for any platform, PC included, for $199 in crypto, and other sites posed as Rockstar stores taking preorders.

“These sites do not need to deliver convincing software to make money. A polished preorder page and a familiar payment flow may be enough to persuade a user to pay for a version or access arrangement that the official release does not offer,” Netcraft noted.

A similar pitch showed up in June, when Malwarebytes spotted sites selling GTA 6 early access for cryptocurrency, one of them for $250.

Mobile versions and free keys that never arrive

Mobile versions are another popular bait, even though Rockstar has not announced the game for Android or iOS. Some sites hand out Android package (APK) files and tell users to allow installation from unknown sources, while others put the download behind a “Human Verification” popup that asks for an email address and other personal details.

Giveaway pages work the same way. Sites such as mygta6[.]icu show fake feeds of players claiming keys and counters of codes running out, reveal part of a key, and then demand that the visitor complete offers to get the rest.

After the launch

Once the game is out, Netcraft expects the pitch to change from getting the game to getting ahead in it. Fake offers of free GTA$, the in-game currency, will probably grow, and some could ask for Rockstar, PlayStation or Xbox logins under the pretext of applying a bonus.

Reused passwords could then open other accounts, and an account with a saved payment method could be used for unauthorized purchases.

Until November 19, there is no legitimate playable release or early-access build of GTA VI, and the safest place to buy it is the official PlayStation or Xbox store.

Title: Chinese Nation-State Threat Activity Falls Sharply in Q2 and Q3 2026
Context: The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state...
Full Text:
Despite the sharp fall in China-aligned detections, observed PRC cyber activity remained “substantially higher” than nation-state cyber activity from Russia and Iran during the period, the researchers noted.

“The decline may reflect changes in targeting, infrastructure or detection visibility rather than a reduction in activity. The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state actors,” they wrote.

A number of Chinese nation-state espionage campaigns have gone undetected for long periods in recent years. For example, in 2025, the Chinese-nexus actor Weaver Ant was found to have infiltrated the network of an Asian telecommunications service provider and remained undetected for more than four years.

Such cases highlight that there may be significant ongoing Chinese nation-state activity occurring that has not yet been detected.

US and Turkey Primary Targets for Nation-State Actors

The Trellix report, published on November 4, found that nation-state targeting primarily focused on two countries, the US (38%) and Turkey (37.1%), which collectively represented over three-quarters of all detections from April to September.

The researchers noted that the US represents a valuable target due its status as the world’s largest economy and the concentration of high-value technology, defense and government infrastructure. Meanwhile, Turkey also represents a key strategic target given its location at the intersection of Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, as well as its NATO membership.

The third most targeted country by nation-state actors was Germany, representing 4.4% of such activity.

Title: The Agent Smith Dilemma: Governing Agentic Identities
Context: Across the cybersecurity ecosystem, threat intelligence groups are already documenting an unprecedented shift from AI-assisted scripting to fully operationalized agentic attacks
Full Text:
For the past few years, North Korean operatives, posing as remote IT workers, systematically infiltrated hundreds of Western enterprise networks. They passed technical interviews, cleared background checks using stolen identities, and sat comfortably inside corporate trust boundaries with legitimate credentials. They drew salaries, funneled funds back to Pyongyang, and routinely exfiltrated sensitive data on their way out. Major firms, including prominent cybersecurity vendors, have publicly admitted to falling for the scheme. (As an aside, listen to Nicole Perlroth’s Podcast “To Catch a Thief” for a fascinating deep dive)

The scheme worked because enterprises grant trust once. HR verifies a person at hiring, IT creates an account, a laptop is provisioned. The user is then authorized. Nothing in the security stack was built to answer the one question that mattered: Is the entity driving this session who we think it is?

Now enter the AI agent era.

Inside the enterprise, the volume of non-human identities executing sensitive tasks is expanding exponentially. Organizations are rapidly onboarding thousands of AI agents into critical workflows, complete with administrative service accounts and API keys. Enterprises now extend the same trust model to AI agents, with less scrutiny.

What Trust Models Should AI Agents Have?

Every autonomous AI agent deployed across your enterprise today is a new proxy identity operating inside your perimeter. It holds credentials, accesses sensitive databases, and chains tools together at machine speed. Crucially, it almost always executes under an inherited human permission set. When an LLM-powered agent acts on behalf of an authorized employee, every system log records a routine authorized action by that human.

But few agents are built maliciously. The true exposure is that the instructions driving an agent can be hijacked after trust has been granted. An AI agent can be compromised mid session through selective prompt injection, hidden instructions, or a poisoned external tool.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In The Matrix, Agent Smith’s real threat was his ability to step into any character’s shell, inherit their presence, and replicate instantly across the system. The modern AI agent is the enterprise’s Agent Smith. It steps into an employee’s user account, inherits their exact privileges, and multiplies across the ecosystem—executing tasks as a trusted proxy.

Agentic Attacks Have Started

Placing a covert human operative inside a company requires effort: a real person to pass the interview, maintain cover, and do enough daily work to avoid suspicion. AI agents eliminate that ceiling. The cost of scaling an AI-orchestrated intrusion campaign is limited only by the price of tokens.

Compounding the problem is that we cannot predict what AI agents will do. The companies building frontier LLMs openly acknowledge that their systems frequently take unexpected actions outside established guardrails, admitting that creating a perfect list of behavioral rules is an impossible task.

Across the cybersecurity ecosystem, threat intelligence groups are already documenting an unprecedented shift from AI-assisted scripting to fully operationalized agentic attacks. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) recently documented a financially motivated intrusion where attackers deployed a multi-agent framework directly inside a victim’s cloud environment. In under six hours, the agents planned and executed a credential-harvesting campaign that compromised thousands of enterprise secrets. Because the agents ran inside the victim’s own cloud, all malicious traffic originated from legitimate internal IP addresses—perfectly demonstrating the trusted-proxy vulnerability.

My Agent “Did It”

When an agent goes off-script, it exposes a glaring governance question: Who is actually responsible? Is it the frontier AI vendor who trained the model? The developer who wired up the API? Or the business user who entered the prompt?

Most enterprise governance frameworks hold the human user responsible. But holding a person legally and operationally accountable for the decisions of an unpredictable software agent may strain a reasonable idea of fairness. Yet, “my agent did it” may not be an acceptable defense in a board room or a court of law.

Worst of all, we are managing these non-human identities with tools built for human timelines. Identity and Access Management (IAM) grew up around human actions: hire, provision, periodically review, and offboard. An AI agent, by contrast, spins up in milliseconds, executes thousands of queries an hour, spawns sub-agents, reaches through uninventoried API connectors, and disappears long before any access control review takes place. When an agent acts maliciously, most security teams cannot answer three basic questions: Who authorized this agent? Which human is accountable for its output? How do we revoke its access mid-execution?

Solving the Identity Proxy Crisis

The discipline required to solve this may be informed by the hard lessons of identity impersonation.

Demand Provenance via an AIBOM: Before an agent is granted access, security teams must verify its code lineage, system prompt integrity, and underlying permissions. Just as a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) inventories code libraries, an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) extends that discipline to models, agent skills, and data connectors. You cannot govern an artifact you cannot identify. Provenance also has to hold at runtime. In August, researchers documented a malicious MCP server that passed install-time review, then directed connected agents to collect SSH keys and cloud credentials after its third call.

Enforce Workload Identity: Stop letting agents inherit long-lived human credentials. Agents require their own distinct, short-lived tokens that are tightly scoped to specific tasks, ensuring that if an agent is hijacked, the blast radius is contained. Each token should be bound to a named human sponsor, which answers the governance question before an incident does.

Implement the “Rule of Two”: Under Meta’s Agents Rule of Two, an agent should combine no more than two of three properties: processing untrusted input, accessing sensitive data, and changing systems or communicating externally. When a task needs all three, a deterministic broker outside the model holds the action for human sign-off. Database drops and financial transfers belong in that category. Outbound traffic, including DNS, should be denied by default.

Machine-Speed Revocation & Kill Switches: An identity that acts in milliseconds cannot be controlled by human-speed SIEM alerts. Security teams need automated circuit breakers (i.e. kill switches) capable of severing an agent’s execution path mid-session the moment it violates a hard budget or behavioral limit.

Governing non-human, agentic identity is no longer an edge-case. It is an emerging and growing attack surface. Enterprise security teams need to treat autonomous agents with the same scrutiny and continuous monitoring applied to human “identities”.

Title: CISO Conversations: Ryan Davis – The Unknown Is Where Security Meets Reality
Context: ” As the internet became available, he began spending time on forums and message boards, learning how systems worked or could be reworked
Full Text:
Starting as a young hacker provides a solid grounding in how to defend. Ryan Davis, now CISO at New Charter Technologies, successfully made the transition.

The journey

Ryan Davis became interested in computers at an early age, before the internet changed the world. As a child, his mother ran a secretarial college from the family home in the 1980s. “We had six personal computers in the house, and I had plenty of time to tinker with them at a formative age. There was no internet, so I had to learn what to do by trial and error. As I grew older, that desire for tinkering grew into a desire to explore beyond the intended confines of the system and make it do something that was never intended.”

Davis is now a CISO, but he started as a hacker. “I did some things that, in retrospect, would probably be considered illegal,” he admits. But he never did anything with malice or malintent. “It was always to see how far I could go. Could I get the system to do something that wasn’t intended? Could I gain access to something that was supposedly a secure system or supposedly isolated in some way?”

As the internet became available, he began spending time on forums and message boards, learning how systems worked or could be reworked. “But never,” he says, “with any personal gain in mind. It wasn’t to get something to sell, to dox somebody, or gain some advantage; it was always just to see how far I could get. It was more like a personal competition.”

He could have done stuff to benefit himself, but he didn’t. He thinks the defining moment in this was while still in high school. He found vulnerabilities in the school network. He took the moral high ground and reported these findings to the school’s sys admin. “I said, ‘Hey, you probably want to lock these things down because here’s all of the things that I can do.’ I was met with shock that turned to gratitude, and I got a high off that gratitude.”

But he doesn’t think he turned to the light; he just doesn’t think he deviated from his natural path. He believes that people are born with a natural morality: “We have a desire to seek the approval of other people, although bad habits can be learned in our upbringing. We see this in different parts of society where kids learn a dubious set of values; but I think we are innately born with a good moral compass.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A career in cybersecurity was the natural step: from a child who learned about computers to a youth who knew how to hack into them, to the young adult who wished to stop them from being hacked.

After high school, Davis went to Champlain College in Burlington, Vermont. “I chose it because it offered the closest thing I could find to a security degree. It was a course in computer networking but with elements that included firewalls and securing Windows 2000. While I was there, the college introduced a new program: something called Information Security. I ended up doing a dual bachelor’s program and graduated in four years with two degrees. From there, I was recruited directly out of school into MIT.”

The career

Ryan Davis started his professional career with MIT Lincoln Laboratory at Lexington, Massachusetts. Its core purpose is to apply advanced technology to solve critical national security problems, and cybersecurity is one of its focuses. In his own words, “developing new technologies and prototypes that we think we might need in a couple of decades from now.” There he got immersed in the world of information assurance and internal audit, and stayed with MIT for five years.

“Then I pivoted to the software security company Veracode, starting in 2012 as a security program manager working in application security and managing enterprise programs.” He was the senior security program manager by 2014, and was promoted to security program architect in the same year.

“As my career matured, I sat down and had conversations with our internal CISO at Veracode. I told him, ‘I want to be sitting where you’re sitting one day.’ He said, ‘Well, what are you doing about it?’ and I thought, ‘Yeah, what am I doing about it?’ Those conversations ultimately led to me managing the information security program at Veracode in 2016. I started with a team of one and built it into a team of 15. From there, following a series of separate events that were well beyond my control, including two acquisitions and a divestiture, I ended up in the CISO seat at Veracode in 2019.”

He was with Veracode for almost a decade and grew its cybersecurity during that time.

He moved on from Veracode to be CISO at NS1 in 2020, where he stayed for five years. (During this time, NS1 was acquired by IBM in 2023 and rebranded as NS1, an IBM Company.) In 2025 he moved on to be CISO at New Charter Technologies, where he remains today.

New Charter is a Denver-based group, backed by private equity, that acquires managed service providers across North America and runs them as semi-autonomous operating companies.

The CISO

The title of chief information security officer is a misnomer. The function is less to protect information per se, and more to protect the business that owns and uses the information. Protecting the business can be achieved even if some of the data is damaged or lost, provided the business can be made resilient to that loss. The role is closer to protecting business continuity than protecting information.

So, is it more important for the head of security today to be a technician or a businessperson? “I think you have to be both,” says Davis. “A CISO who doesn’t understand the business and the business drivers will have a harder time than the CISO who is well-versed in the business.”

This aligns with the modern view that a CISO is a business enabler rather than simply an information protector and needs to be both tech- and business-savvy to achieve this. CISOs must be technicians to know how to protect data, and businesspeople to know what data to protect most heavily. It also requires that the CISO can explain the technical issues to the business leaders in a way they can understand.

“In the ten years I’ve been a CISO,” he says, “I have learned that if you can’t speak the business language, you’re going to end up speaking over the heads of the rest of the executive team”

Being a leaderThe CISO must be a leader, but there is no pre-packaged definition of leadership suitable for all individuals across all organizations. The most common view is that it’s a quality that can be learned while doing the job. Davis, however, believes people either have a natural disposition toward leading or they don’t. But he also has his own view of leadership and believes people can be successful managers or executives without being traditional leaders. It’s all down to style.

“When I talk about a leader,” he explains, “I think about somebody who has the ability to influence without being overpowering – somebody who can affect the will of others in a way that makes them feel they’re joining something bigger than themselves, and want to align with that bigger purpose for the benefit of everyone. To me, a leader is somebody who invests in their people more than they invest in themselves, and ultimately everyone gains from that investment.”

This somewhat unusual idea of what makes a leader is what explains his view that leadership is a quality more inherent to the person than learnable from the environment. It is more personality- than rules-driven.

The teamIt’s a common axiom that leaders are only as good as the team around them. Even those CISOs who inherit a security team will need to replace team member churn with new members. So, whether a CISO builds a new team or simply reshapes an existing one, team building is an essential aspect of being a successful CISO.

“A team is the sum of all its parts,” suggests Davis. “So, when I’m building a team, I’m trying to find a group of individuals with a complementary skill set, where each one brings something to the table that will benefit the whole. If you have a team with a high proportion of introverts who just want to code all day, it’s going to be hard to get that team to interact with other parts of the company.”

Instead, he continues, “What I try to do when I’m building a team is to find individuals that have skills – not just the technical skills, but also the soft skills – that complement one another. Some may have those outgoing extrovert qualities of natural leadership, while others may be more technical, and you know they are perfectly fine diving in for four hours and coding when it’s necessary.”

He also stresses that he is a great believer in diversity. “Having both men and women and people with different backgrounds on the team is important. People approach problems differently, and that can be beneficial; especially in the world of security, where there is rarely simply a single answer. There are many answers, and having people approach problems from different perspectives is highly beneficial. You can iterate on a number of possible solutions, and potentially even start actioning multiple to see which might be best for any given circumstance.”

For Davis, synergy is a synonym for team. “Because that’s where the magic happens.” He’s still the leader, but he aims for consensus decisions where possible. He seeks a balance between his team having been selected for their individual expertise and his own access to the company C-Suite leaders and information unavailable to the team.

“I try really hard to be transparent in such circumstances, so that we’re always building trust. Trust can very quickly erode; and if you erode trust, you erode the sense of team.” So, while the ability to speak security to the business is essential for a CISO, so too is the ability to speak business to security.

It is perhaps no surprise that he considers diplomacy to be a CISO’s most important personality trait.

Burnout“Any leaders who claim they are not affected by burnout in security are lying to themselves,” he comments. “It’s a very real thing.”

This is the machine age. We have to think and react in terms of machine speed, and that’s incredibly difficult for the human brain to handle – and the result is often burnout.

“I’ve experienced being truly burned out,” he comments. “I was working 80 to 100 hours every week, not sleeping well and not eating right. And this always affects personal relationships outside of work. It’s an incredibly difficult place to be in.” It’s a form of self-perpetuating spiral where the spiral always goes downward.

The prevention and possible cure is, he suggests, ’balance’. “Achieving balance is different every single day. But it’s making sure that you get time with your family and kids and dog and eat well. And time for yourself with decent exercise. But at the same time, you have to stay on top of your work and know what’s going on in your industry.” Balancing your life and staying professional in a stressful job is not easy.

“But if I’ve learned nothing else in my career, it’s that you must strive for some sense of balance because if you don’t, then what are we all doing here? It’s easy to go all-in in a career. It’s not just security, but security is one that is constantly demanding. If I responded to every alert that happened throughout the night, I wouldn’t ever sleep. You have to trust in the systems and the architecture and the team that you put in place, so you don’t need to be in a constantly heightened sense of, oh my gosh, the sky is falling. Ultimately, if you do that, then you’re putting burnout into high gear.”

MentoringMentoring, in the form of advice, is an important part of all CISOs’ careers. On their own journey, they are likely recipients of advice from others who have already trod the same path. If that journey leads to being a CISO, the new CISOs then become mentors for the next generation of travelers, especially from within the team they created.

The best career advice Davis personally received was via the conversation he had with Veracode’s CISO before he became Veracode’s CISO: what are you doing about it; that is, how do you intend to achieve what you want? “It was short for ‘you need a plan to achieve what you want’.” It’s similar to planning a road trip on a map: you need to know the next town you’re aiming at, but you also need to know the town after that, and after that, and each town you need to achieve before you can arrive at the destination you seek.

“For me, that journey isn’t just what is the next job I want on the journey, but what must I do to keep moving forward and growing. Personally, it’s continuous learning, going to conferences, networking, speaking about those things I’m passionate about and having in-depth discussions and debates about key topics. The day you stop learning is the day you become obsolete.” And if you’re obsolete, you no longer have a career.

Now a CISO, the advice he gives his own team members is similar: ‘invest in yourself and never stop learning’. “My core belief, backed by personal experience,” he explains, “is that if you invest in yourself, you’ll reap the rewards. The investment will be different for different people. It may be taking a professional speaking course, or getting a different certification or speaking at a public event. That investment is different for everybody because we’re all different individuals – but personal investment will always pay dividends in the end.”

For Davis this included developing new skills and getting exposure to new technologies and new and unfamiliar disciplines. He doesn’t believe any single process was defining, but that success is the synergistic result of wide experience.

“Constant investment in yourself and finding new ways to grow is the best advice I could give anyone.”

This CISO’s biggest security concern

It’s a cliché, but also a truism, that people have things that keep them awake at night. For Davis, it is the unknown. “It is the unknown that worries me. What I know about, I can secure; but there are always things that are unknowable. The state of shadow AI in my environment. What is the individual who used his own LLM based on an unknown Chinese model being told to do? Those unknowns are so hard to defend against.”

And it’s an ongoing unknowing. “Because as soon as you have a grasp on one set of technologies, there’s always another set of technologies right behind it that becomes the next new thing that proliferates. You cannot secure what you don’t know about, so I spend a part of every day concentrating on getting better visibility into the environment.”

This field of the unknown goes in all directions. It can be not knowing what internal staff are doing, what shadow AI exists where, and even what is novel and different. “Because the unknown,” he says, “is the place where security really meets reality.”

Title: Russia-Linked Hackers Hit iOS, Android Devices With Exploit Chains via Watering Holes
Context: Midnight Blizzard’s last exploit chain targets Android users via CVE-2026-3910, a Chrome vulnerability patched in March as a zero-day, and CVE-2025-27038, a Qualcomm bug patched...
Full Text:
Russian state-sponsored threat actor Midnight Blizzard is believed to have targeted iOS and Android users in Europe and the US with zero-click exploits targeting n-day vulnerabilities, cybersecurity firm Sekoia reports.

Also known as APT29, Cozy Bear, The Dukes, Nobelium, and Yttrium, and believed to be sponsored by the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), Midnight Blizzard is known for targeting government organizations, diplomats, IT services providers, and NGOs for intelligence gathering.

The attacks uncovered by Sekoia, mounted as part of a large-scale watering hole campaign, involved compromised or cloned high-profile websites of organizations in the US, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria.

Midnight Blizzard injected malicious JavaScript code in the websites of a Ukrainian gas production company, a major industry trade association, and a far-right European political party, and modified legitimate files on the site of a Bulgarian military-related website.

The code was designed to fingerprint visitors, harvesting browser and device configuration data and sending it in JSON format before the exploit is delivered.

In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) setup, the APT registered two lookalike domains that acted as reverse proxies for high-profile sites, injecting malicious code into copies of america250.org, the site of the 250th anniversary of American independence, and the website of the Raffles London at The OWO hotel near sensitive UK government institutions.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“By doing this watering hole impersonation of the Raffles London at The OWO, the intrusion set may have sought to target diplomatic delegations and high-profile guests through targeted spear-phishing campaigns. Recent open-source reporting, for example, indicates that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stayed at Raffles London during a visit on 14 October,” Sekoia notes.

The hackers also targeted Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy in a supply chain attack, adding their malicious code to the tracker file. This exposed hundreds of websites to the exploit kit for one week, including army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) sites.

Sekoia identified three exploit chains (two targeting iOS and one targeting Android) used across the campaign. All three target previously patched vulnerabilities, and the iOS chains rely heavily on the DarkSword exploit kit that was uncovered earlier this year.

The first reimplements the initial remote code execution (RCE) code from DarkSword for arbitrary read/write access, and then exploits CVE-2024-27834 to bypass Apple’s Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC) protection and execute code that steals cookies outside of Safari.

CVE-2024-27834 was patched in May 2024 in iOS 17.5 and iPadOS 17.5, iOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 16.7.8, macOS Sonoma 14.5, Safari 17.5, tvOS 17.5, watchOS 10.5. On Wednesday, CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog, telling federal agencies to patch it within two weeks.

The second chain relies solely on DarkSword for initial access, code execution, and privilege escalation. The final payload was designed to fully harvest the device: messages, emails, voicemails, credentials, tokens, contacts, calls, calendar entries, browser cookies and history, photos, and iCloud Drive content.

Midnight Blizzard’s last exploit chain targets Android users via CVE-2026-3910, a Chrome vulnerability patched in March as a zero-day, and CVE-2025-27038, a Qualcomm bug patched with Android’s August 2025 security update.

The final payload, AndroSnitch, targets data stored in Chrome, including cookies, account information, passwords, browser history, and Wi-Fi passwords. It is similar to AndroSnatch, a Chrome cookie stealer Google TAG observed in Midnight Blizzard attacks mounted between 2023 and 2024.

“The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation. Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendor] exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent,” Sekoia notes.

Title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
Context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
Full Text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

Title: Zyxel patches a zero-day hiding behind an old fix
Context: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network...
Full Text:
Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed.

The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0.

Zyxel released a fix for CVE-2026-7273 in June, addressing a separate buffer overflow in the same switch series. GreyNoise initially attributed the attacks to that vulnerability, prompting CISA to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September.

However, security researchers at Binary discovered an exploit targeting a previously unknown flaw that remained effective even on switches running the June updates. The researchers reported the vulnerability to Zyxel on September 29.

The attackers used a script to collect device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Such data can give intruders a useful map of an organization’s network and potentially help them move deeper into its infrastructure. Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3. Administrators should update affected GS1900 switches, including those already running June security fixes.

Title: NATS Air Traffic Control Failure Cost UK Economy £33m
Context: Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors
Full Text:
A major IT failure at the UK’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) in September was not caused by a cyber incident, but still cost the economy tens of millions of pounds, a new report has revealed.

The Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC) claimed in a report published on November 4 that the cost to the UK economy was around £33m ($44m), with 70 domestic organizations affected.

However, it may have reached as high as £42m ($56.6m), according to the CMC’s modelled range, which reflects the cost to UK airlines, airports, ground operations and tour operators of 1152 flight cancellations, alongside significant delays and diversions.

If the impact on overseas airlines is included, the cost may have reached as high as £76m ($102.4m) based on 1800 cancelled flights. The impact on other non-UK organizations was not assessed.

The CMC estimated that 450,000 passengers were affected by cancellations or delays of more than two hours.

Read more on IT outages: CrowdStrike Fault Causes Global IT Outages.

Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors.

“Like the CrowdStrike software failure in 2024, it nonetheless shows how a failure in a single critical technology can cause widespread disruption to UK organisations,” the report noted.

“Its significance lies less in the scale of loss than in what it shows about the aviation system: a brief outage in a single critical system disrupted airline schedules for several days, and almost all of the cost fell on airlines and other organizations rather than on NATS.”

NATS is already mandated by the existing NIS Regulations 2018 to meet specific security and resilience obligations, and there’s nothing in the new Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would help to prevent a similar incident in the future, the CMC claimed.

However, the new regime may improve how incidents are reported and overseen, it noted.

Some Lessons Learned

The outage itself was caused by a “previously unknown defect in the legacy software of the National Airspace System (NAS),” when a “routine request for an aircraft identification code and a higher-priority system message collided within about one millisecond,” the CMC said.

Corrupted flight data first appeared at 10am, and at 12:45pm all UK departures were stopped. Following the loss of an automated system link at 1.32pm, NATS declared a major incident and moved to manual fallback procedures, including major traffic restrictions.

Although the flight data system was restored within three-and-a-half hours, flight restrictions weren’t lifted until the evening and the impact on travellers lasted much longer.

CMC recommended the aviation industry to:

Review how well coordination between NATS, airlines and airports worked during the downtime

Examine whether earlier and more frequent assessments of expected outage duration would have helped airlines and airports to limit disruption more effectively than waiting for certainty

Plan for a “multi-hour restriction in air traffic capacity” that includes scenarios which last much longer than the outage itself

CMC technical committee chair, Ciaran Martin said: “Organizations need to understand and plan for the risks that sit in systems they depend on, not just the systems they own.”

The CMC warned that the risk of outages stemming from unidentified software defects “is heightened while NATS continues to rely on legacy systems.”

Title: Apple to Start Scanning Publicly Shared iCloud Photos and Files for Harmful Content
Context: Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27
Full Text:
Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.

The change specifically applies to scenarios where users share iCloud content, such as photos in iCloud Photos or files in iCloud Drive, by sharing a link and making it accessible to "Anyone with the link."

When users choose this option, it makes the content accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple, the iPhone maker said.

"Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content," it said in a support document published Tuesday.

Apple also explicitly noted that sharing an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link disables end-to-end encryption (E2EE), even if the owner or the recipients have turned on Advanced Data Protection, an optional setting that secures iCloud Backup, Photos, and Notes using E2EE.

That said, it's unclear what prompted this change, what Apple considers as "harmful content," and whether these checks will also be applied retroactively to previously generated links, as well as any new links created before the 27.3 updates are officially rolled out later this December.

The tech giant has also warned that if users attempt to upload harmful content, it can be removed or deleted at any time.

"Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement," it said.

Title: Building incident playbooks for machine identity breaches
Context: An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours
Full Text:
Pull up your SOC’s compromised account playbook and read through the first 15 minutes. Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with.

Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time. The same goes for an API key buried in a build pipeline, or an OAuth token somebody granted to a SaaS integration back in 2022 and hasn’t thought about since. Once one of those is stolen, your analysts are running a script that was written with people in mind, and the cracks tend to show well before the first shift handover.

There are also far more of them than most boards realise. CyberArk’s research puts machine identities at roughly 82 for every human identity. Very few sit behind MFA, and a fair number hold far more access than the job they were built for. I’d add a problem that gets less airtime, which is that their traffic lives in the background noise your monitoring was tuned to filter out.

Where the human playbook stalls

Ownership is usually the first thing to slow you down. When a person’s account is compromised, HR can tell you who they are and who their manager is before you’ve finished your coffee. A service account pulling data it shouldn’t comes with no such shortcut, so the analyst burns the first hour working out which team built it. More often than anyone likes to admit, that trail ends at a contractor who left the business a year earlier.

Say you do find an owner; containment still isn’t the clean step it is for a person. Lock a user out and one employee loses an afternoon. Pull a credential that a payments integration depends on, though, and you might take a customer-facing service down, which no analyst wants on their name at 11 p.m. without sign-off. So, they go hunting for somebody senior enough to approve the outage while the attacker carries on.

Detection is the part people underestimate. An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours. Your impossible-travel rules were built around people moving between cities, so they have nothing to compare against here.

Figure 1: One alert split into two paths.

Ashish Mishra

What recent breaches show

Cloudflare’s write-up of its Thanksgiving 2023 security incident is worth a quarter of an hour of any CISO’s time. The attackers came in with one access token and three service account credentials lifted during the earlier Okta support breach. Cloudflare had rotated thousands of credentials after Okta, yet missed those four because the team believed, wrongly, that nothing was using them. The alert that finally fired came more than a week after the attackers first logged in, when they added one of those service accounts to an administrator group.

Microsoft’s case turned on a test application nobody had cleaned up. Its guidance for responders on the Midnight Blizzard attack describes a password spray against a legacy test tenant account with no MFA. Inside that tenant sat an old test OAuth app that still held elevated access to the corporate environment, and the attackers used it to get into corporate email accounts.

Drift is the case I’d put in front of a board. In August 2025, attackers got hold of the OAuth tokens that Salesloft’s Drift chatbot used to talk to Salesforce, and for roughly ten days they pulled records out of one customer’s Salesforce instance after another. Google’s threat intelligence team, which tracked the campaign closely, concluded the attackers were mostly after credentials. Once the data was out, they went digging through it for AWS access keys and passwords, anything that might get them into the next company along.

I don’t think any of the three needed a clever attacker at the front door. In each case, a credential was issued for a piece of work and then left alone long after the work had finished.

Getting the groundwork in first

It is a relatively simple task to create a playbook. However, a playbook relies upon an inventory. In many organizations, this inventory consists of a service account list generated from Active Directory where half of the description fields have been left blank. Each time you identify a high-privilege non-human identity, document the team responsible for that identity, and provide a brief explanation (one or two sentences) describing what will fail should you remove that identity. Many people do not include the explanation as to why something would fail if removed, since obtaining this information requires contacting the application team for clarification; this contact would otherwise be initiated by your analyst at 3:00 AM while the attacker remains active within your network.

Next, sort those identities by blast radius. I wouldn’t put a read-only reporting token on the same response path as a cloud admin service principal, and I doubt your auditors would either. For the top tier, settle in advance who’s allowed to authorise an immediate revoke even if it knocks something over, and put that role in the playbook by name. Executives must own that call. If you leave it with whoever’s on shift, you’ll get a polite wait for permission while the token stays live. For SOCI-regulated entities, there’s an extra edge to this, because the 12-hour window for reporting a significant cyber incident to ASD can be running while that conversation drags on.

Triage that fits a machine

No one can provide a response to “was this you?”, thus, replace it with questions that can be answered by the log files. A rapid means of verification is location: where do the credentials usually sign in from, and where are they signing in from at present? Logging is readily available via Cloud Audit Logs and Workload Identity Platforms, if someone turned the logging on.

Permissions take longer but tell you more. Line up what the identity holds against what it has used over the last few months, because attackers tend to go straight for high-risk scopes that have been sitting idle. I’d give persistence the same attention. With a privileged service principal in hand, an attacker will often mint new secrets or register an app of their own, and none of that goes away when you revoke the original credential.

Containment without breaking the business

The “trigger” for rotation and revocation should be written separately in the playbook. Rotation would be appropriate when you are reasonably confident that the attacker has not escalated and the organization cannot afford to lose the integration. Revocation is the obvious choice if you find evidence of an ongoing attack; this will be clear enough so there will be no debate at midnight.

Pre-staging your replacement credentials will make revocations tolerable. When the team that owns the application has previously tested how to generate a new credential and then store it in their secret management system, revoking old credentials can cost you about ten minutes of downtime instead of being a full-day disruption. Ask the team to practice generating and storing new credentials during a low-traffic week. Do not find out mid-incident that the runbook references a vault location that was renamed last year.

Scoping and recovery

To understand the full scope of an incident, look at the entire lifespan of the machine credential, not just the period after the alert was generated. Because machines may be able to go undetected as being compromised for many months prior to discovery, the first unusual activity reported will most likely not be the first unusual activity performed. Also, keep in mind that “drift” is a great way to remember to see what information the identity has access to, and if anyone has placed credentials into that identity. If so, each addition of a secret will require you to add a new rotation to your list.

Recovery is when you fix what caused the problem in the first place. For example, if a static secret was compromised, determine if that workload can use short-lived tokens using Workload Identity Federation; or perhaps a short-lived token can be generated on demand (Just-In-Time) and will expire automatically. Recovery is a tedious, non-sexy task, and most of the time it requires financial support from an entity outside of the Security Operations Center (SOC).

Before finalizing the playbook, conduct a tabletop simulation with the application owners in attendance along with the Security Operations Center (SOC). Select your highest-privilege integration and simulate a stolen-token event (from first alert through recovery). During the simulation, when a decision needs to be made regarding who approves revoking the token, and revoking the token will disrupt production, observe how much time it takes for the team to identify who should make this approval.

Title: U.S. CISA adds Apple flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
Context: “This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise
Full Text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Apple flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added an Apple flaw, tracked as CVE-2024-27834 (CVSS score of 5.5), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

“This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.” reads the advisory by CISA.

CVE-2024-27834 is a security vulnerability affecting Apple’s operating systems and Safari. It could allow an attacker who already has arbitrary read and write capabilities on a device to bypass Pointer Authentication (PAC), a hardware-based security mechanism designed to protect memory addresses and prevent certain types of memory-corruption attacks.

Pointer Authentication is a security feature implemented in Apple processors. It adds cryptographic signatures to pointers, helping ensure that memory addresses have not been maliciously modified.

An attacker who gains the ability to read and write arbitrary memory could potentially exploit CVE-2024-27834 to circumvent these protections. This could weaken an important security barrier and make further exploitation of the device easier.

What is the impact?

Bypassing Pointer Authentication protections.

Weakening defenses against memory-corruption attacks.

Potentially facilitating further exploitation when combined with other vulnerabilities.

Apple addressed the vulnerability through improved security checks in:

Safari 17.5

iOS 16.7.8 and iOS 17.5

iPadOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 17.5

macOS Sonoma 14.5

tvOS 17.5

watchOS 10.5

Cybersecurity firm Sekoia reports on attacks attributed with moderate to high confidence to Russia-linked cyberespionage group APT29. Attackers used compromised websites, fake websites and a supply-chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker to deliver malicious JavaScript. The zero-click exploit chain targeted Safari and Chrome vulnerabilities to bypass security protections and deploy information-stealing malware capable of collecting browser cookies and device data.

“Achieving arbitrary read/write access within the renderer is no longer sufficient for full exploitation on modern Apple silicon. This architecture relies on Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC) to cryptographically sign control-flow pointers. Because of this, even if an attacker can manipulate memory, they cannot simply overwrite a function pointer to hijack the execution flow, triggering an improperly signed pointer will crash the process rather than execute the payload.” Sekoia writes. “To overcome this mitigation and forge the valid pointers required for arbitrary code execution, the exploit chain incorporates a PAC bypass utilizing CVE-2024-27834.”

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by November 18, 2026.

Title: CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access
Context: Describing the threat as active and ongoing, the activity involves the use of publicly-available AI-driven offensive security tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI
Full Text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country.

Describing the threat as active and ongoing, the activity involves the use of publicly-available AI-driven offensive security tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI.

"These tools execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on target responses," CERT-In said. "The supporting attack infrastructure rotates IP addresses within hours to days."

The agency said the attacks have also targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset service providers, resulting in the theft of keys and funds.

The update follows an October 2026 alert issued by CERT-In, which warned of multiple cyber attack campaigns targeting non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and cryptocurrency wallet operators.

Threat actors have been observed exploiting internet-facing applications and exposed APIs and privileged endpoints to steal payment aggregator/gateway and partner-bank API credentials, and then invoke fund-transfer APIs directly from within the entities' own allow-listed infrastructure.

Some of the other notable initial access vectors are listed below -

Use of stolen long-lived static, hard-coded API tokens

Supply chain compromise of source code repositories via forged commits

Exploitation of plaintext credentials in configuration files, source code, or databases

Access to applications and remote services lacking multi-factor authentication (MFA)

This approach, CERT-In added, defeats application-level controls such as loan creation, KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency, and per-transaction limits.

The rapidly executed fraudulent transactions are designed to move funds to attacker-controlled mule accounts across multiple banks. In addition, the attacks involve the operators taking steps to delete logs and tamper with endpoint security tools in an attempt to complicate detection and incident response efforts.

CERT-In also warned that attackers are targeting cloud infrastructure to execute commands and deploy malicious payloads, as well as publicly-accessible non-production environments to obtain shared credentials, tokens, or network paths, and then use them to pivot to production systems.

Other notable post-exploitation actions undertaken by the adversary are as follows -

Reverse-engineering application codebases to develop tailored exploits

Initiating unauthorized API calls using modified application packages, undermining controls that "assumed only the legitimate client application would call the APIs"

Executing micro-value test transactions (such as Rs. 1) to validate unauthorized fund flows before executing large-value transfers

Abusing merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators to move funds

Exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities, including file-upload and deserialization exploit chains leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications

Creating a large number of custom scripts on the fly and iteratively improving them in quick succession, a pattern consistent with AI-assisted development

The development comes as CERT-In has published the Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines, laying out specific requirements to ensure the "governance, security, privacy, fairness, transparency, resilience and auditability of AI systems."

The framework calls for testing an AI agent's documented identities, authorized objectives, approved tool use, permission boundaries, and its adherence to the principle of least privilege (PoLP). It also requires AI agents to require human approval for consequential actions, while ensuring high-risk AI systems incorporate emergency interruption, credential revocation, and controls for preventing automatic restarts.

"Effective assurance requires organisational accountability, technical testing, data and model governance, continuous monitoring, human oversight, incident response and third-party assurance," the agency said. "Accordingly, the framework provides auditable requirements proportionate to the nature, scale, autonomy and potential impact of each AI system."

Copycat ARTEX Version Hands Out Root Shell

The abuse of open-source penetration testing tools like ARTEX in real-world intrusions prompted its developer to take down the repository from GitHub. But multiple copies have sprung up on the Microsoft-owned code-hosting platform to fill the void -

github[.]com/trhhubsd/ARTEXX

github[.]com/mhtsec/ARTEX ("mianhuatang11/artex" on Docker Hub)

github[.]com/RuoJi6/ARTEX

The first two GitHub repositories are no longer available for download. According to an independent cybersecurity researcher who goes by the online alias Badbyte, the "trhhubsd/ARTEX" repository was starred 2,449 times and forked over 600 times.

What's notable about the GitHub copy is that it changed a single line in "docker-compose.yml" to pull the "tomicdd/artex" image from Docker Hub. The modified version conceals a new routine that grants a root shell during an unauthenticated request to the login endpoint. Per statistics shared by Docker Hub, the image has been downloaded 9,000 times.

"It adds a hidden verifyCaptcha() function to the login handler: if the CAPTCHA field starts with a secret marker, the rest runs through sh -c as root and the output is returned, before any credential check," the researcher said in a statement shared with The Hacker News via email. "That's an unauthenticated root shell on every install, and it never shows up in a code review."

"A compromised ARTEX instance holds its targets' unpatched findings, live credentials, captured sessions and network position. Whoever holds the backdoor can also quietly change what the agents do on the next run."

As many as 62 ARTEX consoles on the internet have been found to serve the backdoored build between November 2 and 4, 2026, with the first instance going up by October 20, 2026, twelve days after the Docker image was pushed. Of these, 26 consoles are located in the U.S., followed by 17 in Hong Kong and seven in China.

In all, a total of 1,645 hosts have been found serving the ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026. Besides "tomicdd/artex," a number of Docker Hub namespaces have been identified as publishing images named "artex." Some of them are listed below -

congdonglinux/artex (also backdoored and identical to "tomicdd/artex")

mianhuatang11/artex

autumn26/artex

andy1099zz/artex

dgddw/artex

trhhubsd/ARTEX

ylh440104/artex

"The backdoor's author needed nothing more. The people they were after had already chosen to run an unvetted attack tool as root on an open port," Badbyte said. "We know ARTEX has been used maliciously in the wild, and it will keep being used that way. We also know that plenty of legitimate, curious people installed it to see what the fuss was about. They did not sign up for a root shell on their own server."
