Title: AI-Powered Ransomware Is Coming for UK Critical Infrastructure, and Europe Is Already the Testing Ground
Context: In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical...
Full Text:
Overview

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has put a date on a threat that security teams across Europe have been bracing for. In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical National Infrastructure by 2028.

That is not a distant, speculative scenario. It is a two-year window, and it lands alongside a second judgement. By 2028, China, Russia and other nation-states will highly likely be using AI-enabled cyber capabilities routinely to pursue geopolitical goals, with the UK facing sophisticated attacks at greater scale and speed.

The review also recorded that UK and EU member states jointly attributed a December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid to Russia's FSB Centre 16. Had it succeeded, roughly 500,000 citizens could have lost power. Europe is not watching this threat from the sidelines; it is where the playbook is being tested.

Key Takeaways

2028 is the marker. The NCSC judges AI malware will highly likely be used in ransomware against UK CNI before the end of 2028.

Europe's grid is already a target. Russia's FSB Centre 16 was attributed to the December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid, and a July 2026 advisory from 18 partners in 12 countries flagged the same group exploiting vulnerable routers to reach CNI networks worldwide.

China is best positioned to use AI against CNI. The NCSC rates China's activity as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK.

AI speeds up old tricks rather than inventing new ones. For large organizations, 88% of incidents the NCSC handled began through just four initial access vectors.

A "patch wave" is coming. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery will shrink the time defenders have between disclosure and exploitation.

The gap is widening. Organizations with legacy technology and slow remediation will become the preferred targets of both states and criminals.

The 2028 Warning

The NCSC's assessment is precise about where AI makes the difference. It calls AI an almost certain "force multiplier" that improves reconnaissance, social engineering, vulnerability discovery and exploit development. The biggest effect, it says, will be faster and larger versions of existing tactics rather than brand-new attack vectors.

Ransomware is where that acceleration hits CNI hardest. The review expects criminal adoption of AI to raise the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and exploitation. It also warns that open-source AI tools built for security researchers are likely to be repurposed to automate criminal workflows, cutting costs and raising attack volumes against less resilient targets.

The agency is careful not to overstate today's reality. Its Incident Management team has begun to see attackers using AI tools, but none of the observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Human operators remain essential, and the NCSC notes that losing control of an agentic AI is likely to hinder threat actors from reaching their goals.

The review's pessimistic 2028 scenario shows why that caveat may not last. In it, frontier AI is available to everyone from state actors to novice hackers, jailbroken models are sold in criminal marketplaces, and attribution becomes harder as capability spreads. It even describes a realistic possibility of an automated cyber actor operating beyond its operator's control. Cloud-controlled CNI and AI-driven robotics raise the chance that a digital compromise causes physical harm.

The NCSC stresses this is an illustration of the cost of inaction, not a forecast. But it is a scenario written by the agency responsible for defending UK infrastructure, and it is set just two years out.

Europe: The Proving Ground for CNI Attacks

If the UK is looking at 2028, continental Europe is already living with the threat. The NCSC names Russia as the most audacious cyber threat to the UK today. GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler goes further in the review's foreword, warning that tactics Russia developed against Ukraine are now being turned more widely on states and their institutions.

Three data points from the review frame the European picture:

Poland's energy grid (December 2025). The UK and EU member states formally attributed the attack to FSB Centre 16. If successful, it could have cut electricity to around 500,000 people.

Router exploitation on a global scale (July 2026). The NCSC and 18 international partners from 12 countries issued a joint advisory on FSB Centre 16 actors exploiting vulnerable routers to target CNI networks worldwide. On the same day, the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including criminals running proxy networks linked to Russian intelligence.

Operational technology in crosshairs. The review points to recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) as evidence that organizations failing to modernize are falling behind.

The pattern matters for anyone running energy, water, transport or telecoms in Europe. Grids, interconnectors and supply chains cross borders, and a disruptive attack in one country can cascade into its neighbors. The review also describes how cyber threats to the UK can escalate rapidly and without warning during periods of geopolitical tension.

Add AI to this mix and the timeline compresses. A state actor that today relies on patience and known router flaws could, with AI-assisted discovery and exploitation, find and weaponize new weaknesses across thousands of European edge devices far faster than defenders can patch them.

China is Best Positioned to Turn AI on Critical Infrastructure

While Russia is the loudest threat, the NCSC sees China as the most capable. It judges that China highly likely has both the intent and the best position to use AI against CNI and other strategic targets. Its frontier AI programmes are expected to sharpen vulnerability identification, targeting efficiency and access operations.

Data sits at the center of that strategy. The review describes China collecting large volumes of information from the UK and elsewhere, then using it to train models and improve capability. In the AI era, stolen data is no longer just espionage material; it is fuel.

The UK has already acted on this. In December 2025, it sanctioned two China-based firms: i-Soon, which targeted more than 80 government and private IT systems globally, and Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has linked to the Flax Typhoon intrusions. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 partners across nine other countries published guidance on the covert networks most China-linked actors use to hide their activity.

The 2028 scenario adds a further concern: China, as a leading developer, may help spread advanced AI-cyber capability to other actors, letting them hide in the noise and making attribution harder for European defenders.

AI Runs the Old Playbook, Only Faster

The most useful finding in the review is also the least dramatic: attackers are still getting in through the basics. Over the past year, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks. Of these, 337 needed its direct support, and 80 were classed as nationally significant.

For large organizations, 88% of incidents started through four initial access vectors:

Exploiting public-facing applications

Phishing

Misuse of valid accounts

Exploiting external remote services

Even state-linked intrusions often used flaws for which patches already existed but had not been applied quickly enough. As the review puts it, sophisticated actors do not need to be sophisticated to gain initial access; their skill shows in what they do once inside.

This is exactly where AI changes the economics. The NCSC expects AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to give attackers more chances to hit systems before owners patch them. It is urging every organization to prepare for a "patch wave": a surge of security updates across the technology stack, many of them critical, as AI exposes years of technical debt.

Two further risks deserve attention:

Shadow AI. Staff moving sensitive data to personal devices to use unsanctioned AI tools leaves organizations blind to where that data goes, and open to both APT groups and criminals.

The widening gap. Mature, well-resourced organizations will use AI to detect and fix faster. Those running legacy systems will fall further behind and become more attractive targets.

The financial stakes are already clear. UK government research cited in the review puts the annual cost of malicious cyber activity to UK organizations at about £14.7 billion. The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover alone cost the company around £196 million in direct costs and contributed to UK GDP growing just 0.1% in Q3 2025.

How the UK Is Fighting Back With AI

The NCSC's answer is to meet machine-speed attacks with machine-speed defense. Several initiatives in the review stand out:

Cyber Shield. A joint NCSC and DCMS programme to build a national agentic cyber defense ecosystem over five years. The NCSC supplies the platform and intelligence, while defensive agents are built by the security market and open-source community. Early phases focus on detection and blocking, where automation is already practical.

Project DROMOS. Launched in 2026 by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre and the AI Security Institute, it used frontier AI models to review government codebases. Expanded into live environments, it surfaced hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities.

National Detect Strategy. A pilot aiming, by 2030, to ensure defenders across critical systems can detect and respond to known vulnerabilities and attacker techniques at organizational, community and national scale.

Regulation and benchmarks. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill brings new sectors into scope and adds national security powers. The new CAF Core Profile sets a minimum resilience baseline for essential services.

There are early results. Under the Government Cyber Action Plan, the median time to fix domain-related vulnerabilities fell from 50 days to 8. The Early Warning service now covers 19,922 organizations, up 52% on last year.

For Europe, the lesson is that partnership is now part of the defense. The review highlights the world's first AI security standard developed through ETSI, the European standards body, as proof that allies can shape AI security while the technology is still evolving.

National defense at machine speed also depends on seeing adversaries before they reach the network. Groups like FSB Centre 16 and China-linked operators plan, recruit, and trade access in places most defenders never look. As AI makes attribution harder, government agencies, national CERTs, and defense bodies need intelligence that tracks threat actors across the open, deep, and dark web and connects that activity to the infrastructure being targeted. Cyble Hawk is built for exactly this. It gives national security teams sovereign threat intelligence, adversary profiling, and investigative support. That means early warning of campaigns against critical infrastructure and stronger attribution when an attack does land. Book a demo to see how your agency can move from reacting to incidents to anticipating them.

Recommendations for CNI Operators in the UK and Europe

The NCSC's core message is that AI did not create these weaknesses; it is exposing them faster. Operators of critical infrastructure should act on the following now:

Harden the edge first. Inventory and patch internet-facing applications, VPNs, routers, and remote access services. These are the routes FSB Centre 16 and others are actively exploiting.

Prepare for the patch wave. Build processes to test and deploy security updates more often, faster and across suppliers. Track time-to-remediate as a board-level metric.

Kill password-based access where you can. Move privileged and remote users to phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, and audit valid accounts for misuse.

Segment IT from OT. Limit the paths from corporate networks to PLCs and industrial control systems, and monitor those boundaries continuously.

Govern AI use internally. Map what data AI tools and agents can access, what actions they can take, and how they are monitored. Close off shadow AI with approved alternatives.

Rehearse recovery, not just prevention. Test ransomware response playbooks against scenarios where operational systems must run during disruption. Use the NCSC's guidance on recovering from highly disruptive attacks.

Lock down the supply chain. Require baseline controls such as Cyber Essentials, or equivalent standards in EU frameworks, from suppliers with access to critical systems.

Use threat intelligence that moves at AI speed. Monitor for exploitation of newly disclosed flaws, stolen credentials, and chatter about your sector, so you can act before an incident escalates.

Start post-quantum planning. The NCSC wants discovery and migration planning finished by 2028, priority migrations by 2031 and full migration by 2035.

Conclusion

The NCSC has given Europe a deadline. By 2028, AI-powered ransomware against UK critical infrastructure moves from possibility to expectation, and state actors will be using AI as a routine part of their operations. The Poland grid attack and the global router campaign show the targeting is already in place; AI simply adds speed and scale.

The agency's own framing is a "moment of choice." Organizations that modernize, patch fast, and build resilience now will be able to absorb what comes next. Those that defer will find AI exposing their technical debt faster than they can repay it.

For CNI operators across the UK and Europe, the next two years are the window to close the gap. Continuous visibility into emerging vulnerabilities, active exploitation and threat actor activity will be central to staying ahead of attacks that move at machine speed.

Title: U.S. Charges Canadian Man in Alleged Hack of University Supercomputers
Context: These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials
Full Text:
A Canadian man was extradited to the U.S. to face charges over hacking universities and hijacking their computers to mine cryptocurrency.

A Canadian man, Ryan James Roach (35), has been extradicted to the United States to face charges tied to a hacking operation that targeted universities and other schools. Roach was extradited on October 28 and now faces federal charges alongside Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario.

The indictment alleges that, from June 2016 to December 2019, the two men hacked computers, stole login details, and used victims’ machines to mine cryptocurrency for themselves.

“They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials.” DoJ states. “Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts. Some of the computers damaged by the defendants were located at an institution of higher learning in the Western District of New York.”

The targets were not random home PCs. Prosecutors say the pair went after U.S. schools with supercomputers, including institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts. Some affected computers belonged to a higher-education institution in western New York.

“To carry out the scheme, Roach and Stubbings surreptitiously accessed victim computers without authorization, deployed malware to gain control, stole victim login credentials, exfiltrated the data to servers that they controlled, and forcing victim computers to use their processing power to mine cryptocurrency for the financial benefit of the defendants.” DoJ continues.

That is a lot of effort to turn someone else’s research hardware into a personal crypto rig.

The alleged method was also more involved than a single phishing email. The indictment says they looked for weaknesses in victims’ networks, used servers and compromised machines from one victim to hide their tracks, and then moved through the network once inside. The duo used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network.

The charges include conspiracy to obtain information from and damage protected computers, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer. Each carries up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Prosecutors also allege the pair damaged at least 10 protected computers in one year and caused at least $5,000 in losses.

Roach appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Mark W. Pedersen and is being held pending a detention hearing. Extradition proceedings for Stubbings continue in Canada. The FBI, the Justice Department’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, and the Office of International Affairs worked on the case.

For security teams, the useful part is not the alleged crypto-mining. It is the reminder that universities remain attractive targets because they hold powerful computing resources, broad networks, and plenty of people with access. Patch quickly, watch for unusual processing load, and treat credential theft as a serious incident rather than a nuisance.

“The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.” DoJ concludes.

Title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
Context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
Full Text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

Title: Attackers turned OpsShield’s trusted update channel into a supply-chain attack
Context: ” What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution...
Full Text:
The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process.

This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers.

The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys.

Ultimately, the breadth of this unsanctioned access underscores the continued fragility of the software supply chain, as well as the vulnerability of security tools themselves.

“The real danger here is that attackers were able to turn a trusted security update mechanism into a vector to break into servers,” said Erik Avakian, a technical counselor at Infotech. “The software that’s supposed to protect those servers became the source that compromised them.”

The anatomy of the attack

OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software. Its cPGuard product is a security suite, malware scanner, and firewall designed for Linux web hosting servers.

The company disclosed that, between November 1 and 2, attackers were able to gain unauthorized access to the OpsShield update distribution infrastructure, and, for about 70 minutes, pushed out a malicious update.

The threat actors began by probing OpsShield’s billing portal, registering a customer account under a false identity, and ordering a free cPGuard trial. They then sent crafted requests that allowed them to gain the ability to run commands on the server to collect data. They used stolen access keys to publish fake updates that ran as root (the highest level of admin privilege), and to copy sensitive files and make copies of three OpsShield cloud servers.

About 2,950 customer servers ran the fake update, exposing password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, and shell history, OpsShield reported. Attackers also accessed about 7,900 billing portal accounts containing customer names, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.

OpsShield says it is still reviewing the exact request that provided access, and has patched two possible entry points and verified related vendor components “line by line.” It closed the attacker’s account, revoked the stolen update-storage key as well as “every cloud API token and access key on our account.”

The company also removed the attacker’s secure shell (SSH); deleted the clones of its servers created by the attacker plus any snapshots; turned on stronger login protection and replaced every SSH key and password; reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated all keys; and began rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers with tighter PHP and firewall settings.

The company has also published clean updates: v5.88.26, which removes the hidden root shell; plus a follow-up which removes the scheduled task left by the attacker. Further, it began re-issuing all cPGuard license private and public keys so that the copies the attacker gained access to stopped working.

The company advised admins to:

Update cPGuard to the latest version, then confirm that /etc/cron.d/i93677, /var/tmp/.i93677/ and /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh are gone; delete them if not;

Change root passwords and every local user password on the server;

Generate new root SSH keys and remove old ones from every server that trusted them; until the keys are changed, treat the servers as compromised;

Change MySQL root passwords and any database passwords and rotate any password, API key, or token existing in root shell histories;

Reset the OpsShield billing portal passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.

Finally, it said, “if we told you the attacker logged in to your server by hand, rebuild it from a clean backup taken before 1 November.”

OpsShield being transparent, but the impacts are still real

“Frankly, few vendors write a breach disclosure this candid,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “OpsShield deserves a lot of credit for that.”

However, he pointed out, the worst kind of breach is the one a security tool delivers. Update channels are left unlocked on purpose, and security tools run as root because they have to see everything, “so the fake update ran as root too.”

For a hosting provider, one server can hold hundreds of customer websites and databases. A MySQL root password opens all of them, and a root SSH key grants access to every other server that trusts it. Shell history also often contains typed passwords and tokens.

The downstream customer may be hit hardest while knowing the least, Dickson pointed out, as most website owners have no idea which security agent their hosting provider runs. Every server that updates itself trusts the vendor’s pipeline.

OpsShield describes itself as a small team selling to smaller hosts at a low price, which is the uncomfortable truth of the supply chain, Dickson said. “Your exposure is set by the smallest vendor holding root on your servers, not the largest.”

Avakian agreed that this serves as a reminder that an enterprise’s software supply chain is only as secure as the systems, identities, and processes behind it. “You can do everything you can to secure your own infrastructure and still get compromised through a third-party supplier you trust.”

What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution mechanism to turn the vendor’s own trusted infrastructure against its customers, he noted.

Third parties extend risk, which is a fact that organizations still underestimate, he said. “Enterprises need to pay much more attention to third-party and supply chain risk management.”

Zero-trust a must-have

Avakian also pointed out that the impact on downstream customers could go well beyond initial compromise, as stolen credentials can be used to carry out further attacks. Enterprises should take a zero-trust approach that includes their software suppliers and the updates they rely on.

“Just because an update comes from a trusted source doesn’t mean you can assume it’s safe,” he said. Enterprises should take a closer look at vendor risk, protect privileged credentials, and examine software integrity. Also, continuously monitor for unexpected behavior after an update and be ready to isolate systems quickly if and when something goes wrong.

“You have to plan for the possibility that even a trusted supplier can be compromised,” he emphasized. “And you need to practice those types of scenarios as part of a regular table-top exercise program.”

Dickson advised starting with an inventory, and knowing every vendor agent running with root or administrator privilege, as each one is an update channel. Customers should ask vendors where update publishing keys live and what separates them from customer-facing systems, watch outbound traffic from servers, keep secrets out of shell history, and treat SSH keys as credentials with an expiration date. Downstream customers should ask their host directly whether it runs cPGuard, then change their own passwords.

“The most dangerous software on your server may be the software you trust to update itself,” he said. “Choose those vendors as if they hold root, because they do.”

Title: Vercel rolls out new protection against stolen session cookie attacks
Context: The new feature, announced by Vercel's CTO Malte Ubl on X, binds a login session to the user's device with a private key stored in a TPM, so even if the session cookie is...
Full Text:
Vercel is gradually rolling out Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) on its platform as a key defense against information stealer malware.

The new feature, announced by Vercel's CTO Malte Ubl on X, binds a login session to the user's device with a private key stored in a TPM, so even if the session cookie is stolen, it can't be reused on another device.

Vercel is a cloud platform developers use to deploy and host websites, web applications, and AI agents. The company also develops the popular Next.js web framework.

Its latest announcement concerns logins to Vercel's platform at vercel.com, where developers manage their projects and deployments.

"DBSC works by storing a private key in your device's TPM (the same device that the fingerprint sensor or similar biometric devices on your laptop or phone uses) and using that key to sign your cookie," explained Ubl.

"The private key can never be retrieved ever again. Not by us, not by you, not by the malware."

Vercel's DBSC rollout also complements Chrome's App-Bound Encryption, which makes it harder for infostealer malware to extract browser cookies. DBSC adds another layer of protection by preventing stolen session cookies from being reused on other devices.

DBSC currently works in Chrome on macOS and Windows, but the rollout is gradual to ensure edge cases involving OAuth apps are handled appropriately.

Separately, Vercel is rolling out a similar protective technology called DPoP for the Vercel CLI.

Security Review also lands

Earlier this week, Vercel launched Security Review in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams, adding a feature to Vercel Agent that scans code changes on every push to connected GitHub repositories once enabled.

The new system uses code and team-defined policies to flag issues such as missing authorization checks and exposed secrets.

If permissions allow, the Vercel Agent can validate and commit fixes.

Vercel says Security Review scans will be free until November 10, 2026, while agent-generated fixes will be billed separately.

Ubl said that Vercel's security team shipped this new feature internally a couple of months back, and it has already proven its worth, so the platform decided to make it broadly available.

In April, Vercel suffered a security breach impacting a subset of customers, in which attackers gained access to its systems by compromising an employee's Google Workspace account at Context.ai.

Vercel said the attacker used that access to reach internal systems and view environment variables that hadn't been marked as sensitive.

A threat actor impersonating ShinyHunters attempted to sell the allegedly stolen source code, access keys, and database data.

Full Text:
Election Day brings typical cyber threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. Hackers tamper with European refrigeration systems. OpenAI faces questions over years of security warnings. Nvidia reportedly restricts business with Chinese data center customers. Binance details a six-billion-dollar heist attributed to North Korea. Barracuda patches critical security flaws. Gartner predicts an engineering-heavy future for security operations. Canadians face charges for hacking U.S. universities. Our guest is Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

Today is Wednesday November 4th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Election Day 2026 brings a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation.

Election Day 2026 brought a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. But the biggest technology story emerging from the midterms may be voters' growing resistance to artificial intelligence.

According to Nextgov, election officials reported unsuccessful attempts to penetrate online services, including efforts to guess login credentials. One state election office experienced five spikes in traffic to its ballot drop-box locator, which subsided after officials implemented a CAPTCHA. As of Tuesday evening, election security analysts had received no reports of foreign influence operations.

Meanwhile, ballot scanner malfunctions in New York's Westchester County quickly became fodder for election conspiracy theories. Officials initially attributed rejected ballots to problems with their thickness. Voters were instructed to deposit affected ballots in secure emergency bags for later counting. Despite no evidence of deliberate interference, misleading claims spread rapidly on X, reaching as many as 100 posts per minute.

Beyond election security, voters delivered a significant political setback to the technology industry's ambitious AI expansion.

Axios reports that roughly two dozen ballot measures restricting data center development appeared headed for approval. In Texas, Democratic gubernatorial winner Gina Hinojosa campaigned on maintaining a construction moratorium until lawmakers address environmental and infrastructure concerns.

With Democrats also winning key races in Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona, analysts estimate nearly two-thirds of planned U.S. data center capacity for 2028 could face delays.

The emerging message from voters: They're increasingly concerned about AI's impact on electricity prices, water supplies, and their communities. Silicon Valley may have enormous ambitions, but it turns out the people living next door to those data centers get a vote, too.

Hackers target refrigeration systems across Europe.

Hackers are targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, remotely changing temperature settings and forcing supermarkets to throw away spoiled food.

Attacks reported in November affected stores in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Germany, along with food suppliers in the UK. In some cases, attackers switched refrigeration equipment into defrost mode or disabled temperature alarms. Retailers have responded by disconnecting vulnerable equipment from the internet.

The attacks have also raised concerns about medical supplies. In France, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration equipment supplied to the French Blood Establishment, changing freezer settings from minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees. An alert technician caught the problem before it disrupted operations, according to French health officials. There's no confirmed loss of blood plasma or harm to patients.

Authorities haven't identified the perpetrators or established whether the incidents are connected. French cybersecurity officials are urging organizations to secure remote access to refrigeration controllers, update firmware, and eliminate default passwords.

The incidents demonstrate how compromising ordinary industrial equipment can have very real physical consequences.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses that could expose sensitive AI research to competitors and foreign governments.

According to Reuters, concerns included broad employee access to internal code repositories, sensitive research documentation, and inadequate security reviews of internal tools. Some employees believed leadership prioritized development speed over security.

Those concerns gained urgency following several incidents, including the arrest of a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a listening device in an executive conference room, and researchers using a rival AI model to access employee accounts and internal systems.

OpenAI disputes suggestions that it neglected security, pointing to restricted repositories, increased investment, and regular reviews. The company reportedly reassigned a quarter of its production engineers to security improvements in August.

The larger challenge: protecting increasingly valuable AI technology without slowing the research that makes it valuable.

Nvidia sets limits on Chinese data center customers.

Nvidia is reportedly imposing new restrictions on data center customers that provide computing services to Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, Nvidia has told operators they must limit Chinese customers to no more than 49 percent of their overall business, with the remaining 51 percent coming from non-Chinese companies.

The policy would require data center operators to track how much business they conduct with Chinese firms, potentially complicating operations for providers serving customers in both China and elsewhere.

The Financial Times says Nvidia's sales representatives and regional teams have communicated the restrictions directly to customers, but the company apparently hasn't issued formal written documentation.

The reported move introduces a new limitation on how Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure can be used, adding another consideration for data center operators navigating business relationships with China.

Binance describes the $6 billion North Korean heist.

North Korea has launched several missiles toward the sea, hours after rejecting FBI accusations that its hackers stole more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Pyongyang denies responsibility and says the accusations undermine prospects for renewed diplomacy with Washington.

Meanwhile, Binance has revealed how the attack unfolded. Hackers spent months compromising three engineers' computers, using malicious software disguised as developer tools and a fake job interview featuring a rigged coding assignment.

Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. The company hasn't explained precisely how the AI tool was abused.

Binance says approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted, and affected systems have been rebuilt.

Barracuda patches Email Security Gateway vulnerabilities.

Barracuda Networks is urging customers to patch two vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances that could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges.

One critical flaw enables unauthorized changes to global configurations, while the second allows users with administrator permissions to inject operating system commands.

Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces. Chaining the vulnerabilities could allow them to bypass authorization controls and gain root access.

The company has released patches and recommends updating firmware, applying security fixes, and restricting administrative access to trusted internal networks.

Gartner predicts SOCs will shift toward more engineers.

By 2028, security operations centers could employ 50 percent more engineers than analysts, according to a new Gartner report. The shift reflects AI's growing ability to handle routine security alerts, freeing human analysts to focus on investigating cases, making decisions, and coordinating responses.

Gartner predicts SOCs won't necessarily shrink. Instead, engineers will increasingly build, test, and refine AI workflows, while analysts expand into threat hunting and exposure management.

The transition creates challenges for entry-level analysts, who traditionally learned their craft by processing alerts. Organizations will need new approaches to training and developing expertise.

Gartner also recommends replacing traditional alert-volume metrics with measures of case accuracy and decision quality.

By 2030, the firm expects SOCs to become more proactive, continuously testing their own defenses rather than primarily responding to alerts.

Canadians are indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities.

Two Canadian men have been indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities to steal data and mine cryptocurrency.

Prosecutors say Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings targeted institutions in four states between 2016 and 2019, deploying malware, stealing credentials, and exploiting university supercomputers. They allegedly used servers registered under false identities and compromised systems to conceal their activities.

Roach has been extradited to the United States, while Stubbings awaits extradition. Both face up to ten years in prison and fines of $250,000 if convicted.

AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

WIRED's Will Knight decided to see whether artificial intelligence could outperform him at fantasy soccer. He assembled a team of AI agents, handed them control of his lineup, and waited for the tactical brilliance to begin.

Their opening move? Bench Erling Haaland, one of the world's most prolific goal scorers. Not exactly an auspicious start.

The AI eventually reconsidered, but its subsequent decisions haven't been particularly impressive. After several weeks, Knight's AI-managed team still hasn't outperformed the average fantasy squad.

Meanwhile, researchers studying AI forecasting have found that leading models can sometimes outperform ordinary people at predicting events, although expert human forecasters generally remain formidable competition. Some experiments suggest AI is closing that gap.

Knight suspects AI could eventually become an unbeatable fantasy manager. But he's not particularly enthusiastic about that prospect. After all, fantasy sports are supposed to reward human judgment, even when that judgment is spectacularly wrong.

Title: Zyxel fixes zero-day exploited to hack nearly 1,000 network switches
Context: Attacks linked to zero-day flaw On June 16, 2026, Zyxel released security updates addressing CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the same...
Full Text:
Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that hackers exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management interface that allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to execute operating system commands using specially crafted HTTP requests.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 switch models, and Zyxel released security updates on October 22 and published a security advisory on November 3.

However, the vulnerability was initially mistaken for an older flaw that Zyxel had already patched months before the attacks began.

Attacks linked to zero-day flaw

On June 16, 2026, Zyxel released security updates addressing CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the same GS1900 switches.

Starting around August 17, cybersecurity company GreyNoise observed a suspected Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala exploiting Zyxel switches, reporting that the attackers compromised 996 devices across 48 countries.

The threat actors exploited the flaw to execute commands remotely before downloading a script that collected device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information.

GreyNoise linked Kapibala to the Red Heron hacking campaign, which Acronis previously reported was exploiting a critical vulnerability in the self-hosted Git service Gitea.

When GreyNoise disclosed the campaign on September 21, it attributed the exploitation to CVE-2026-7273, the vulnerability Zyxel had patched in June.

That same day, CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring federal agencies to address the flaw.

However, researchers at firmware security company Binarly discovered that the exploit used in the attacks actually targeted a separate, previously unknown vulnerability that remained unpatched.

While investigating Red Heron infrastructure linked to the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT rootkit, Binarly researchers found an exposed archive containing an obfuscated Python exploit targeting Zyxel GS1900 switches.

After analyzing the exploit, the researchers found that it specifically checked for firmware versions patched for CVE-2026-7273, indicating the exploit had been developed or updated to target those versions.

Binarly confirmed on September 28 that the exploit remained effective against all ten firmware releases patched for CVE-2026-7273.

The researchers determined that the earlier security update added checks to prevent a buffer overflow, but attackers could bypass them by corrupting a parameter counter before it was validated.

This allowed the exploit to overwrite memory and execute commands without authentication, even on switches running the earlier security updates.

Binarly reported its findings to Zyxel on September 29, and the vendor confirmed the new vulnerability on October 11, assigning it CVE-2026-107441.

Zyxel classified it as a separate flaw because the exploit also abused missing validation of HTTP parameter lengths.

On October 22, Zyxel released new firmware updates that limit parameter sizes and validate the parameter count before copying data into memory, preventing the exploitation technique.

While the recovered exploit specifically targeted firmware patched for CVE-2026-7273, it remains unclear whether it was deliberately developed to bypass those updates or exploited a related vulnerability that the earlier patches failed to address.

Administrators of affected Zyxel GS1900 switches are advised to install the latest firmware updates to protect against CVE-2026-107441.

Title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
Context: Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their...
Full Text:
Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.

Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”

In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.

Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.

Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.

Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.

Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.

“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”

Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

Title: PolinRider Loader Reappears in Hijacked npm Packages
Context: Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases...
Full Text:
TL;DR

Sonatype Research Labs identified concealed runtime loaders in 12 npm releases across 10 hijacked packages.

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to decode payload-server IP addresses from Ethereum transactions sent by the same hard-coded wallet previously reported in PolinRider activity, then retrieve, XOR-decode, and execute JavaScript. Six conceal the loader in eval(atob(...)); six use a character-permutation bootstrap and the JavaScript Function constructor.

The manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. The code can run when an affected entrypoint is loaded or, for server-hemera-mongo, when the bundled application starts.

Check direct and transitive dependencies, lockfiles, internal npm mirrors, and build records. If affected code ran, treat the host as compromised and investigate its processes, network activity, and accessible credentials.

Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases

On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases across 10 hijacked packages. The examined releases contain two loader variants that use the same Ethereum sender wallet and payload-retrieval infrastructure. Sonatype tracks the finding as sonatype-2026-010515.The affected packages support unrelated developer functions, from Redux integration and health APIs to browser activity tracking, utilities, and server examples. Their shared issue is concealed behavior embedded in code that otherwise serves those ordinary purposes.These releases don't rely on a consumer-side installation script to activate that behavior. An application can reach the code when it loads an affected package; the server-hemera-mongo releases run it as the service starts.

Affected Releases

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

The Shared Loader Uses Ethereum Transactions to Find Remote Code

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to query public Ethereum RPC endpoints, with a Blockscout API fallback, to locate a transaction sent by the hard-coded wallet 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. The loader interprets the first four bytes of the transaction's recipient address as a primary IPv4 address and the next four as a secondary address. It retrieves XOR-encoded JavaScript from the primary address over plain HTTP on TCP port 443, using the paths /0x/cls and /0x/ls.

After XOR-decoding the responses, the loader passes the JavaScript retrieved from /0x/cls to eval in the application process and to a detached node -i process through piped standard input. The JavaScript retrieved from /0x/ls is passed only to a detached node -i process. The child processes are unreferenced, allowing them to continue independently of the application process.

The Ethereum wallet acts as a dead-drop resolver: the operator can advertise a new payload-server IP address by sending another transaction without updating the malicious packages. Blocking an individual server therefore does not disable the loader's ability to discover a replacement.

Six Releases Conceal the Ethereum Loader With a Different Bootstrap

Six releases use a character-permutation bootstrap designed to reconstruct and execute an Ethereum-based loader: @adminide-stack/utils@0.0.16-130, cdeops@13.5.31, @adminide-stack/forms-core@5.1.9-alpha.3, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser@12.0.194, @cdmbase/wiki-browser@12.0.18-alpha.53, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser@12.0.23-alpha.3. The decoded loader bodies recovered from these six releases are byte-identical. They differ from the loader in the six Base64-wrapped releases but use the same Ethereum wallet, retrieval paths, and XOR keys.

In utils@0.0.16-130, an obfuscated routine follows the package's logger code. It permutes and decodes an embedded blob, obtains the JavaScript Function constructor indirectly, and executes the decoded content.

In cdeops@13.5.31, an obfuscated bootstrap appears in client.js before the module's normal delegation to global.require('cdeops/client'). It decodes embedded content and executes it dynamically, then continues to the expected client delegation. The hidden execution is separate from the documented purpose of that shim.

Shared Wallet and C2 Infrastructure Link the Releases to PolinRider

Sonatype Research Labs independently decoded the loaders in all 12 releases and recovered the same hard-coded Ethereum sender wallet, 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. This exact wallet appears in GitGuardian's October 27, 2026 report, "GhostAction Crosses Paths With PolinRider: Inside the October Escalation," where it is identified as the Ethereum resolver used by PolinRider loaders found in compromised GitHub repositories. Those earlier loaders also retrieved stages from /0x/cls and /0x/ls on port 443, matching the retrieval paths and port in the npm samples.

The connection extends to the payload-server infrastructure. Greenflagged'sanalysis of these npm releases decoded transactions from that wallet and reported 95.135.181.151 as the advertised C2 address at its November 3 observation. GitGuardian had already listed the same IP on port 443 as a fallback C2 in a PolinRider persistence script. The exact wallet match, overlapping server infrastructure, and matching stage-retrieval paths support linking these malicious npm releases to previously documented PolinRider activity. This connection does not depend solely on similarities in obfuscation, and it does not definitively establish that PolinRider and GhostAction share an operator.

The Malicious Code Doesn't Wait for an Install Hook

The package manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. Execution occurs when the runtime reaches an injected JavaScript file. For example, require('cdeops/client') selects the affected client.js, while the package's ES module import maps to a separate client.mjs file. In server-hemera-mongo, the injection is in dist/main.js, the application bundle referenced by its start script.

Assess exposure by correlating dependency records with execution evidence. Lockfiles identify resolved dependency versions, while cached artifacts and download logs help trace package acquisition. Build commands, application configuration, process telemetry, and runtime logs help establish whether an injected JavaScript file was executed.

Disabling npm install scripts does not address code that runs during module loading or application startup. The relevant question is whether the affected package code ran in a developer environment, CI worker, build host, or deployed service.

What Teams Should Do Now

Organizations should take these steps to identify affected systems and limit further exposure:

Find affected versions: Check direct and transitive dependencies, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, internal npm mirrors, caches, build records, and artifact metadata.

Evaluate repository protections:Determine whether your repository manager or dependency firewall blocked these releases before they reached developers or build systems. Review download and policy logs to identify any deliveries, and ensure all eight versions are blocked from future use.

Remove affected dependencies:Replace affected versions in projects and prevent internal mirrors and caches from serving them. Preserve copies needed for investigation, and use replacement versions that have been independently verified as clean.

Determine whether the code ran: Check which entrypoint the application loaded and whether the runtime could execute the injected code. Correlate this with process and network activity. A lockfile entry does not prove the malicious code ran, and an import error does not prove it didn’t. The import may have failed after the injected code executed.

Investigate affected hosts:If the code ran, treat the host as compromised. Look for detached node -i processes launched by another Node process with piped standard input, and plain HTTP requests to TCP port 443 using /0x/cls or /0x/ls. Payload requests carry a Sec-V header containing A10-npm_inject in the six Base64-wrapped releases, A10-II in utils@0.0.16-130, or A10-E in cdeops@13.5.31. Use these indicators alongside process ancestry, timestamps, and dependency records to identify affected systems.

Assess access and rotate credentials: Identify the credentials and systems available to the affected process. Rotate credentials where exposure is possible, including publishing credentials, source repository access, cloud keys, and CI secrets.

The operator can change the remotely served JavaScript without publishing another npm release. Use available process, network, build, and runtime records to determine what affected systems executed and which credentials and resources those processes could access.

For ongoing details and response guidance, see the Sonatype Security Event and Sonatype Guide research.

Thanks to Sonatype Research Labs' Adam Reynolds for analysis of the affected npm releases and their PolinRider activity. Connect with Adam on LinkedIn.

Title: DreamHost confirms data breach exposed FTP logins and webmail sessions
Context: The company says it has blocked the attackers' access and addressed the vulnerability exploited in the attack
Full Text:
DreamHost is warning of a data breach after attackers gained access to its File Manager platform for two months and stole customers' FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords.

This follows the American web hosting provider and domain registrar's announcement that it suffered a cybersecurity incident requiring users to reset their email and FTP/SFTP passwords.

In a data breach notification, DreamHost now says the breach extended from August 2026 to October 23, 2026, the day it was discovered.

"We discovered that an unauthorized third party accessed the server that runs our web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com," reads the notification.

"The unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in that software and was able to access the FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords of individuals who logged into this File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026."

In addition, DreamHost says the intruder may have also accessed webmail systems, exposing session information, including credentials, for a limited number of users.

The firm said the attack appears deliberate, and its staff has been working nonstop to contain it fully.

At this time, DreamHost said it found no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing/payment details, which an external provider handles.

The company says it has blocked the attackers' access and addressed the vulnerability exploited in the attack.

The company also stopped active sessions for potentially affected users and invalidated passwords.

BleepingComputer has contacted DreamHost multiple times with questions about the incident and the exact number of impacted accounts, but our inquiries have gone unanswered.

Recipients of the notifications are advised to check website files for unauthorized changes, review webmail forwarding rules and filters, and change passwords on any other accounts where they may be using the same credentials.

To mitigate the risks from this exposure, DreamHost offers impacted individuals one year of credit monitoring and identity theft protection through Equifax.

Letter recipients are also urged to consider placing a fraud alert or asking for a security freeze on their credit report.

Full Text:

In this article

A fake $750 Apple Cash offer funnels users toward app and game promotions

Its device checks, countdown, and “spots left” claims aren’t real

Users get no reward and may share information or spend money in games

A page we found promises a $750 Apple Cash reward if you complete a quick “device verification.” There is no reward, and the page does not verify your device. Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links.

The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it.

The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash

Why Apple makes such good bait

Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks.

Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention.

The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context.

Apple Cash isn’t an Apple Gift Card

The page blurs two different things:

Apple Cash is money you send, receive and spend through Apple Wallet.

An Apple Gift Card adds money to your Apple Account balance for Apple purchases.

Apple warns that its gift cards can only be used for Apple purchases, and that someone asking you to pay them with one is probably a scammer. But neither Apple Cash nor an Apple Gift Card comes from a website that “unlocks” it after you install an app.

The fake site leans hard on Apple’s name. It calls the app it promotes an “Official Apple Partner” that is “Verified by Apple Cash,” and its footer claims “Copyright © 2026 Apple Inc.” None of that is true.

A “verification” that verifies nothing

We looked at the code behind the page’s three steps: Eligibility Check, Verify Device and Claim Reward.

The eligibility check is a timer. The four items that tick green, including “Location: United States,” are just labels that light up on a schedule. The page never checks where you are or what device you use. Everyone passes in under four seconds.

It tells users to download an app for “device verification”

The device verification is an app install. The page tell users to download an app called Reco Social, then tells them to create an account, and install and play a game. We found no evidence that Reco Social or its developer created or operated the fake reward page.

When you tap Download & Open App, the page opens a link in a new tab. Five seconds later, it starts showing “Verifying device…”. Nothing is being verified. The page has no way of knowing whether you installed anything, created an account or played a game.

The reward is the same link again. Ten minutes after you tap the button, the page moves on by itself and announces “Device Verified Successfully,” whether or not you installed anything. The Claim Your $750 button doesn’t add anything to your wallet. It opens the same link as the download button.

Fake urgency

The page is built to stop you from thinking too long:

“Only 47 spots left today” always starts at 47. It drops by one every 30 seconds and stops at 3, so it never runs out.

The “claimed $750” pop-ups are generated at random from a list of 15 first names and 15 US states, with a random “minutes ago.” Every visitor sees a new one every 8 to 15 seconds.

The 10-minute “Session Expires” countdown doesn’t end anything when it hits zero.

Who gets paid?

The download button doesn’t go directly to the App Store. It first goes through a tracking link on taprkr[.]com. These links can be used in affiliate marketing to credit clicks and installs to whoever sent the traffic.

The link carries a label, “recosocial-cpr.” CPR can stand for “cost per registration,” a deal where a promoter earns money when someone signs up. That label alone doesn’t confirm how this offer pays.

The destination varied in our tests. The link led to an offer labeled “playful-rewards-revshare” on iPhone and an ad network on PC. A revshare (revenue share) deal usually pays the promoter a cut of what users later spend, such as on in-app purchases.

The tracking labels suggest that promoters may earn money from registrations or spending in promoted apps, but they don’t confirm how this offer pays. Users don’t receive the promised $750.

We have no evidence that Reco Social or any app at the end of these links is behind the fake Apple page. Deceptive affiliate promoters can send traffic to legitimate apps because they may earn money for installs or signups regardless of how users were persuaded.

The page also loads a TikTok tracking pixel, which advertisers use to measure campaigns. This could mean the operators are measuring traffic from TikTok, but it doesn’t show where the link was shared.

What’s the harm if it’s “just” an app install?

Compared to a page that steals passwords or card numbers, this one can look harmless. But you still pay a price:

You give away personal data. Creating an account means handing over your email address, phone number or social login to a service you only signed up for because of a lie.

You may be encouraged to spend. Many mobile games make their money from in-app purchases, and with a revenue-share deal, someone profits when you spend.

You may be set up for the next scam. Fake reward offers often come in chains. The next one may ask for your Apple Account details, card number, or a “small processing fee.”

You lose time chasing a reward that was never coming.

How to stay safe

Keep these points in mind if you come across an Apple Cash or other Apple-related offer online:

Don’t expect an app install to pay you in Apple Cash. Be suspicious of any “Apple” offer that asks you to download a third-party app, create an account or play a game to receive Apple Cash or an Apple Gift Card.

Verify Apple Cash only in Settings. The real identity check is in Settings > Wallet & Apple Pay > Apple Cash. Treat any website or message that asks you to “verify” Apple Cash somewhere else as suspicious.

Be extra careful around launches and holidays. iPhone Duo deals, giveaways and preorder offers will keep circulating. Go to apple.com or the Apple Store app yourself instead of following links.

Check the address bar. Apple’s website is apple.com. A page on a domain like applecashgiftcard[.]com is not Apple, however much it looks like it.

Treat countdowns and “spots left” as red flags. Fake urgency is there to rush you past the moment you’d ask, “Why would anyone give me $750 for this?”

Already installed an app from a page like this? You didn’t earn a reward, so you can delete the app. Delete any account you created through it, cancel any subscriptions in your App Store settings, and change that password on any other accounts where you reused it.

Never pay with gift cards, and never pay to receive a prize. As the FTC puts it, “No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.” If a “reward” asks for a fee, your card details or gift card codes, it’s a scam.

Report it. Apple asks people to forward suspicious Apple-themed messages to reportphishing@apple.com. You can also report the ad or post to the platform where you saw it and, in the US, report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

How Malwarebytes helps

Malwarebytes can help block known scam pages. Use Browser Guard with a supported browser, or Web Protection in Malwarebytes for iOS when browsing with Safari.

If you’re not sure whether a link, text or offer is real, you can ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you click.

Title: Cyberattack disrupts blood storage refrigeration systems in France
Context: Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which was outside the company's direct control
Full Text:
France's national blood service has confirmed that a cyberattack targeting a refrigeration equipment provider raised temperature and defrost settings at three of its facilities, threatening stored blood products.

The French Blood Establishment (Établissement français du sang or EFS), which manages blood collection, processing, and distribution across France, said the incident occurred on November 2 and affected systems used to monitor and control cold-storage chambers.

According to a statement published on November 3, EFS was not directly targeted in the cyberattack, but was instead its refrigeration supplier.

While EFS has not named the affected supplier, European refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld Rentals confirmed in a statement that a cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software had affected a limited number of its refrigeration units.

Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which was outside the company's direct control.

"The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the company said.

"Only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected, and Coolworld responded promptly and took appropriate measures."

The company said it is working with affected customers but will not comment on individual cases.

At EFS, the incident raised temperature and defrost thresholds in affected cold-storage chambers to extremely high levels.

These facilities store blood products before they are distributed to hospitals, as well as biological samples maintained by the EFS.

EFS says its monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the temperature change, allowing staff to fix impacted equipment or transfer products to other refrigeration facilities.

"No health impact has been identified, and no loss of blood products has been reported," EFS said in its statement [translated from French].

The organization confirmed that plasma bags intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines were either transferred or secured, preventing damage to the products.

Blood collection and distribution operations have continued without interruption.

EFS says its technical teams are working with France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the Ministry of Health, and it has strengthened monitoring of refrigeration equipment and temperatures.

The incident follows a wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, where attackers remotely manipulate temperature settings or activate defrost functions that turn off cooling.

In October, cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration systems at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, including Intermarché, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, Leclerc, and Super U.

In those attacks, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration controllers running older Danfoss software and remotely activated automatic defrosting functions, raising temperatures and forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen products.

These attacks targeted Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers, which are used to monitor and manage cooling equipment remotely.

A second wave of attacks occurred this month, affecting more than 115 stores across Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Estonia.

Some refrigeration systems were shut down entirely, while others had their temperature settings changed remotely.

At one Swedish supermarket, the system reportedly began generating heat, while another store reported that temperatures were changed to 50°C (122°F).

Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel previously said that attackers behind the November incidents exploited the same vulnerability used in October's attacks against French supermarkets.

In 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) disclosed two vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451.

The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely on vulnerable systems, potentially giving them control over refrigeration equipment.

However, it has not been confirmed whether these vulnerabilities are being exploited in the attacks.

Title: mSecure tells users to change passwords but won’t say why
Context: But make sure another working sign-in method is available first
Full Text:
Password manager mSecure has warned current and former customers to protect the confidential information stored in its app after detecting “suspicious activity.”

But its advice about what users should do comes without an explanation of what happened or whose information might be at risk.

The warning leaves users to decide whether to replace credentials—and whether it’s safe to store replacements in mSecure.

While those are perfectly reasonable questions, mSecure’s warning does not answer them.

In an email published by The Hacker News and sent to customers on November 3, mSecure’s developer, mSeven Software, said:

“mSeven Software (‘mSeven’) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application. In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist.”

The notice recommends that customers “immediately take steps to protect all confidential information” stored in mSecure. Those steps:

“may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys.”

But the notice does not identify the suspicious activity, when it occurred, which systems were involved, or whether anyone accessed customers’ stored information. The Register, which also reviewed the email, noted that the company had not explained whether customers’ secrets were exposed.

How to be safe

Because the scope of the incident is unknown, we recommend prioritizing your most important accounts while mSeven investigates.

Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident.

Users should not have to wait for a completed forensic investigation before receiving useful guidance. They need to know who should act, which credentials need attention, and whether the tool they would normally use to manage those changes remains safe to use.

Until mSeven provides those answers, our advice is to prioritize your most important accounts, replace the relevant credentials through official services, and avoid destructive account resets:

Change passwords through each service’s official website or app, beginning with your primary email, financial accounts, work accounts, and accounts used to recover access to other services. Use a new, different, strong password for each.

Review two-factor authentication stored in the vault. If that could be compromised by unauthorized access, consider re-enrolling that account’s authenticator through the service’s security settings.

For passkeys stored in mSecure, use each website or app’s account-security settings to remove the old registration and create a replacement with a different provider as a precaution. But make sure another working sign-in method is available first.

Think carefully about where replacement credentials go. The notice does not establish whether saving new credentials in mSecure is safe. For users rotating important accounts now, using a different password manager temporarily is a reasonable precaution.

We’ll keep you posted if we learn more about this incident, so stay tuned.
