Title: SonicWall Won't Patch EoL GMS Flaws That Could Expose Files, Alter Database Records
Context: The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from...
Full Text:
SonicWall has warned of two vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that it said will not be patched.

Details of the security flaws, which affect SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions, are below -

CVE-2026-109593 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An unauthenticated file read vulnerability that could allow an attacker with network access to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information.

CVE-2026-109594 (CVSS score: 6.8) - A post-authentication SQL injection vulnerability that could allow an authenticated attacker to access or modify information stored in the GMS database under specific conditions.

"The affected product has reached End-of-life (EoL)," SonicWall said in a Tuesday alert.

"As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities. Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

The development comes less than a month after SonicWall shipped fixes for CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that could have allowed an attacker to reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from Singapore and the U.S. since October 9, 2026. As many as 30 exploitation attempts were registered on November 3, 2026.

Title: NIKKE PC game launcher hacked to spread remote access, data-stealing malware
Context: The developers of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE have confirmed that hackers tampered with the game's PC launcher scripts in a supply-chain attack, distributing malware capable of...
Full Text:
The developers of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE have confirmed that hackers tampered with the game's PC launcher scripts in a supply-chain attack, distributing malware capable of stealing credentials and cryptocurrency wallet data.

According to a notice published on X, a client update was issued on November 4 at 02:30 (UTC +9) to address the issue.

"We have identified an issue indicating that the PC Launcher's script files may have been tampered with by a third party," reads the statement on X.

"Accordingly, client fixes and an update were implemented on November 4 at approximately 02:30 (UTC+9). We are currently investigating the scope of the impact caused by this issue, and we will provide further details regarding follow-up measures in a separate notice."

Goddess of Victory: NIKKE is a popular sci-fi shooter RPG developed by the South Korean firm Shift Up for Windows, iOS, and Android.

Its publisher, Level Infinite, reported more than 45 million downloads since its launch in 2022, while Google Play alone reports 10 million downloads.

Malicious launcher scripts delivered backdoor

Although Level Infinite has not disclosed many details, a report on GitHub by independent security researcher MotherSphere alleges the incident involved four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite's official content delivery network (CDN).

According to the researcher, the files were modified on September 27, 2026, to inject malicious JavaScript that downloaded additional code from attacker-controlled servers whenever players opened the game launcher.

The injected code was hidden within legitimate JavaScript files and used obfuscation to conceal the domains insightjs[.]com and insightjs[.]org, from which the malicious code was downloaded.

BleepingComputer examined two of the modified JavaScript files and confirmed that they contained an obfuscated loader designed to retrieve and execute additional code from these domains, falling back to the second domain if the first was unavailable.

According to MotherSphere's analysis, the downloaded code abused the launcher's native functionality to retrieve and execute a malicious LuaJIT payload called insight.bundle, which installed a remote-access agent referred to as K2F.

The backdoor allowed attackers to remotely execute commands, browse and download local files, capture screenshots, collect NIKKE account credentials, and steal information stored in web browsers.

The malware also supported an additional command to install a malicious Windows DLL named platform_experience_helper.dll that could remain active after the game launcher was closed.

BleepingComputer analyzed strings extracted from a DLL sample uploaded to VirusTotal and found code indicating that the malware can steal cryptocurrency wallet data from browser extensions, including MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, and others.

The DLL contained functionality to intercept sensitive wallet information, including recovery phrases and private keys, potentially allowing attackers to steal cryptocurrency.

However, it is unknown whether the attackers deployed this additional component on infected systems or successfully stole cryptocurrency from players.

The researcher claims that Level Infinite replaced three of the impacted JavaScript files on November 3 with clean versions. However, they claim a tampered copy of the fourth was reportedly still being served to users as of 22:26 GMT.

This suggests that at least one compromised script may have remained accessible after the company deployed its client update.

The researcher also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) that users can check to determine whether the malicious Lua agent executed on their computers.

One indicator is the string k2f_chan registered in the Launcher/intl_service/debug.log file within the NIKKE installation directory.

This entry indicates the malicious Lua agent executed, but it does not confirm whether the DLL was loaded as well.

BleepingComputer also found that the insightjs[.]org backup domain is now serving code that displays a security warning inside the game launcher.

The warning, displayed in English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, tells players to immediately close the launcher and refrain from opening the PC client until the publisher confirms the issue has been resolved.

The message confirms that this is not an official announcement from the game's publisher, so it unclear who currently controls the domain or when the malicious payload was replaced with the warning.

BleepingComputer has contacted Level Infinite for comment on MotherSphere's findings, but has not received a response by publication.

Potentially affected players should run a full system scan using updated antivirus software.

Those who find they were compromised should reinstall Windows, and change passwords and other sensitive credentials from a clean device.

Researchers Uncover Prompt Adware Hidden in OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit
Context: " As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research.

Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses.

"The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service."

Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails.

The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top."

Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering.

However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026.

It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants.

What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface.

"The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said.

While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks.

"As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

Title: mSecure password manager hack prompts password reset warnings
Context: 8M records exposed The MFA Gaps Attackers are Still Exploiting Hackers disrupt refrigeration systems at European supermarkets BAE Systems cyberattack disrupts US federal court...
Full Text:
mSeven Software is warning current and former mSecure password manager customers to change passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys following a cyberattack in which a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database..

In a security notification sent to customers on November 3 and shared with BleepingComputer, the company said it recently discovered suspicious activity involving its mSecure password management application.

"mSeven Software (“mSeven”) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," reads the mSecure security notification.

"In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist. You are receiving this email because you are a current or former mSecure customer."

The notice did not provide any details as to what systems were compromised, whether customer data was stolen, and how many users were impacted.

However, the company urged all current and former customers to immediately protect confidential information stored in the password manager.

"This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys," continued the security notice.

mSecure is a password manager that allows users to store passwords, passkeys, financial information, and other sensitive data in encrypted vaults that can be synchronized across devices.

According to mSeven's security documentation, mSecure uses AES-256 encryption and a zero-knowledge architecture that encrypts data locally on users' devices before transmitting it to the company's servers. The company says it cannot access customers' decrypted vault contents.

These security protections have led to confusion among customers about why they are being advised to change all their stored passwords and authentication if their data was encrypted before being uploaded to the company's servers.

Encrypted password database reportedly stolen

While the original notification had few details, customers have shared responses reportedly received from mSeven's support team indicating that a hacker stole an encrypted database from mSecure Cloud.

In one support forum post, a customer shared a response stating that the stolen database contained information belonging to current and former mSecure users.

According to the response, mSeven discovered the theft and subsequently notified customers.

The response also stated that the company had no evidence that the attacker accessed the confidential information stored within the encrypted database.

"Please note, this issue only pertains to users that were synching with the mSecure Cloud," reads the response shared by the customer.

The company also reportedly said it had implemented additional security measures and had no evidence that the mSecure application was currently unsafe to use.

Other customers reported receiving similar explanations, including confirmation that the incident was limited to users who synchronized their password databases through mSecure Cloud.

However, customers have expressed frustration over the company's lack of transparency about the breach and the potential risks to their stored credentials, particularly as mSeven has not publicly explained how the breach occurred.

While mSeven reportedly has no evidence that attackers accessed the encrypted information, stolen password vaults can still pose significant risks if attackers can crack weak master passwords through offline attacks.

This was shown in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults.

Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak master passwords to access stored credentials, private keys, and recovery phrases.

BleepingComputer contacted mSeven Software with questions about the incident, the stolen database, and the potential impact on customers, but has not yet received a response.

Title: US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
Context: Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive...
Full Text: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023. Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began. The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters. Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia. Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors. According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information. Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government. Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023. The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials. On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000. "Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

Title: China-Aligned Group Abuses Sogou Input Method to Deliver Malware
Context: A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application...
Full Text:
A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application traffic into a malware distribution channel.

ESET researcher Anh Ho detailed the activity in research published on November 4, naming the group SlippyNunchucks and tracing its activity to at least September 15, 2023. ESET assessed with high confidence that the group is associated with a nation-state surveillance effort aligned with Chinese government interests.

The campaign began on July 1, 2026, when users of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language keyboard app owned by Tencent, began receiving DarkVigil implants. The number and geographic spread of victims initially led ESET to suspect an exploit.

Hijacked Sogou Traffic Reached Six Countries

A Sogou component fetched a brand-promotion configuration from a Sogou server over unencrypted HTTP. Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking redirected those requests to attacker-controlled servers, which returned a malicious configuration.

That configuration made the app download the DarkVigil implant and place it where Sogou's own components would run it, giving the malware persistence without a separate mechanism.

ESET does not know where the DNS manipulation occurred. Possibilities include routers set up with malicious DNS settings, routers implanted to hijack DNS and interception at internet service provider (ISP) level.

Victims were in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and Oman. They included a multinational gambling organization operating from Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Hong Kong, an internet café in Dubai and a university student in Denmark, though ESET gave no victim count.

Read more on China-aligned update hijacking: PlushDaemon Hackers Unleash New Malware in China-Aligned Spy Campaigns

Tencent Fixes Sogou as ESET Flags Remaining Gaps

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular .NET toolset with more than 20 plugins. Darktrace had linked FDMTP to Mustang Panda with moderate confidence, but ESET said its telemetry showed no overlap with that group and tracks SlippyNunchucks separately.

Before the Sogou campaign, the group's only publicly identified distribution method was a supply-chain compromise of QuickFox. ESET linked the gambling-sector targeting to China's gambling restrictions and to China-aligned groups' apparent support for law enforcement action against Chinese individuals tied to regional fraud.

ESET reported the issue to Tencent on September 11, and Tencent acknowledged it on September 21. Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released in late October, moved the affected requests to HTTPS and enabled certificate pinning.

ESET said the downloader component still does not validate downloaded file types or restrict where files are saved.

The fix closes the unencrypted request the attackers abused. Where their DNS hijacking took place remains unknown.

Title: APT29-Linked Hackers Hijack Web Analytics Script to Deliver iOS and Android Exploits
Context: 7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft
Full Text:
The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker.

"The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android."

The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026.

A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors -

Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript

Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria

Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js"

Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort.

"It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said.

"However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites."

Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data.

On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified -

Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft.

Class B, which targets iOS devices running iOS 18.5 and exploits the DarkSword exploit chain comprising CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 to deliver JavaScript malware for full device data exfiltration. This includes SMS messages and iMessages; Apple Mail Envelope Index and Protected Index SQLite databases; voicemail; WhatsApp and Telegram databases; iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords; contacts; call history; Safari browser history and cookies; photos; and data from Apple Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive.

Class C, which targets Android devices running Chrome versions from 139 through 145 (but explicitly excluding version 143 for reasons that remain presently unknown) and exploits CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to achieve remote code execution, sandbox escape, privilege escalation, and ultimately deliver AndroSnitch to collect Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords.

In all three cases, the exfiltrated data is sent to the "ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12" endpoint. The Android attack chain incorporates a check to determine whether the targeted device is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra by examining its model identifier (i.e., SM-S938B). If the device matches, the exploitation activity is terminated.

AndroSnitch derives its name from its similarities to ANDROSNATCH, a Chrome cookie-stealing payload that Google documented in August 2024 in connection with a suspected APT29 watering hole campaign, which targeted Android users visiting a Mongolian government website by leveraging a Chrome exploit chain involving CVE-2024-5274 and CVE-2024-4671.

"This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendors] mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets," Sekoia said. "The adoption of packaged N-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation."

Coruna and DarkSword Kits Evolve

The development comes weeks after iVerify and Report URI detailed the P7 variant of DarkSword being delivered via half-click attacks that leverage ad-based infrastructure. In one case, the exploit is said to have been propagated through a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup and served from "ad-track[.]live."

The other pathway is part of a criminal campaign dubbed DeadTag, in which attackers acquire expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that are still loaded by thousands of websites. The idea is to serve malicious JavaScript to iPhone visitors and silently do the attacker's bidding.

"It checks who's visiting," Report URI said. "Search engines, security scanners, automated browsers and anything else that looks like a bot gets nothing."

The script then interacts with the attacker's server, which then decides the destination to which each visitor has to be redirected. The iPhone exploit paths that take advantage of DeadTag lead to the Coruna exploit kit for older iPhones running iOS version 13 to 17.2.1 and DarkSword P7 for iOS devices running 18.4 to 18.7.

"These are not phishing pages or fake app downloads, both kits attack the browser itself," Report URI's Scott Helme said. "Simply opening the page is enough for your device to be compromised. There's nothing to tap, you don't need to click any link, nothing to install and no warning. If the iPhone is running a vulnerable version of iOS, the kit breaks out of the browser and installs spyware on the device."

Other schemes lead to decoy Google redirects, betting and casino scam sign-up pages, search advertisements for car deals and dentists, and fake surveys and "you've won" prize pages. More than 660 expired and re-registered domains are part of the DeadTag network.

According to an analysis published by Zimperium zLabs, campaigns distributing Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits have continued to evolve, with 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code as of October 2026.

Although Coruna was initially developed by a nation-state actor for highly targeted operations, its subsequent leak following initial disclosure has made the toolkit widely accessible to multiple threat actors for their own campaigns.

In many cases, the lure sites have been found to explicitly instruct visitors to exit their in-app browser or alternative iOS browser and open the link in Safari so as to trigger the exploit chain depending upon the device operating system.

"Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations)," security researcher Santiago Rodriguez said. "Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain."

"The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and – in several instances – compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes."

Title: Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper
The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th)
Context: This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail
Full Text:
One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.

Today, I noticed a slight resurgence in scans targeting e-mail scripts on our honeypots. Today, there are numerous scripts like the old "formail" scripts, and it is hard to link a specific vulnerability to any of these scans. But my main suspect is spammers looking for webforms that allow setting arbitrary "To" headers. The URLs I am seeing:

"/sendmail.php" "/test-mail.php" "/testemail.php" "/config/mail_config.php" "/mail_config.php" "/email-test.php" "/mailtest.php"

In particular, the "Test" part of the filename suggests that the attacker is not looking for production scripts, but for test scripts left behind during development. This, along with the requests for credential/secret files that top our "Leaderboard," points to a more fundamental issue: Code hygiene. Do not leave behind development artifacts that should never have reached a live website.

For example, some excerpts from a random "mailtest.php" script that came back in a Google search [mailtest]:

<?php

/* DONT FORGET TO DELETE THIS SCRIPT WHEN FINISHED! */

$server = array( 'HTTP_HOST', 'SERVER_NAME', 'SERVER_ADDR', 'SERVER_PORT', 'SERVER_ADMIN', 'SERVER_SIGNATURE', 'SERVER_SOFTWARE', 'REMOTE_ADDR', 'DOCUMENT_ROOT', 'REQUEST_URI', 'SCRIPT_NAME', 'SCRIPT_FILENAME', ); $to = ( isset( $_GET['email'] ) ? $_GET['email'] : FALSE ); $subject = 'Mail Test Successful for ' . $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']; $message = '';

??????? foreach ( $server as $s ) { $message .= sprintf( '%s: %s', $s, $_SERVER[$s] ) . PHP_EOL; };

$success = mail( $to, $subject, $message, $headers );

The comment at the top says it all: This is not meant for production use, and even on a development site, it should likely be deployed only briefly for debugging. The script takes any "To" address from the "email" GET parameter and exfiltrates/displays part of the server configuration. It can be useful to scan your own hosts for some of these URLs as an additional control, but you really want to catch these issues during application deployment.

[CVE] https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2000-0411 [mailtest] https://gist.github.com/Porrapat/60ed7411d933122fc481

Title: Fake software installers are turning your PCs into profit centers for hackers
Context: The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly
Full Text:
Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent.

The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post.

The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly.

“Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said, adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign.

Fake installers used for real money

The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software, games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads.

The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software.

Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session.

The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates.

Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing.

A third installs utility-style software associated with Advanced Windows Manager and Windows Manager. These applications may participate in advertising, software distribution, or affiliate-driven monetization.

Microsoft urges defenders to scrutinize unofficial software

Microsoft recommends preventing downloads from untrusted sources, particularly cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, and activation tools.

Organizations using Microsoft Defender Antivirus should enable cloud-delivered protection, maintain tamper protection, and configure reputation-based protection to block untrusted applications and downloads, the company said. It also recommends evaluating Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that restrict executable files based on prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria.

For detection and investigation, organizations were advised to check execution from Inno temporary directories, especially when files such as “eld*.exe, set_*.exe”, “FirstFast[1].exe”, or “SecondRunner[1].exe” appear.

Microsoft also recommends correlating outbound requests containing “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution” or “r=offer_execution_fail” with process activity, scheduled-task creation, and software installations.

Unexpected WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, or VirtualBox installations warrant investigation, it said.

Defender XDR customers can use Microsoft’s published advanced hunting queries to identify related activity, while a list of indicators of compromise (IOCs) was also shared to help defenders outside the Microsoft ecosystem.

Title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
Context: If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it
Full Text:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux. It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google.

Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38. It will become available on Google Play over the coming days.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look.

Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

CVE-2026-121229: Memory corruption in ANGLE, which could allow a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

ANGLE is Chrome’s graphics translation layer. A buffer overflow occurs when a program puts more data into an area of memory than it can hold, overwriting data in adjoining memory. An attacker can exploit this to make the vulnerable process run malicious code.

Chrome vulnerabilities that enable remote code execution outside the browser sandbox are particularly valuable to attackers because they can turn a visit to a malicious or compromised website into direct code running on the underlying operating system, often without requiring additional exploitation steps.

CVE-2026-121035: Use-after-free in Prerender.

Chrome’s Prerender component helps pages open faster by loading and preparing a page in the background before you navigate to it. If you then visit that page, Chrome can display the prepared version almost instantly instead of loading it from scratch.

This goes beyond just downloading content: Chrome also starts rendering the page and running its JavaScript.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

Dawn powers WebGPU in Chrome, allowing websites to use a device’s graphics processor for rendering and computational tasks. It checks and translates WebGPU instructions into commands that the device’s underlying graphics system can understand.

Title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
Context: Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe
Full Text:
A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

Title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
Context: " Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs
Full Text:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.

Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.

XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.

Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

Title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
Context: With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat...
Full Text:
Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.

One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.

No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip.

The runtime is the application, not the pipe

The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model.

A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go.

Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing.

The inspection point is also a target

In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector.

None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure.

A millisecond verdict needs a memory

Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do.

Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist.

What real agent runtime looks like

Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block.

Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy.

Do not buy the end state

Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly.

What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime.

The first ninety days, in order

A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this.

Window

The work

How to know it is real

Weeks 1 to 2: get the number

Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic.

Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps.

Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations

Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first.

A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?"

Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path

Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults.

Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block.

The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance.

Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge.

Seven questions that sort vendors

Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists.

Ask

What a good answer looks like

Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO?

Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot.

For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain.

A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score.

Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents?

Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one.

When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain?

Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one.

What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict?

Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone.

What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised?

A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly.

How long until I see my real agent inventory?

Days. A quarter is a different product.

Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days.

Title: Police Seize 100+ Servers After Four-Year Investment Fraud Probe
Context: A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers...
Full Text:
A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

Title: Fake Interview of Software Engineer Led to Binance Mega-Heist
Context: Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking...
Full Text:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.

Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.

“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.

“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Read more on crypto theft: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency.

The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.

An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.

The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.

The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations

On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.

The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.

Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.

After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.

“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.

Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

Clean-Up Time

Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.

It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.

The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.

Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.

“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.

“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."

Title: Russian Police Arrest 3 Suspected VasyGrek Hackers, Dismantle Criminal Infrastructure
Context: Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection
Full Text:
Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure.

Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software."

In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware.

The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control.

"The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web."

The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value.

According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents.

Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities.

In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device.

The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors.

"The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said.

"The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis."

The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT.

While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf.

Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access.

"Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire.

"A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."
