Identity tripwire appendix

Tripwire

Suspicious interaction

Recommended response

Decoy service account

Authentication from any source or destination outside its tightly defined baseline

Generate an alert and apply a virtual fence

Dormant privileged account

Login attempt against a disabled, unused, or never-used account

Deny the request and investigate the originating identity and host

Decoy SPN/Kerberos path

TGS request for a decoy service identity from an unexpected system

Alert on possible service-account discovery or credential theft and virtually fence it

Tier-0 access edge

Non-admin identity attempts authentication to domain controllers or identity infrastructure

Block inline and surface the full attempted path

Legacy protocol path

NTLM or other weak protocol used against a sensitive resource from an unusual source

Deny or segment the protocol-level access and generate an alert

Executive/admin breadcrumb

Title: Serial ransomware crook gets 70 months behind bars for Nefilim, Hive roles
Context: One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto...
Full Text: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs. Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain. The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands. One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack. Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected. Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue. Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023. According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic. Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022. Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages. “Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said. “Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.” Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025. In announcing Stryzhak's sentencing, the Justice Department took the opportunity to remind the public that rewards totaling up to $11 million are available for qualifying information about alleged Nefilim operator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk and other key ransomware suspects. ®

Title: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

Japan Inc Under Fire

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

Title: AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes
Context: This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that...
Full Text:
Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for artificial intelligence (AI) scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point as AI is now embedded throughout the patient lifecycle, accessing more data than most organizations can secure.

This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns.

A recent Proofpoint report, "2026 Study on Cybersecurity in Healthcare" warned that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions, and more importantly, how they are protecting those tools, explains Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint. Some Proofpoint customers use the OpenEvidence open-source AI tool for research and diagnoses because it can integrate with Epic Systems, a widely used platform for Electronic Health Records (EHR).

"The challenge is making sure physicians aren't putting sensitive information into that tool, so it does get challenging," Biddle tells Dark Reading. Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury like a left tibia fracture could qualify as Protected Health Information (PHI).

That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself, advises Biddle.

What Do CISOs Want to Know about AI in Healthcare?

AI's use is spreading fast and that complicates how organizations think about risk. Tony Sabaj, head of Americas channel SEs at Check Point, says AI's pattern-recognition capability is already improving clinical care, catching early signs in cancer screenings, triaging critical patients, and reviewing electrocardiograms to "generate reports faster and with more accuracy."

Beyond the clinic, health insurers are using AI for claims processing and fraud detection, and like other industries, healthcare is building digital twins to model operational scenarios at scale.

Related:Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era?

Some of AI’s most visible momentum is in reducing administrative burdens including documentation that converts clinician-patient conversations into draft notes, scheduling, intake, coding, and patient communications, says Cindi Carter, global chief information security officer (CISO) at Check Point. But she warned it's also being used behind the scenes to support operational planning, research, and cybersecurity.

Organizations often sort AI tools into "medical" or "administrative" buckets. The first consists of diagnostic AI or treatment recommendation systems, while the latter includes intake forms or scheduling. Carter is concerned that these labels may undermine the downstream risks administrative tools can still pose because a "documentation tool can still influence what becomes part of the medical record" and lead to clinical consequences.

In pharmaceutical and precision medicine, AI investment is outpacing security investment, Sabaj says. And as AI reaches further into healthcare, organizations need to ensure existing regulatory frameworks keep pace. Guardrails often center on protecting data leakage, but safeguards should also ensure that if AI is taking any kind of medical action, it's limited to known parameters, he recommends.

Related:How the CISO-CMO Alliance Builds Trust Before Crisis Strikes

"We continue to see breaches of medical information and AI has the potential to exacerbate this issue," Sabaj tells Dark Reading. To get ahead of the threat, some hospitals are building their own AI tools, using open weight models and training large language models on proprietary data rather than relying on public platforms to handle sensitive PHI.

Carter's concerns extend beyond confidentiality. Despite progress, AI is known to hallucinate. What if AI produced an inaccurate summary, omits an important detail, or acts on manipulated information? The organization can lose confidence in the information supporting care without a record ever being stolen, she adds.

The CISO question then becomes broader, shifting from "What data left?" to "What can this system see, what can it change, and can we reconstruct what happened?" she says.

"In healthcare, we are protecting sensitive information and the integrity of decisions that depend on it," she explains.

Leading Causes of Major Healthcare Breaches

In the relatively short time span since rapid AI adoption took off, Phil Englert, VP of medical device security at Health-ISAC, has already observed changes that will affect how much sensitive data floods systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated, when a cyber incident occurs, organizations frequently lose patient identifiers, medical records, insurance details, and other clinical or financial data— all considered PHI.

Englert cited recent Health and Human Services data that shows hacking and other IT-related incidents continue to be the leading causes of major healthcare breaches. Denver Health Medical Plan reported a breach Oct. 1 that affected 238,083 individuals, triggered by an exposed vendor access key through AI platform SquareML.

This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that an organization's security posture is often only as strong as that of its partners."

While organizations need to secure AI within their own environments, they also need to protect themselves against it as threat actors use it to craft more convincing and effective social engineering attacks, warns Englert. Healthcare organizations are seeing increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, deepfakes, voice impersonation attacks, and QR-code phishing— any method to exploit human trust in a sector driven by speed and precision.

While healthcare organizations can't seem to shake the ransomware threat, which "remains one of the most damaging facing the sector," AI-enabled attacks are a top cybersecurity concern for 2026, he adds.

"Cyber Safety is Patient Safety"

Implementing effective guardrails has proved significantly challenging. Carter offers five recommendations informed by the governance and lifecycle risk themes in the Joint Commissions and the Coalition for AI Health guidance: Visibility, boundaries around data and actions, evidence from vendors, validation and meaningful human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Organizations should maintain AI inventory and give staff a straightforward way to disclose unsanctioned uses as shadow AI risks pummel the sector. Limiting what data AI can handle e is also essential; Carter recommends that access to information should not automatically confer authority to update records, send communications, or initiate transactions.

"AI compresses the time between a mistake and material loss," Carter warns. That should be reflected in organizations' safeguards.

Implementation also depends on organizational maturity. While talking with security officers across the industry, Proofpoint’s Biddle observed varying levels of AI adoption. Some are quite far in the process, while others are still cautious and taking it slow, she adds. She points out healthcare does tend to lag behind other industries when it comes to technology.

Many organizations lack resources but continually face disruptive attacks that severely affect patient care. "It doesn't seem to be getting any better, unfortunately, "Biddle says .

Getting better requires money, but when CISOs stand in front of the board and request investments to shore up defenses, they are often hit with: “Why do you need to spend this amount?” says Biddle. It's difficult, because they are competing with budget dollars for life-saving devices, she says.

"But I would say: Leverage the impact of cyber safety," Biddle adds. "Cyber safety is patient safety."

Title: Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang’s systems
Context: Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector
Full Text:
A Ukrainian man has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison for his role in a series of ransomware attacks.

36-year-old Artem Stryzhak became an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group around June 2021, receiving an 80% cut of the ransoms he managed to extort in attacks against hospitals, government organisations, law firms, and businesses around the world.

The rest of the ransom would go to Nefilim's administrators - including fellow Ukrainian Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who was charged last year in relation to attacks against hundreds of corporate victims using the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware, as well as Nefilim.

At the time of writing, Tymoshchuk is not in US custody and a US $11 million bounty has been offered by the US State Department for information leading to his arrest.

Nefilim was not the only ransomware gang that Stryzhak worked closely with. He was also an early affiliate of the Hive ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation which targeted businesses and, in particular, organisations working in healthcare.

The FBI later warned that Hive had extorted US $100 million from businesses and organisations globally in a period of just 18 months.

According to the US Department of Justice, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators were behind Hive ransomware attacks against a number of victims, including law firms, a dentist's office, and a healthcare provider, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector.

In January 2023, it was revealed that a multinational law enforcement operation had secretly penetrated the Hive ransomware operation in late July 2022, capturing decryption keys and quietly passing them to victims so they did not have to pay a ransom.

The DOJ said that the operation saved corporate victims of Hive over US $130 million in ransom payments.

At the time I speculated that the take-down of Hive may lead to the identification and possible apprehension of some of those involved in Hive ransomware attacks. In June 2024, Stryzhak was arrested in Barcelona, and subsequently extradited to the United States where he pleaded guilty.

The infiltration into Hive's infrastructure took place in 2022. Stryzhak was arrested in 2024, and sentenced in 2026. If there's a lesson for ransomware affiliates who think they got away with it, it's that law enforcement is prepared to be patient, and the evidence does not go away.

That's something that Volodymyr Tymoshchuk may also want to consider.

Title: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries
Context: Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections
Full Text:
Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections.

In research published October 27, Check Point said it had tracked the campaign, which it calls Yoba, for two months, though an earlier variant posing as the Cursor coding agent appeared in early June. The fake projects impersonated artificial intelligence (AI) applications including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus.

Their releases sat in GitHub repositories with GitHub Pages landing pages, and some of the repositories appeared among Google’s top results, most likely through search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning.

Yoba Uses Signed Binaries to Hide Malicious Components

The fake applications bundled legitimate signed OpenAI and Anthropic executables with a malicious dynamic link library (DLL). Check Point found that the signed Setup.exe files loaded the malicious component through DLL sideloading, a technique often used to bypass security protections.

The malicious DLL, dubbed YobaDropper, ran several checks before deploying a second-stage loader, including the name of its host process and whether it had administrator privileges.

It also checked keyboard layouts to avoid machines in Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries other than Ukraine and used lengthy sleeps to frustrate automated analysis. Check Point said the actor showed indicators suggesting Russian origins.

The dropper then created a directory under ProgramData, copied a legitimate Windows executable into it and used Scheduled Tasks to establish persistence, with a task running under the Local System account and disguised as a Microsoft task.

Read more on fake AI tools spreading malware: Attackers Combine ChatGPT Feature Abuse With ClickFix to Deliver Trojan Malware

YobaLoader Uses Telegram and DNS to Fetch Payloads

The second-stage YobaLoader used Telegram and encrypted Domain Name System (DNS) lookups, known as DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), to obtain instructions without dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, according to Check Point.

It took an image from a Telegram channel and used data from it to generate domains through a domain generation algorithm.

It then queried Google’s DoH service for encrypted data stored in DNS records, which was cryptographically validated before the loader retrieved and decrypted the next-stage payload.

Check Point advised organizations to be cautious when installing AI applications from unverified repositories and to restrict the execution of software from unknown sources.

The observed payload was an XMRig cryptominer, but the researchers said YobaLoader is a generic loader, so future waves could deliver other executable or PowerShell payloads.

Title: Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots
Context: Cyber Risk Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Threat Intelligence Vulnerabilities & Threats News Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots The threat actor...
Full Text:
A threat actor lurked behind more than 30 different AI bots to find and steal exposed credentials, continuously scanning for sensitive data without success. The findings highlight a growing problem for organizations: distinguishing between which AI agents belong in their networks and which may be malicious.

A scanner impersonating 32 bots — including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta, and others — hunted for exposed credentials to various organizations, according to a report published today by CQ Prime Research, part of Cequence Security. The scanner requested files from affected organizations — which spanned retail, financial services, telecommunications, energy, and software — that hold passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

The scanner has been running since late September and was still active as of late October, according to the researchers. They identified the activity on Oct. 21, discovering that on a single day this month, 48% of Cequence-protected organizations received the malicious AI bot traffic.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The findings highlight a growing challenge for security teams at a pivotal time, as businesses must figure out which AI agents to trust and permit access to their services.

"Attackers can test every one of those allow and deny decisions, and Cequence is seeing them probe which agents a business trusts, then impersonate the agents they expect to get through," Will Glazier, director of CQ Prime threat research and data science, wrote in the report.

Malicious Scanner Gives Itself Away

The scanner operates by firing off a burst of 50 to 190 requests in about 8 seconds and then moving on, working through targets one at a time, around the clock. Fortunately for the organizations affected, nearly all of the requests were blocked or failed, according to the report.

"It sends random nonsense paths first to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique," Glazier wrote.

CQ Prime Research identified the traffic as malicious through some telling behaviors that undermined the scanner's attempt to blend in with other traffic. The scanner rotates through about 32 bot identities evenly, which real bots do not do, according to the report; one machine claimed to be an agent from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity, all within seconds.

The attacker also used the contact address of Anthropic's crawler for all of its fake Claude identities, even when posing as different Claude agents, which shows the text was copied and not unique to each agent, according to CQ Prime Research.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

The scanner also makes requests for configuration files, cloud credential files, and private SSH keys, from a list of about 90 paths, while never identifying itself or providing a contact address. Legitimate Internet-scanning services would never need these files and always identify themselves.

"The requests gave it away," observes Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solutions management at security firm Black Duck, which means "what Cequence documented is the test, not a breach."

Financial Accounts at Risk

However, what happens when AI agents scanning a network get through? This is what organizations are facing, particularly banks and financial institutions, with growing concern among experts that rogue agents are already logging into customer accounts at these organizations without them knowing. The result of such activity could cause global economic fallout.

For now, CQ Prime Research found that at financial services firms, AI agents acting for customers represented fewer than 1 in 4,000 requests. "The agents banks worry about most log in with a customer's own credentials through an ordinary browser and don't announce themselves," Glazier wrote in the report.

At this point, financial institutions should be starting to take action to identify which AI agents are legit and which aren't. But acting now already could mean they're playing catch-up to the activity of threat actors, observes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability

"Banks are currently scrambling to figure out which AI bots belong on their networks, but cybercriminals have already moved on to the next phase," he says. "They are no longer trying to break into these systems. Instead, they are simply logging in disguised as trusted AI agents."

Defending Against AI Agent Impersonation

To mitigate the growing threat from AI bots and agents, security leaders must treat AI agents, API keys, and service accounts with the same operational rigor as human administrators, Barney suggests. "That requires eliminating implicit trust across every access path," he says.

Indeed, organizations should not trust a bot's claimed identity on its own, according to CQ Prime Research, and they should verify agents through signed requests, published address ranges, or direct integrations.

They also should monitor for behavior that does not match the claimed identity, "such as an AI assistant requesting configuration or credential files," Glazier wrote.

Organizations also should stop leaving static credentials in vulnerable files where scraping bots can easily find them to eliminate obvious security gaps. Instead, Barney says, "Security teams must move away from long-lived local credentials in favor of centralized, zero-knowledge secrets vaults."

Title: JFrog Names Nine Global Winners for Inaugural Software Supply Chain Excellence Awards
Context: This year’s JFrog Software Supply Chain Excellence Award winners are working to reduce their exposure to these emerging threats by building a system of record that governs and...
Full Text:
JFrog announced completion of the first-ever Software Supply Chain Excellence Awards, recognizing the teams who have turned their software supply chain into a competitive advantage – unifying development, security and operations around a governed, automated ecosystem that delivers trusted software at scale.

The nine honorees span the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, across three categories: Unified Platform, Trusted AI Adoption, and Software Supply Chain Security.

“Agents now write, review and deploy code faster than ever, while malicious AI models, agent skills and extensions are turning up in the registries developers use daily. Increasing regulations require proof at every step – from code to runtime,” said Roie Shorer, Chief Growth Officer at JFrog. “The companies that pull ahead in the AI era will be those going beyond simply automating for speed and scale. They will be the ones who can see exactly what’s shipping and why, as they bring trust, control and adaptability to their development operations. This year’s winners didn’t just add tools; they established a single source of truth where developers, security, and compliance teams can operate using the same data and the same rules. We’re very proud of all of them and thrilled to be part of their journey.”

Software supply chains are being put under new strain as developer teams grapple with AI-era software challenges. In its 2026 Software Supply Chain Security report, JFrog identified over 900 malicious AI agent skills carrying high-impact payloads alongside 495 malicious AI models on Hugging Face and 56 malicious extensions on OpenVSX. Attackers are no longer just targeting code; they are targeting the autonomous tools that write, review, and deploy it.

This year’s JFrog Software Supply Chain Excellence Award winners are working to reduce their exposure to these emerging threats by building a system of record that governs and secures artifacts from end-to-end – mastering the AI surge with speed and trust.

THE CONVERGENCE AWARD

The Convergence Award recognizes teams that unify a fragmented software delivery workflow – bringing previously disconnected repositories, scanners and tools into a single governed system of record.

Here are the winners:

Ford (Americas): Ford Motor Company has more than 15,000 developers spread across 80-plus global plants, which previously ran on separate repository tools and scanners with no shared visibility between them. By consolidating operations into a unified ecosystem with the JFrog Platform, Ford reduced tool sprawl and turned multiple blind spots into a single pane of glass view for IT and security teams. As a result, the team now manages more than 43 million artifacts on the JFrog Platform with 99.99% uptime. The team credits the consolidation with recapturing an estimated $8 million a year in developer productivity.

SCHOTTEL Industries (EMEA): Schottel replaced fragmented artifact storage and open-source consumption with the JFrog Platform. Over six months it delivered more than 32,000 artifacts, curated over 2,300 open-source packages and automatically blocked more than 900 risky ones. Manual dependency approval processes that previously delayed developers by months were replaced by automated governance and security controls, enabling faster adoption of new technologies while helping maintain its compliance and security standards.

Rakuten Symphony (APAC): Rakuten Symphony runs 28 self-hosted JFrog Enterprise+ instances across India, Japan and Singapore, that are all connected by JFrog Federated Repositories into one collaborative environment. With JFrog Curation and JFrog Advanced Security moving controls to the point of ingestion, the company cut manual triage efforts by roughly 60% in a single month across more than 600 releases, reclaiming more than 500 engineer-hours and pre-triaging over half of its vulnerability workload automatically.

THE TRUSTED INTELLIGENCE AWARD

The Trusted Intelligence Award recognizes teams that bring enterprise-grade governance to AI and model lifecycles, helping trust extend far beyond just supporting application code.

Here are the winners:

NVIDIA (Americas): Models repositories are under enterprise identity control, with a shared curation and scanning policy,which means a downloaded model faces the same checks as a package before it reaches production.

NVIDIA brought its AI model distribution surface under a governed perimeter by applying curation, scanning, and policy enforcement directly to its model mirrors. Thousands of AI model seats are now managed inside a controlled, auditable boundary, transforming what was once an unmanaged distribution surface into a demonstration of DevGovOps operating at true enterprise scale. To get there, NVIDIA leveraged JFrog Curation and JFrog’s scanning and policy tools, piloting them on the infrastructure through which its AI models flow.

Husqvarna Group (EMEA): Husqvarna’s autonomous divisions, across forest, garden and construction equipment, had accumulated overlapping scanners with limited shared visibility into software supply chain risk. After consolidating around the JFrog Platform and introducing software package scanning and policy-based controls earlier in the software development lifecycle, builds were progressively onboarded, providing teams with greater visibility into open-source dependencies and a more consistent approach to software component governance. Title: AI Is Turning CISOs Into Business-Risk Translators, Says Nvidia’s Head of Cyber
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
In the AI era, cybersecurity leaders must explain how AI-related risks connects to business goals and help executives understand who is responsible for accepting those risks, according to Nvidia’s head of cybersecurity policy, Mark Weatherford.

Speaking at ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Weatherford argued that the broad adoption of AI in the workplace, including in cybersecurity workflows, has transformed the CISO role from a security gatekeeper to a business-risk translator.

As organizations weigh AI adoption, CISOs must help executives understand the tradeoffs and clarify who owns the risk, he said.

Weatherford recalled a board meeting where a CISO struggled to explain the relationship between security and the business. Ultimately, the board challenged the CISO on their understanding of the company’s business model. This event, he said, had a negative impact on the perception the board had of the CISO’s credibility and ability to protect the business.

Weatherford said the exchange taught him that CISOs need to understand how their organizations generate revenue, not only how to protect them.

He added that business perspective is especially important as organizations weigh the potential benefits and risks of AI.

For instance, boards may worry that moving too slowly will cost them competitive advantage, Weatherford said, while moving too quickly can mean deploying tools without appropriate controls or an understanding of the risks.

While he argued that CISO rarely owns the business risk from deploying things like AI, he emphasized that modern CISOs must interpret that risk and make sure leaders understand who owns it.

Balancing AI Innovation With Cybersecurity Risks

Weatherford described two main challenges CISOs face with AI.

First and the “pace of technological change” makes their work more challenging.

Second, CISOs need to focus both on “security for AI and AI for security,” protecting the AI systems their organizations deploy while also considering how AI can support security operations.

Combined, these challenges mean traditional cybersecurity approaches may no longer be sufficient, he argued.

“If you’re not doing pentesting 24/7, 365, you’re probably behind the curve,” he said.

Weatherford also cautioned against investments driven by “fear of missing out.”

Leaders, he said, should do business due diligence before spending heavily on AI. CISOs can contribute by preparing concrete proposals for reducing risk. He recommended putting together a short plan that describes the proposed work and the resources it would require.

Vendor evaluation is another area where CISOs need to apply judgment. Weatherford said he looks for AI-native products that address security problems, rather than older products with AI added on.

He urged CISOs to consider supply-chain dependencies, too. Multiple vendors may depend on the same suppliers, creating single points of failure that can affect more than one product or service. Some dependencies may sit several tiers down the supply chain, beyond the suppliers an organization knows it relies on directly.

Weatherford’s advice for keeping pace with these changes was to stay curious and keep learning and even relearn things as technologies evolve.

For instance, he encouraged CISOs to “learn one new thing every week,” suggesting focusing on one AI topic at a time, such as model context protocol (MCP), prompt injections or sandboxing.

Finally, Weatherford recommended CISOs to join and create formal and informal peer communities. He mentioned that he created a CISO Exchange Network in which he invited CISOs from Nvidia’s major partners, customers and suppliers, where they share experience, concerns and tips.

Full Text:
One of the world’s largest natural gas suppliers has notified an undisclosed number of customers that their personal data may have been compromised in a recent breach.

French multinational Engie employs over 90,000 people across 30 countries, supplying gas, nuclear power, and renewables. Its revenue in 2025 was almost €72bn ($80bn).

According to screenshots of the customer notification posted to X, the compromised data could include: full name, postal and email address, telephone number, unique IDs for energy supply (PCE/PDL), customer ID, and contract number.

The firm confirmed that no banking data was involved in the breach.

Read more on cyber-attacks impacting French firms: French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Engie urged customers to be on the lookout for potential fraud and phishing stemming from the incident.

“A malicious person could use the information mentioned above to impersonate you or use your personal details to contact another organization in your name, obtain additional information, or attempt to make a payment,” it warned. “Fraudulent emails may appear to come from trusted sources, such as organisations you know, in order to deceive you.”

According to a statement from the firm sent to Infosecurity, its own IT systems weren’t compromised. Engie blamed a third-party marketing platform used by its partners which was then compromised by threat actors.

“Engie recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers in France,” it explained.

“As soon as this activity was detected, the relevant access was disabled. At the same time, Engie launched an in-depth technical investigation to understand the circumstances of the incident, accurately assess its scope by identifying customers potentially affected, and ensure that the situation was fully secured. Enhanced monitoring measures were also put in place.”

No Group Has Claimed Responsibility

At the time of writing, no extortion group had admitted responsibility for the breach, which Engie said is now contained.

However, in October last year, extortion group Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters listed the firm on its leak site, after compromising over 100 Salesforce instances and claiming to have extracted more than one billion records.

In that incident, Engie’s US retail energy business Engie Resources was the victim, with the group claiming to have obtained 3GB of data.

According to claims data from insurer Resilience shared with Infosecurity, no UK or European energy and utilities clients have reported ransomware since July 2025.

European claims with a recorded cost involved only fraud or exposed customer data. That contrasts with the US where ransomware comprises around 70% of incurred losses across claims on record in the sector, Resilience said.

Title: Banks are blocking AI agents from customer accounts
Context: Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help
Full Text:
This week, Axios reported that major US banks were detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. In many cases, customers have given the agents their usernames and passwords so they could act on their behalf. This kind of access can violate a bank’s rules.

Bianco Research president Jim Bianco raised the question during Unchained’s Bits + Bips livestream on October 26:

“Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?”

Bianco described traditional finance’s business model as “based on laziness.” Customers may leave idle cash in low- or no-interest bank accounts rather than move it into a money market fund. An AI agent could make that move for them. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said.

The banks offer a different explanation. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow just any outside agent into its systems because doing so was “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

Both explanations can be true: banks can want to retain deposits while also facing real security problems when software acts through customers’ accounts.

Handing over your banking login introduces another service into the security chain. A vulnerability in that service could expose your credentials or allow your account to be misused. And as Bank of America reportedly pointed out:

“If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”

That’s the bank’s stated position, not a universal ruling on consumers’ legal rights. Still, it’s a warning worth taking seriously.

Pros and cons

An AI agent with permission to make purchases might find and buy an item at a lower price. But giving an agent access to your bank account also means sharing sensitive banking information with a third party. We’ve seen shared AI chats become searchable online too.

Axios reported that many banks allow, or are moving toward allowing, read-only access. This can let a tool analyze transactions without giving it permission to move money.

That’s an important boundary, but it doesn’t make the information harmless. An agent that can read bank statements may still disclose them if it’s compromised or manipulated. Preventing transactions and protecting confidentiality are separate security goals.

How to keep control of your money

For consumers, the practical question is not whether banks have perfectly selfless motives. It’s what access you’re giving away, and what could happen if the agent makes a mistake.

Don’t paste banking passwords or security codes into a general-purpose AI assistant. Major banks have explicitly warned customers against sharing their credentials.

Use your bank’s approved connection methods rather than giving an agent your login. Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help.

Give agents access to as little sensitive information as possible. An assistant comparing publicly advertised savings rates doesn’t need your bank statements. OpenAI recommends limiting agents to the data and credentials they need for the task.

Review consequential actions yourself. If an agent asks for confirmation, check exactly what it intends to do and what information it will share. Don’t treat a confirmation prompt as a formality.

AI can make it easier to compare financial products and spot opportunities you might otherwise miss. But an assistant that finds a better rate and an agent that can act inside your account are different propositions.

Let it help with the homework, but be cautious about handing it the keys.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Title: Cisco open sources tool for detecting AI agents on hacking sprees
Context: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging...
Full Text: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse. It’s called Project Quarry, and it aims to provide a “shared language” for evaluating agent behavior, along the lines of what Snort, which Cisco also maintains, did for detecting malicious network traffic and what YARA did for rule-based malware identification. Most detection tools rely on specific interactions with an AI model or agent. Did it attempt prompt injection? Or did the agent call an attack tool? “But what is missing is the entire context under which something may occur,” Amy Chang, head of AI threat and security research at Cisco, said in an exclusive interview with The Register. She likened this to credit card fraud detection. Without context, individual transactions such as a small test charge or a single purchase in a location far away from a card-holder's usual location may not raise any flags. “And then you try again,” making another fraudulent purchase, “and that went through, too. So now I’m gonna buy the PS5,” Chang said. “Those are the things that Quarry addresses by taking into consideration the entire agent session,” she explained. “One tool call may seem in-scope until you realize that that next step is taking that information and sending it to an attacker-controlled inbox or server.” Even data theft is a sequence and not a single agentic action. Agentic AI security firm Invariant Labs demonstrated this with a proof-of-concept attack against GitHub's MCP server that hijacked a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue, and coerced it into leaking data from private repositories. Simply reading a configuration file, or sending a request to an external endpoint may be legitimate agentic actions. However, combining the two can lead to data exfiltration – and shows “why action relationships matter,” wrote Chang and fellow Cisco researchers Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, and Konstantin Berlin in a blog post about Quarry shared with The Register ahead of publication “A policy can produce a finding when the trace shows a sensitive file read followed within a defined window by an external send,” they wrote. “The risk comes from the relationship between the two actions, so the finding should preserve evidence from both." Quarry covers single- and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs. In addition to the open source code itself, the project’s GitHub repository includes installation instructions, supported Python versions, plugins for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, configuration examples, rule-writing guidance, and a rule starter pack. For instance, with the rule pack, “If a base-64 encoded malware is somewhere in the tool call, that would result in a block,” Chang said. The rule format looks similar to a YARA or Snort rule, with a header that details the traffic to examine, content to match, and metadata for tracking the rule. Here’s a Quarry rule that flags an agent that reads a credentials file: While the Cisco Ai researchers have not run Quarry against data describing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, they suggest that if the intrusion had been read as a complete, step-by-step record of a single session, there were several points where the AI agents’ steps would have given a Quarry rule something to act on and flag for humans. For example, Quarry would probably have flagged internet access from a sandbox. “The rule can flag specific tool calls that reach an external server asset that wasn’t in the task’s allow list,” Chang said. “Another one would be credentials found and used somewhere else.” According to OpenAI’s technical report about the Hugging Face intrusion, this is exactly what happened on July 10, when an agent validated 14 exposed Hugging Face tokens with write access and shared them. “The rule would flag that there was a credential in the tool result that then called an outside service, which is likely not within the parameters of what you would want to do in this case,” Chang said. “We don't want you to go and search for credentials that may have been leaked or inadvertently exposed and then utilize them to conduct a task.” The Cisco team is quick to say that rules along are not a substitute for chain-of-thought monitors, or other forms of human oversight – but they do help record a pattern that other teams can then “review, test, and apply to their own agents,” they wrote. Herein also lies the benefit of open source, and a collective approach to defending against adversarial use of AI, Chang said. “Do we have all the answers? No,” Chang said. “We all see slices of the problem, and it’s important for us to share what we see.”®

Full Text: UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data. Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised. A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected. 123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker. "Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said. "Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts." They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in. There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too. "The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us. "In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked. "That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us." The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU. The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners." 123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification. The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution. "If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone. "We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account. "We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®

Title: Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature
Context: Cybersecurity Operations Cyber Risk Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Threat Intelligence News Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around...
Full Text:
A two-month operation in Africa led to the arrests of nearly 1,500 cybercrime suspects across 20 African countries and the US, the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds, and the shutdown of nearly 11,000 malicious networks.

The third annual roundup of cybercriminals and financial scammers, dubbed Operation Serengeti III, aimed to take down groups responsible for ransomware, phishing, and cyber-enabled fraud, Interpol stated. The operation expanded the impact of cyber-focused investigations from previous law enforcement efforts in 2024 and 2025, which netted 1,006 suspects in the original Operation Serengeti and 1,209 suspects in last year's effort, dubbed Operation Serengeti 2.0.

The increasing arrests show that the national law enforcement partners are becoming more mature in their investigative practices and collaboration across jurisdictions, says Neal Jetton, director for cybercrime at Interpol.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

"Rising arrest figures reflect stronger enforcement activity, not a change in the scale of offending," he says. "The success of law enforcement efforts should be judged by whether fewer people are victimized over time and not by the number of suspects arrested or victims identified during a specific operation."

The crackdown came as cybercriminals in the region continue to develop more sophistication in their operations, with a survey of African members finding that 72% of the 36 African countries have discovered a criminally operated scam center and more than half of cybercrime cases involved the use of AI — 8% frequently and 47% occasionally, according to Interpol's "African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026."

The data highlights the rapid improvements in cybercriminal infrastructure, says Jacomo Piccolini, vice president of global data partnerships at Team Cymru.

"Scams that once looked like individual schemes now run like businesses, with recruitment pipelines, international staff, and, increasingly, trafficked workers," he says.

Busting Transnational Criminal Orgs

In Uganda, for example, two transnational criminal organizations (TCOs) used a rotating call-center model with scripted communications, fraudulent websites, and fake trading platforms to convince elderly victims in Asia to invest in their financial scams, Interpol said in a statement on Operation Serengeti III's impact. Ugandan law enforcement authorities successfully dismantled the fraud rings, arresting 365 foreign nationals, consisting almost entirely of citizens from various Asian nations, Interpol's Jetton says.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

In another arm of the operation, national police arrested nine suspects in Angola, dismantling two illegal cryptocurrency mining sites and seizing more than 2,000 devices used to mine crypto along with six illegal power transformers valued at more than US $1 million. Cybercriminal mining operations are a common way to generate cryptocurrency, the favored method of cashing out on illegal schemes, Jetton says.

"Cryptocurrency played a significant role in moving the proceeds," Jetton says. "It is now the principal rail for this type of fraud."

In Nigeria, police shuttered two fraud operations: One using 2.1 million email addresses to create a large-scale phishing and business email compromise (BEC) operation, while another scheme focused on international investment fraud and garnered at least US $2.4 million in profits, Interpol stated.

The schemes showed off the role that AI is taking in enabling cybercriminal campaigns. The phishing and BEC campaigns used email addresses and AI agents to scrape information from LinkedIn and other social media to identify high-value targets, Jetton says.

"AI enabled the threat actor to create highly personalized phishing emails by mimicking the writing style of executives, colleagues, and suppliers," he says, adding that "AI helped criminals manage and prioritize millions of email addresses for large-scale campaigns and, in some cases, combined with voice cloning, deepfake videos, and AI chatbots to make social engineering attacks even more convincing."

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

Maturing Collaboration Between Law Enforcement

Law enforcement collaboration is making the individual nations more effective in tackling transnational cybercrime. With international partners, the individual countries are able to gain intelligence on signs of cybercriminal activities in their country, says Team Cymru's Piccolini.

"The biggest change is timing. Since Serengeti 2.0, investigators have gone in with intelligence on suspicious IP addresses, domains, and command-and-control servers before the operation begins, along with training in open source, crypto, and ransomware investigation."

Without such collaboration, TCOs could evade repercussions, especially if they limited their activities to impacting only citizens of other nations, as in the case of the Asian investment fraud ring.

"Actors targeting victims in Europe and North America use infrastructure spread across multiple jurisdictions, which makes it harder to pursue through any single country," Piccolini says. "That’s a big part of why international operations like Serengeti, with partners who can see across borders, matter so much."

Both Interpol and Team Cyrmu stressed that several operations are ongoing, with investigators continuing to use seized data and other information to pursue suspected cybercriminals.

Title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
Context: A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second
Full Text:
Executive Summary

In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY, a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer.

Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it.

INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean.

The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it.

Key Takeaways

Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected.

The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere.

Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated.

Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console.

The Campaign So Far

INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY.

The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password-gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts.

Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product

The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second.

Detection

Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel.

Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them.

For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs

By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else.

Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list.

A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it.

Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You

FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so.

Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added.

What Keeps It There

Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below)

The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be.

Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works

First move

Why it fails on its own

Delete the webshell

Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags.

Patch FreePBX

Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system.

Change the admin password

The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login.

Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it.

Preserve first

The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run:

Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below.

Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times.

Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs.

Then clean, in this order

Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref.

Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local.

Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled.

Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php.

Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host.

Conclusion

The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account.

The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR.

The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure.
