Title: Quantum-resistant signing on AWS, Part 2: Enforce your ML-DSA algorithm policy with SCPs and IAM
Context: Review these controls periodically and pair the deny-list with detection so a variant outside your policy surfaces quickly rather than waiting to be discovered
Full Text:
You want to set a cryptographic algorithm policy and stop non-compliant choices from being made in your Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment. This post shows you how. As you adopt post-quantum cryptography, one of the first decisions you face is which algorithms and parameter sets fit your business needs, balancing security against signature size, key size, and performance. Your cloud environment’s job is to let you express that decision and enforce it consistently, so an approved choice stays fully usable while an excluded one cannot be introduced. This post works through one concrete example on AWS: taking an organization’s cryptographic algorithm policy and turning it into preventive and detective controls. The same patterns apply to whatever your approved set is today and whatever it becomes as standards evolve.

This post is Part 2 of a two-part series on quantum-resistant signing on AWS. Part 1, Build a software supply chain with ML-DSA, is for builders and constructs an end-to-end ML-DSA signing pipeline for binaries, container images, and software bills of materials. This part is for the security, governance, and compliance teams who decide which algorithms that pipeline, and everything else in the organization, is permitted to use, and who need that decision enforced.

AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the ML-DSA digital signature scheme (FIPS 204) through three parameter sets, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87, targeting NIST security categories 2, 3, and 5. All three are strong, standardized choices. Each one trades signature size, key size, and speed against security margin, the amount of cryptographic strength a parameter set holds in reserve above its target security category. ML-DSA-44 is the most compact and fastest. ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 carry a larger security margin, which is what you want for signatures that must stay trustworthy over a long lifetime.

Throughout this post, the examples use the same example policy: an organization that has standardized on ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 and wants ML-DSA-44 kept out of its approved set. That is a standardization decision, not a judgment that ML-DSA-44 is insecure (see the following note). Wherever you see ML-DSA-44 in the controls that follow, read it as the variant your policy doesn’t include; the mechanics are identical for any allow/deny split you choose. The approved set here is also the one the Part 1 architecture deploys: ML-DSA-87 for the root certificate authority (CA) and ML-DSA-65 for the subordinate CA and the code-signing key. Part 1 makes the choice; this post makes it stick.

Note: ML-DSA-44 is a valid choice. ML-DSA-44 is a fully NIST-standardized parameter set (FIPS 204) at NIST security category 2, which targets roughly 128-bit-class classical security (category 2 is benchmarked against the collision resistance of SHA-256). It produces the smallest signatures and public keys of the three variants (a 1312-byte public key and 2420-byte signature) and is the fastest to sign and verify, which makes it a strong fit for constrained devices, high-volume signing, and bandwidth- or storage-sensitive workloads. You would choose ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 instead to gain extra security margin for long-lived signatures or to align with an internal standard, not because ML-DSA-44 is weak.

What success looks like

The approved variants (ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 in the example) remain fully usable throughout. What you want to rule out is the introduction of a variant outside the policy (here, ML-DSA-44). Concretely, within the AWS service surfaces in scope, principals shouldn’t be able to:

Create ML-DSA-44 key material

Use existing ML-DSA-44 keys for signing or verification

Stand up private certificate authorities (CAs) that would introduce ML-DSA-44.

And any drift from those settings should be detected.

Scope and limitations

These controls operate on AWS service APIs, principally AWS KMS, AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA), and AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). They don’t and can’t govern cryptography that runs on compute you control. For example, OpenSSL or an application might perform ML-DSA-44 signing on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, container, or AWS Lambda function. Protocol-level use, such as OpenSSH’s hybrid ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 public key authentication, is also outside the reach of Service control policies (SCPs) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and isn’t addressed in this post.

Certificate material brought in through acm:ImportCertificate or iam:UploadServerCertificate is also not algorithm-aware (see the Private CA section). Other TLS-terminating or signing services (for example Amazon CloudFront and Amazon API Gateway) and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere aren’t covered in this post and should be assessed separately. (Part 1 of this series uses IAM Roles Anywhere with ML-DSA certificates; controls for that service are out of scope here.)

These controls are intended to be applied as defense in depth. You can apply all of them or only a subset, depending on how prescriptive you want to be:

A blanket SCP at the organization root prevents member accounts from creating or using ML-DSA-44 keys. (SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so workloads there aren’t restricted.)

An SCP at a production organizational unit (OU) restricts keys only in production accounts.

If you need flexibility inside an account, use IAM permission boundaries instead of account-wide settings enforced through an SCP.

Choose the combination that matches your operating model. The policy examples here are written to apply across all AWS Regions. If you need to scope a control to specific Regions, add an aws:RequestedRegion condition.

The policies in this post are illustrative starting points. Authoring, validating, and maintaining the specific SCPs, IAM policies, and permission boundaries for your environment is your responsibility. Test all policies in a non-production environment before deployment and adjust example values (such as policy names and key Amazon Resource Names (ARNs)) to match your organization’s approved standards.

A note on cryptographic agility

Your algorithm policy isn’t fixed forever, and these controls shouldn’t be either. The point of expressing the policy as AWS controls is that you can revise it as your needs and the relevant standards change, tightening, loosening, or swapping the approved set without re-architecting. Treat the examples here as a template you adjust to whatever your current policy is.

A deny-based control that names specific algorithms is, in effect, an allow-list of everything it does not name. The risk is default-allow: any parameter set you have not explicitly denied is permitted, so a newly introduced variant, including one you have not yet evaluated, becomes usable until you notice it and add it to the deny list. Deprecation of an already-approved variant is easy to handle in this model, because you simply add the deprecated variant to the deny list. What the model does not catch on its own is the arrival of something new. Review these controls periodically and pair the deny-list with detection so a variant outside your policy surfaces quickly rather than waiting to be discovered.

The alternative is to write the condition against the approved set rather than the excluded one. A Deny that uses StringNotEquals with a list of approved key specs fires when the request’s key spec matches none of them, so a new or not-yet-evaluated variant is blocked by default until you add it. That closes the default-allow gap, at the cost of a policy update before anyone can use a newly approved variant. The family-level SCP in Part 1 of this series takes this shape: it denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML_DSA_*. The examples in this post take the other shape and name the excluded variant, so that approved variants stay usable without a policy change. Both are valid. Choose based on whether you would rather block something new first and approve it later, or notice it first and decide then.

{ "Sid": "OnlyApprovedMlDsaVariants", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_*" }, "StringNotEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": ["ML_DSA_65", "ML_DSA_87"] } } }

The StringLike clause scopes the statement to ML-DSA key specs so it doesn’t affect other key types; the StringNotEquals clause denies any ML-DSA variant outside the approved list.

Just as algorithms and key sizes will be introduced over time, or move from approved to unapproved, so will AWS service operations. The set of operations through which an ML-DSA-44 key can be used today (AWS KMS Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey) reflects current service capabilities and might expand as AWS releases new features. If your policy is to block use in addition to creation, you should periodically review the list of operations you restrict, because services evolve over time.

Background: Key spec compared to signing algorithm

AWS KMS support for ML-DSA introduces three key specs—ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87—that all use a single post-quantum signing algorithm: ML_DSA_SHAKE_256. This distinction drives which controls are effective.

kms:KeySpec: Reflects the KeySpec property of the key. It’s evaluated both on CreateKey (the requested key spec) and on AWS KMS key resource operations that act on a specific key, including Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey. This makes kms:KeySpec a reliable lever for both preventing creation of ML-DSA-44 keys and restricting use of existing ones, because it can single out ML_DSA_44 from ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87.

kms:SigningAlgorithm: Reflects the signing algorithm supplied on Sign and Verify, which is ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 for all three variants. It therefore can’t distinguish ML-DSA-44 from the approved variants and shouldn’t be used for this purpose.

The practical consequence: for keys held in AWS KMS, preventing ML-DSA-44 key material from being created is the most robust single control. If no ML-DSA-44 KMS keys exist, none can be used for signing through AWS KMS and none can become the subject key of a certificate. CA keys and TLS server keys are separate material: AWS Private CA generates and holds a CA’s key pair in its own HSMs, and ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded TLS certificates carry their own keys, so those surfaces are governed by the AWS Private CA and certificate controls later in this post. Where ML-DSA-44 KMS keys already exist, their use can additionally be restricted with kms:KeySpec.

Organization and account-level blocking using SCPs

SCPs can be applied at the organization root or to a specific OU to restrict ML-DSA-44. Placement determines the effective scope: it applies organization-wide when attached at the root; attached to an OU, it applies to the accounts within that OU. An SCP is the broadest-scope preventive control available.

Note that SCPs apply to member accounts and OUs but not to the organization’s management account, so avoid running ML-DSA-44-capable workloads in the management account, where an SCP will not restrict them.

The following example SCP denies both the creation of ML-DSA-44 keys (kms:CreateKey) and their use (kms:Sign, kms:Verify, kms:GetPublicKey), matching on the ML_DSA_44 key spec in each case. The creation deny stops new keys from being created; the usage deny covers keys that already exist, whether created before the SCP was attached or living in an account that later joins the OU, because kms:KeySpec is also evaluated at request time on those usage operations.SCPs are guardrails: a Deny in an SCP can’t be overridden by any IAM policy within member accounts.

Attach the following SCP at the organization root (or relevant OU):

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } }, { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "kms:Sign", "kms:Verify", "kms:GetPublicKey" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

Scope the usage deny to the three key-spec-aware actions. Limit the use of Deny to kms:Sign, kms:Verify, and kms:GetPublicKey (testing confirmed kms:KeySpec is evaluated on all three). Avoid a blanket kms:*: a wildcard that would also catch management operations such as DescribeKey, DisableKey, and ScheduleKeyDeletion, which you need to inspect or clean up those same keys, effectively locking you out of managing the keys you’re trying to remove. If you use multi-Region keys, also add kms:ReplicateKey to the creation deny: replicating an ML-DSA-44 primary key creates a new ML-DSA-44 key in another Region, and kms:KeySpec is evaluated on ReplicateKey as well.

Combining with a family-level guardrail. This SCP governs which ML-DSA parameter set is allowed; it says nothing about RSA or ECDSA. Part 1 of this series includes a complementary SCP that denies creation of any signing key whose key spec isn’t ML-DSA. Attached together, they require every new signing key to be ML-DSA and to be an approved variant.

Operational considerations. A blanket Deny at the organization root is the strongest control but has trade-offs: it removes any ability to create ML-DSA-44 keys anywhere in scope, with no exception path, which can block legitimate testing and might cause infrastructure as code (IaC) or pipeline runs that attempt ML-DSA-44 creation to fail. To preserve flexibility, consider scoping the Deny to a production OU and using IAM permission boundaries (see the following section) in build and non-production accounts.

What the caller sees. When an SCP denies a request, the caller receives an AccessDenied error indicating an explicit deny in a service control policy. For same-account and same-organization requests, the error includes the type of the denying policy and, as the enhanced error messages roll out across services, its ARN. The error doesn’t expose the SCP policy contents, and the user being blocked often can’t see the SCPs applied to their environment. Document the SCP ARN and its purpose internally so support teams can map an AccessDenied quickly.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS (principal-level)

The following IAM policy blocks ML-DSA-44 at the principal level. It is the identity-based counterpart to the SCP shown earlier, useful when you want per-account or per-role control rather than an organization-wide guardrail. Attach it to the IAM role or user you want to constrain.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

Key points:

The condition value is ML_DSA_44 (underscores, not hyphens).

This policy blocks CreateKey only. To also block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys at the principal level, add the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey deny shown in the Restricting use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys section.

For comprehensive, non-overridable coverage, deploy as an SCP rather than relying solely on principal-level policies.

IAM permission boundaries

IAM permission boundaries set the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to an IAM role or user and can be used as an alternative or complement to using SCPs. The effective permissions are the intersection of the identity-based policy and the boundary, and a Deny in a boundary can’t be overridden by an attached policy. Boundaries are useful where you want per-account or per-role flexibility (for example, in build or non-production accounts) rather than a blanket, multi-account deny.

Operational consideration. A permission boundary only takes effect on principals that have it attached. To rely on boundaries as a control, you need a mechanism to enforce the boundary on all IAM principals programmatically. One example enforcement mechanism would be an SCP that denies iam:CreateRole, iam:CreateUser, iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary, and iam:PutUserPermissionsBoundary unless the approved boundary is set (using the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key), and denies iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary and iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary outright so the boundary can’t be removed after the fact. You would also want to probe for non-conforming principals periodically and respond, perhaps by automatically attaching the PermissionsBoundary. IAM users shouldn’t be used, but the enforcement should account for the possibility that they exist.

Because a boundary only sets a ceiling and does not itself grant anything, it opens with Allow on all actions, then denies ML-DSA-44 key creation specifically. The following permission boundary denies creation of ML-DSA-44 keys:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowAll", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" }, { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyCreation", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "kms:CreateKey", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

To also block use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys for the principals carrying this boundary, add the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey deny statement shown in the following section (which also uses kms:KeySpec).

Restricting use of existing ML-DSA-44 keys

As described in the Background section, kms:KeySpec is also evaluated on Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey, reflecting the KeySpec of the key being used. You can therefore deny those operations when kms:KeySpec equals ML_DSA_44 while continuing to permit ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87. The IAM policy below, attached to an IAM principal, does exactly that.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyMLDSA44KeyUsage", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": [ "kms:Sign", "kms:Verify", "kms:GetPublicKey" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:KeySpec": "ML_DSA_44" } } } ] }

This deny can also live in an AWS KMS key policy. The same kms:KeySpec deny can be placed directly in the key policy of an AWS KMS key. A key policy is a resource policy, so the statement must include a Principal element. Identity policies and SCPs do not name principals to which they apply. A deny in the key policy is a resource-side backstop that protects a specific key, while an SCP gives non-overridable organization-wide coverage. To turn the previous example into an AWS KMS key policy, add a Principal element to the statement (for example "Principal": {"AWS": "*"}, or a more specific principal), and keep the rest of it the same.

Additional approaches

Depending on your goals you might also want to remove the key material itself rather than only deny its use. Remember that it is difficult to know what data has been signed by a specific key, unless you track that somehow. Deleting a key that was used will make signature verification impossible. Take great care to make sure keys are not used before deleting them.

Disable or schedule deletion of the keys. Disabling stops key use immediately and is reversible. Key deletion is definitive but irreversible after the waiting period, so confirm before scheduling.

Deny Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey by specific key ARN. You can target named keys rather than the whole key spec. To do this, you would list the exact key ARNs in the Resource element of the IAM policy (no condition key required). This is effective for targeting a single key specifically, but it is difficult to maintain lists of key ARNs. Use this strategy sparingly. If you’re considering using an IAM policy naming a key ARN, remember that a Deny in the key policy of the target key accomplishes the same goal and is attached to the key itself.

Finding existing keys (only needed if you disable or delete). A Deny in an IAM policy or SCP, based on kms:KeySpec, doesn’t require you to know which keys exist – it applies by key spec at request time. If you want to disable or delete existing ML-DSA-44 keys, you need to locate them. AWS KMS has no server-side filter for key spec, so you must enumerate keys with ListKeys and call DescribeKey and inspect each KeySpec. This client-side filtering pattern is common across AWS APIs and is well supported by pagination in the AWS SDKs. You can also use AWS Config to record and query KMS key resources.

Reference: Choosing a KMS key spec – kms:KeySpec condition key

Approved ML-DSA variants and control of AWS Private CA

AWS Private CA sets a certificate authority’s (CA’s) signing algorithm at creation time, in the CertificateAuthorityConfiguration parameter of CreateCertificateAuthority (valid values include ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87). There is currently no condition key for the algorithm, so an SCP cannot enforce signing algorithm. The approach in this section controls who can create CAs and pins the algorithm in that trusted path, backed by AWS CloudTrail-based detection.

Recommended approach

Restrict who can create CAs. Deny acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority broadly via SCP, and allow it only for a small set of trusted roles or an approved provisioning pipeline. This removes the ability for arbitrary principals to stand up a CA with an unapproved algorithm.

Pin the algorithm in the trusted path. Have that approved pipeline or infrastructure-as-code template hard-code SigningAlgorithm to ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 in CertificateAuthorityConfiguration. Because AWS Private CA exposes no algorithm condition key, this provisioning path is the enforcement point. Note that the CA’s algorithm pins the signature on the certificates it issues; the subject key in each certificate comes from the CSR, which AWS Private CA copies without validating its algorithm, so pin the CSR key algorithm in the same issuance pipeline.

Control the trust chain. On the PKI side, only add approved CAs to your trust stores and issuance hierarchies, and do not trust or subordinate CAs that could issue ML-DSA-44. This prevents an unapproved CA from being introduced into a trusted path.

Detect drift. Use CloudTrail to capture CreateCertificateAuthority calls and AWS Config to flag any CA whose configuration uses ML_DSA_44, so an unapproved CA is caught quickly.

Part 1 of this series shows what this looks like in practice: it creates an ML-DSA-87 root CA and an ML-DSA-65 subordinate CA with CreateCertificateAuthority, activates them, and distributes the resulting chain to verifiers. In the model described here, those are the calls that only your approved provisioning pipeline is allowed to make.

Setting the ML-DSA value in CertificateAuthorityConfiguration. The same variant goes in both the KeyAlgorithm and SigningAlgorithm fields (for example, KeyAlgorithm=ML_DSA_65 with SigningAlgorithm=ML_DSA_65). Note a difference in signing algorithms between AWS KMS and AWS Private CA. With AWS Private CA, the SigningAlgorithm takes the variant value directly (ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, and ML_DSA_87), and doesn’t accept ML_DSA_SHAKE_256. In contrast, AWS KMS uses ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 as its signing algorithm. Be aware that some older AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) builds omitted descriptions of the ML-DSA variants from the built-in CLI help, so don’t rely on the help in the AWS CLI to determine valid values. For more information, see CertificateAuthorityConfiguration API Reference.

Known limitation. Some surfaces have no algorithm condition key, so you enforce them through provisioning and detection rather than policy. acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority has no condition key for the algorithm, and acm:ImportCertificate and iam:UploadServerCertificate are not algorithm-aware, so a disallowed signature setting on a created, imported, or uploaded certificate cannot be blocked by an IAM policy or SCP condition. Govern these through your provisioning process, restrict who can call them, and deny the import and upload actions entirely where they are not required. The controls above remain the available mitigation.

In particular, iam:UploadServerCertificate doesn’t support any method to prevent use of particular algorithms, and AWS doesn’t recommend using this API to generate and upload certificates. This API predates ACM and exists mainly to cover AWS Regions or partitions where ACM is not yet available. While a new Region or partition is being built out, workloads can still need a TLS server certificate before ACM support has shipped there, and uploading a certificate to IAM gives you a place to store and reference it in the meantime. Once ACM is available in that Region, you should use ACM instead. Outside that narrow case, deny iam:UploadServerCertificate unless it is genuinely required.

ACM-issued leaf certificates. A CA’s own key and signing algorithm are separate from the leaf certificates that ACM issues from it. If you use ACM to request leaf certificates, you can constrain the leaf’s key algorithm with the acm:KeyAlgorithm condition key on acm:RequestCertificate. This lets you allow-list approved algorithms for leaf certificates using SCPs or IAM policies, similar to the AWS KMS examples earlier in this post. Be aware that, at the time of writing, ACM doesn’t offer ML-DSA leaf certificates. So a policy like this is a forward-looking defense-in-depth control rather than an immediate ML-DSA-44 risk. The IAM example below is illustrative (using example approved algorithms). Since this is an evolving part of the service, be sure to validate this in your environment before relying on it.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "RestrictACMLeafKeyAlgorithm", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "acm:RequestCertificate", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringNotEqualsIfExists": { "acm:KeyAlgorithm": [ "EC_secp384r1", "RSA_2048" ] } } } ] }

This example uses StringNotEqualsIfExists so it denies only requests that specify a disallowed algorithm. With plain StringNotEquals, a request that omits acm:KeyAlgorithm would also be denied, because the missing key makes the condition evaluate true. Choose the operator that matches whether you want to block requests that leave the algorithm unspecified.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 usage in TLS for NLB and ALB

Elastic Load Balancing, for both network load balancers (NLB) and application load balancers (ALB), terminates TLS on behalf of your applications. The certificates used by these listeners are requested through or imported into ACM, or uploaded to IAM. A listener’s configured security policy and its certificate determine what’s offered during negotiation. At the time of writing, ACM requests and imports accept RSA and ECDSA keys only, and NLB and ALB listeners accept RSA and ECDSA certificates only, so no ML-DSA certificate can be bound to a listener today. As with the ACM leaf-certificate policy earlier, the controls in this section are forward-looking defense in depth rather than a mitigation of an immediate ML-DSA-44 risk.

Certificate controls (the effective mechanism for ML-DSA-44)

Because the listener API calls reference a certificate only by ARN, you can’t write an SCP on CreateListener, ModifyListener, or AddListenerCertificates that inspects the certificate’s algorithm. IAM conditions can’t reference attributes of a separately-referenced resource. Keeping ML-DSA-44 out of TLS therefore relies on there being no ML-DSA-44 certificate material to associate:

Configure your private CA to issue only ML_DSA_65 or ML_DSA_87 certificates, and control who can create CAs.

Prevent ML-DSA-44 key creation in AWS KMS, so that no KMS-held ML-DSA-44 key can become the subject key of a certificate. TLS server keys for ACM-issued, imported, or uploaded certificates are not KMS keys; those are governed by items 1 and 3.

Control imported and uploaded certificates through your provisioning process or deny the import and upload actions where not required, as described in the AWS Private CA section.

Detective controls

CloudTrail records the certificate and listener API calls in this section: certificate creation and import (acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority, acm:ImportCertificate, iam:UploadServerCertificate) and listener configuration (CreateListener, ModifyListener, AddListenerCertificates). Whether the algorithm shows up in the event depends on what the call itself carries. Creation calls that take the algorithm as an input record it: kms:CreateKey logs the KeySpec, and acm-pca:CreateCertificateAuthority logs the signing algorithm. That makes CloudTrail effective for catching the creation of ML-DSA-44 key material or a CA. A listener binding references its certificate only by ARN, so the certificate’s algorithm does not appear in that event. To evaluate the algorithm of a bound or imported certificate, use AWS Config resource evaluation as the detective backstop.

Summary for TLS

The primary preventive control is the certificate material itself: with no ML-DSA-44 CA, no ML-DSA-44 KMS key, and certificate import and upload controlled, no ML-DSA-44 certificate can be issued or bound. Where you also operate an allow-list of permitted TLS security policies, the elasticloadbalancing:SecurityPolicy condition key (on CreateListener and ModifyListener) can additionally constrain which TLS policies listeners can use.

Summary of controls

The following table maps the example policy (allow ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87, exclude ML-DSA-44) to the available controls. Modify the controls to limit use to the approved set of algorithms your policies require.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to use ML-DSA as an example of turning a cryptographic algorithm policy into enforceable AWS controls. The key lever is the kms:KeySpec condition key: it keeps your approved parameter sets (ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87) fully usable while preventing the creation and use of a parameter set you’ve excluded (ML-DSA-44) on the CreateKey, in addition to the Sign, Verify, and GetPublicKey operations, where kms:SigningAlgorithm can’t tell the variants apart. Applied as defense in depth across SCPs, IAM policies, permission boundaries, and KMS key policies, and extended to the surfaces that have no algorithm condition key (AWS Private CA, certificate import, and Elastic Load Balancing TLS) through provisioning controls plus AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config drift detection, these controls give you a consistent way to keep an unapproved variant out of your accounts.

The pattern isn’t specific to ML-DSA-44. Title: Luna Moth Leaks Shed Light on Ransomware Group's Inner Workings
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Leaked files have disclosed the inner workings a major ransomware group, which demonstrates a multi-layered, businesslike approach to its operations.

The analysis by Check Point researchers has revealed information on the instructions the Luna Moth group provides to ‘staff’ on how to best emotionally manipulate their victims into providing remote access to their enterprise machines and how the work is divided up between a social engineer and the hands-on keyboard attacker.

The documents were leaked to an anonymous onion site called “The Luna Moth Files” in early October 2026 and claim to contain internal files and chat logs of Luna Moth, commonly also known as Silent Ransom Group (SIG). The group is also tracked by cybersecurity analysts as Chatty Spider UNC3753.

Analysis of the files by cybersecurity researchers at Check Point, published on October 9, has exposed what appears to be the inner workings of the Silent Ransom Group, with ‘staff’ working on several stages of the operations which are designed to steal confidential information and extort financial payments from victims using blackmail.

The operation begins at a planning stage, in which criminal operators identify organizations and individuals to target, with the required business context to ensure that the initial contact appears entirely legitimate before the victim is persuaded to communicate over the phone.

In many cases, the attacker poses as IT support or an IT security worker, using the persona to convince the target to provide remote access to their computer via a remote access software tool. This provides the attacker with initial access to the network, which can be abused to move around and even escalate their privileges.

According to the leaked documents, the attackers are provided with scripts to follow which take into account common responses and reactions from their victim. This includes advice on how the caller should handle a victim who isn't trusting or otherwise resistant to the attacker.

IT Support for Cyber Scammers

One element of the social engineering attacks which the leaks appear to have revealed is that when the attackers are on the phone to the victim posing as the IT support worker, the caller isn’t acting alone.

The documents appear to suggest that while one individual is actively speaking to the victim to reassure them and keep them calm, it’s another individual who is actually using the remote software. According to the leaked files, the two cyber-criminals coordinate their efforts using a group messaging service.

“If authentic, the exposure shows that Luna Moth should be understood less as a conventional ransomware crew and more as a specialized data-extortion business whose core platform is the coordinated manipulation of trust,” said the Check Point report.

Given how the activity directly targets people, researchers warned that technical controls are not enough to keep organizations safe from the threat posed by cyber extortion activity which operates in this way.

Steps organizations can take to help protect staff from falling victim to campaigns like this include encouraging employees to verify any unexpected IT requests through a separate, known channel before approving a remote session and to limit which remote access tools employees can install.

Title: Silverfort Secures AI Agents on Google Cloud in Runtime with Agent Gateway Integration
Context: An expanded collaboration with Google Cloud The Agent Gateway integration is not Silverfort’s only collaboration with Google Cloud
Full Text:
Today, Silverfort announces an integration that brings its runtime Identity Security approach to Agent Gateway, part of Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise, giving teams real-time visibility into AI agent activity and enforcing access decisions as they happen.

After Silverfort was named in Google Cloud’s Next ’26 announcement among the partner services bringing identity and governance administration to Agent Gateway, it is time to announce the new milestone we have been building toward, and it lands at exactly the moment enterprises need it.

A milestone for securing agentic AI

Agent Gateway is a genuinely significant piece of infrastructure. Announced in preview at Google Cloud Next ’26, it provides “an open, extensible, scalable way to enforce centralized governance policies to securely connect agents, models, and tools across runtimes.”

For an Identity Security company, that is exciting news. Every agent interaction can be configured to flow through Agent Gateway, which makes it the natural place to apply Identity Security controls at scale. Silverfort now secures the AI agents running there by connecting directly into the platform’s control plane, so agent owners never have to route traffic through a separate gateway.

Why AI agents change the identity problem

Organizations are adopting AI agents faster than most identity and security teams can inventory, monitor, or control them. These agents authenticate into systems, access sensitive data, and take actions across cloud and SaaS environments, often with broad privileges and limited oversight. The result is a rapidly expanding identity attack surface that traditional security tools were not built to address.

Agents also do not fit neatly into traditional security models. Unlike a human user who logs in once and works within predictable patterns, agents can chain actions across services, escalate broadly privileged credentials and tools, and behave in ways that are difficult to predict or trace. That leaves most organizations unable to answer basic questions: how many agents are running, who owns them, what they can access, and which ones are overprivileged.

These risks also arrive from two directions at once. Alongside the exposure created by an organization’s own agents, adversaries are now using AI-powered attack models built to probe, exploit, and move laterally at machine speed. They are not the same problem, but they converge on one control plane: what an identity is permitted to access, and what it is allowed to do. When agents are overprivileged and attackers are autonomous, the window to act is very small.

What Silverfort delivers on Agent Gateway

Visibility into agent activity

Silverfort automatically discovers AI agents operating through Agent Gateway and maps each one back to its human owner for clear accountability. Security teams get a complete view of agent behavior, ownership, permissions, and access paths across Google Cloud and beyond.

Runtime enforcement controls

Silverfort evaluates agent requests against access policies at the Agent Gateway layer before they reach downstream systems, limiting unauthorized privilege escalation and risky agent overreach. If an agent attempts to access a dataset, SaaS application, or internal resource outside its approved permissions, Silverfort evaluates that request in real time and enforces the appropriate policy response. Unauthorized attempts are stopped in line rather than detected after the fact.

Risk-based prioritization

Not all agents carry the same level of risk. Silverfort analyzes agent exposure based on privilege level, access patterns, and connections to sensitive resources. Overprivileged agents, dormant credentials, and high-risk access paths are flagged and prioritized so teams can focus remediation where it matters most.

Granular access policies and detailed audit trails

Policies are defined by agent identity, target application, and action type, and are managed from a centralized dashboard. Access requests are allowed or blocked in real time, and all agent activity is auditable and tied to enterprise identity governance frameworks and to the human using the agent.

Because the controls sit where agent traffic already flows, organizations gain all of this without deploying additional infrastructure or redesigning how their agents are built. Developers keep building. Agents keep running.

Meeting agents where they actually run

AI agents do not all run the same way, so Silverfort delivers runtime enforcement in two complementary ways. The Silverfort MCP Gateway is a universal inline enforcement layer between agents and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers they access, built for custom and open-framework agents operating outside closed, vendor-specific ecosystems.

By connecting directly into the control plane of leading agentic platforms, Silverfort enforces policy without requiring agent owners to route traffic through a separate gateway. That’s the right fit for cloud-managed enterprise environments where scale, platform resilience, and zero workflow disruption are critical.

An expanded collaboration with Google Cloud

The Agent Gateway integration is not Silverfort’s only collaboration with Google Cloud. In June, Silverfort launched an integration with Google Security Operations that pulls live identity risk into SecOps playbooks and pushes enforcement back the other way, letting analysts raise a user’s risk indicator or tighten a service account policy from inside a response case. It ships through the Google Cloud partner integrations catalog.

Both integrations point in the same direction: identity telemetry and runtime enforcement reaching Google Cloud teams inside the tools they already run.

One platform for human, machine, and AI agent identities

AI agents do not operate in isolation. They share access paths with human users, service accounts, and other non-human identities, and they often create overlapping risk across all of them. A compromised or overprivileged agent can become a path to lateral movement, privilege escalation, or data exposure, and protecting the agent alone without visibility into the identities around it leaves gaps that attackers will find.

Silverfort brings AI agents into the same Identity Security Platform used to protect human and non-human identities across cloud and on-premises environments. Because those controls apply at runtime, they hold against both pressures – an agent drifting outside its approved scope, and an attacker moving at machine speed with credentials it should never have been able to use. Enterprises rarely run a single agentic AI platform, and enforcement extends across the wider ecosystem regardless of where agents run.

Availability

The Silverfort integration with Google Cloud’s Agent Gateway is now live. Organizations running AI agents on Google Cloud can get started without installing additional software or making code changes to existing workflows. Visibility and runtime protection begin on day one.

This is the beginning

Agentic AI is moving from experimentation to production faster than any enterprise technology in recent memory, and identity is where its security will be decided. Bringing runtime Identity Security to Agent Gateway is a significant step, and one of many we intend to take as the agentic ecosystem grows.

If you’re new to Silverfort, see how we secure AI agents across every platform and request a demo today. For current customers, click here to get started with the integration now.

Title: Net Closes Around ShinyHunters with Another FBI Arrest
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The FBI has arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive on suspicion of involvement with the ShinyHunters group, which was responsible for a major breach at the bureau last month.

FBI director, Kash Patel, confirmed the arrest on X October 9, without naming the individual in custody.

“Our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor,” he said on X (formerly Twitter).

“This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly.”

Read more on ShinyHunters: ShinyHunters Claim Hack of Rival Ransomware Gang Clop.

However, court documents indicate the identity of the person arrested as Edward Dubrovsky, a cyber founder and investor based in Toronto.

He has been charged with conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats.

Dubrovsky, 54, is reportedly a former managing director at incident response firm Cypfer and currently associated with cyber-consulting firm CyberSteward.

He appears to be a self-styled expert in negotiating with cyber extortionists, as evidenced by a book he authored, Cyber Extortion Strategic Response. The book is marketed as a “practical manual for leaders on managing coercive events, negotiation and settlement strategies.”

Arrests Mounting for ShinyHunters

Dubrovsky is the latest of a number of recent arrests as the FBI seeks to hit back at the group responsible for a serious data breach in September 2026.

Dutch police arrested convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the incident.

Saif Al-din Khader (aka Rey), who is 17, was taken into custody in Jordan on September 29 and is said to be cooperating with the FBI’s investigation.

That came after ShinyHunters exploited a vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft to compromise the agency's jobs site, and then pivoted to its AWS GovCloud servers to extract 2-3TB of data.

Experts believe it could be one of the most damaging government breaches in recent history, if reports are correct that the hackers made off with names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers, and emergency contact details for thousands of FBI employees, including those in counter-intelligence work.

It has been reported that an Accenture contractor has been removed from their work with the bureau after failing to patch the vulnerability which was subsequently exploited by ShinyHunters.

Cypfer Statement on Association with Dubrovsky

Cypfer contacted Infosecurity to provide the following statement regarding its association with Dubrovsky:

"In response to recent reports associating Edward Dubrovsky with CYPFER, the company clarifies that Mr. Dubrovsky served as a Managing Director from May 2022 through December 2025, at which time he left the firm. Mr. Dubrovsky has had no affiliation, operational role or relationship with CYPFER since that time, and contrary to certain reporting, was never a founder or co-founder of the company," the firm wrote.

"CYPFER remains steadfastly committed to the highest standards of integrity, ethical business practices and federal-grade governance across all global operations, continuing our mission to protect and defend our clients worldwide."

This story was updated on October 13 at 16.35 BST to incorporate Cypfer's statement.

Title: Karaoke Giant Reveals Data Breach Impacting Eight Million
Context: “According to NCG, between October 1 and October 2, 2026, a malware infection was discovered on one of their employees' devices (a PC), and the device was isolated from the...
Full Text:
One of Japan’s biggest karaoke box operators has revealed a data breach at a supplier which it claims may have exposed personal information of over eight million customers.

Daiichi Kosho has several popular brands including Big Echo, one of the country’s largest karaoke box chains, and also manufactures karaoke entertainment systems.

It published a statement on October 8 claiming an incident at Nippon Columbia Group (NCG), a Japanese entertainment group which handles customer information for the firm.

“According to NCG, between October 1 and October 2, 2026, a malware infection was discovered on one of their employees' devices (a PC), and the device was isolated from the network on October 2. Following an investigation into the scope of the impact by NCG, we received a report from NCG on October 5,” it explained.

“Personal data related to work outsourced to us was temporarily stored on the device in question, and we cannot rule out the possibility that this data may have been leaked.”

Read more on data breaches: KDDI Breach Affects Six Japanese ISPs, Exposes 14.2 Email Credentials.

NCG has reset affected passwords and is investigating the cause of the incident as well as whether data was compromised or not, the notice continued.

“Based on the information we currently have, approximately 8,724,000 customers who registered or made reservations at our stores may have had their names (registered names), genders, dates of birth, email addresses, and telephone numbers leaked to external parties,” it warned.

Daiichi Kosho urged customers to be on the lookout for possible phishing attempts using this personal information.

“Please be extremely careful of suspicious emails, SMS messages and phone calls, and do not open any links or attachments that you do not recognize,” it said. “We will never ask you for your password or credit card information. We ask for your continued caution.”

The majority of those impacted by the potential breach are customers of Big Echo (5.6 million) and the company’s DK Dining brands (3.5 million). Other affected businesses include Mega Big, Banana Club, Karaoke Club Dam and B-Garage.

Daiichi Kosho has opened a toll-free number for any concerned customers to get in touch while it confirms what happened.

Japan in the Crosshairs of Cyber-Attacks

The news comes after several cyber-attacks in recent weeks that have rocked the country.

In September, two major railway operators in the Tokyo region revealed separate incidents. Subway operator Tokyo Metro said an unauthorized third party had accessed the email addresses of 59,000 passengers signed up to its Metpo loyalty scheme.

At around the same time, Keio Corporation revealed a ransomware attack, although it’s not clear whether any data was compromised.

Car-rental company Times Car announced on September 25 that an unauthorized third party gained access to its website, leading to the compromise of personal information on 6.6 million members and former members.

Last year a major ransomware attack on food and beverage giant Asahi Group Holdings severely disrupted operations.

Japan has long been playing catch up on cybersecurity, due partly to chronic skills shortages and poor governance.

A new Active Cyber Defence law which came into force on October 1 will empower the Self Defense Forces (SDF) and police to proactively access and neutralize hostile foreign servers, but it may do little to improve cybersecurity posture in regular organizations, especially SMBs.

Context: According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward
Full Text:
Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

Edward Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile.

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

Image: Courtlistener.com

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

Title: The Flax Typhoon gets a cold front.
Context: Reports include vulnerability details, proof-of-concept exploits and, when available, suggested fixes. Attackers exploited multiple zero-days earlier this year, including vulnerabilities used to install custom malware and others that CISA later linked to ransomware operations.
Full Text:
An international coalition disrupts Chinese state-backed hacking operations. Officials dismantle cybercrime centers in Ghana. Anthropic launches initiatives aimed at quicker remediation. A maximum-severity SonicWall vulnerability is under active exploitation. The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act remains in legislative limbo. Ransomware spikes. Attackers exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS backup software. Midnight Mimosa targets cheap Android device firmware. Prosecutors saddle a money mule. Maria Varmazis joins Dave to continue our CyberWire’s 10th anniversary celebration with a conversation about public-private partnerships. Open AI does the math.

Today is Friday October 9th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

An international coalition disrupts Chinese state-backed hacking operations.

An international coalition has disrupted infrastructure used by Integrity Technology Group, a Chinese cybersecurity company that U.S. officials say supports state-backed hacking operations. The Justice Department seized websites supporting two Integrity Tech tools, Microscan and FishHub, used in the long-running Flax Typhoon campaign.

Microscan automated reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against targets including power companies, airports and other critical infrastructure. FishHub helped attackers conduct phishing operations and deploy malware after gaining access to victim networks. Authorities say Chinese actors have also targeted poorly monitored edge devices to maintain persistent access, potentially positioning themselves to disrupt critical infrastructure later.

Agencies from the U.S., Australia, Japan, the U.K., Spain, New Zealand and Canada contributed to a detailed advisory describing Integrity Tech’s tools and operations.

Officials dismantle cybercrime centers in Ghana.

Ghanaian authorities say they dismantled suspected cybercrime centers in the Greater Accra Region, arresting eight suspects and rescuing 120 people believed to have been trafficked and forced into online fraud, including romance scams. Investigators seized 136 phones, 130 laptops, networking equipment, vehicles and other evidence.

The operation has also prompted a dispute over who was in charge. FBI Director Kash Patel portrayed the raid as part of the bureau’s global “Operation Blackout,” but Ghana’s Cyber Security Authority says the operation was planned, coordinated and executed by Ghanaian authorities. The CSA acknowledged intelligence support from the FBI and Britain’s National Crime Agency, while stressing that foreign agencies cannot independently exercise police powers in Ghana. Most of those rescued were Nigerians, and authorities are working to repatriate them.

Anthropic launches initiatives aimed at quicker remediation.

Anthropic has launched two cybersecurity initiatives aimed at turning AI-discovered vulnerabilities into fixes more quickly. Its free OSS Scanner lets open source maintainers opt in to periodic scans using Anthropic’s most capable models. Reports include vulnerability details, proof-of-concept exploits and, when available, suggested fixes. To speed disclosure, reports are sent without human review, meaning some may contain errors, though Anthropic expects a true-positive rate above 90 percent.

The company is also launching its Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, bringing Claude models, engineers and threat research to companies that secure operational technology. Anthropic says OT vulnerabilities are particularly challenging because industrial systems often can’t be taken offline for patching. The initial program includes security vendors, consultancies and industrial manufacturers, with plans to expand to additional partners and sectors.

A maximum-severity SonicWall vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers appear to be targeting a maximum-severity vulnerability in SonicWall SMA1000 remote-access appliances just days after a patch became available. CVE-2026-102255 affects the WorkPlace interface on several SMA1000 models and could allow an unauthenticated attacker to make the appliance access internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

Security firm Previdian says its honeypots detected exploitation attempts consistent with the flaw, though researchers haven’t confirmed that those attempts successfully compromised systems. Shadowserver is tracking more than 400 internet-exposed SMA1000 appliances, but it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

The activity continues a rough stretch for SonicWall’s SMA1000 line. Attackers exploited multiple zero-days earlier this year, including vulnerabilities used to install custom malware and others that CISA later linked to ransomware operations.

The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act remains in legislative limbo.

More than a year after permanent authorization for the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 expired, Congress remains deadlocked over its future. CISA 2015 protects companies from certain liabilities when they share cyber threat indicators with the government or one another. Short-term extensions have kept those protections alive, but tied them to recurring government funding battles.

Senate Homeland Security Chairman Rand Paul continues to block a long-term extension, seeking an amendment restricting government efforts to influence social media content moderation. Bipartisan proposals in both chambers would extend the law through 2035, but none has advanced.

The Cyber Threat Alliance says uncertainty hasn’t dramatically reduced existing information sharing, though it may discourage new participants. Its president, Michael Daniel, favors a medium-term extension that would give Congress time to modernize the law for AI-era threats, including information about attacks such as model distillation.

Ransomware spikes.

Ransomware activity reached a record high in the third quarter of 2026, according to Comparitech, which counted 2,627 claimed attacks—up 27 percent from Q2 and 61 percent year over year. Only 247 have been confirmed by the targeted organizations.

Finance and technology saw the sharpest quarterly increases, while education, healthcare, government and utilities also experienced substantial growth. Comparitech suggested advances in AI could be helping attackers scale and accelerate their campaigns.

Researchers also noted growing use of triple extortion, in which attackers encrypt systems, steal data and then pressure individuals or customers connected to the victim. The average ransom demand was about $602,000.

Qilin and The Gentlemen were the most prolific groups, while the United States accounted for 1,066 claimed attacks, or 41 percent of the worldwide total.

Attackers exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS backup software.

Attackers are exploiting two unpatched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS backup software to gain unauthenticated remote code execution. Huntress says CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 affect even the latest version and have targeted at least five organizations. Attackers chained the flaws to deploy webshells, conduct reconnaissance, install XMRig cryptocurrency miners and establish persistence. With no patch available, Huntress recommends restricting the AhsayCBS management interface to trusted IP addresses or requiring VPN access and checking systems for compromise.

Midnight Mimosa targets cheap Android device firmware.

Bitdefender has uncovered Midnight Mimosa, a supply-chain malware campaign affecting low-cost Android devices built on MediaTek platforms. The malware is embedded in device firmware before sale, giving it system-level privileges and persistence that survives normal uninstall attempts. Operators can remotely install or remove apps, grant permissions and load additional code, enabling ad fraud, click fraud and botnet activity.

Bitdefender has observed thousands of affected devices across more than 150 countries over two years, with Western Europe and the Americas particularly represented. Researchers also found 13 Google Play apps containing related ad-fraud code, though without the firmware malware’s privileged access.

Midnight Mimosa can temporarily disable Google Play and Play Protect while installing additional payloads, giving its operators extensive control over compromised devices from the moment they’re activated.

Prosecutors saddle a money mule.

A Ukrainian-Russian dual citizen has pleaded guilty to helping run Your Mule Cashout, a money-laundering operation that processed millions of dollars for cybercriminals worldwide. Prosecutors say 42-year-old Oleg Korniev helped manage the organization, which operated since 2007 and recruited more than 15,000 U.S. money mules through fake job offers.

The mules received stolen funds in their bank accounts and wired the money to cash-out contractors in Eastern Europe. YMCO allegedly processed more than $10 million stolen from over 750 U.S. bank accounts.

Korniev admitted the operation caused more than $14.7 million in actual and intended losses and that he laundered at least $7 million. He pleaded guilty to charges including money laundering, identity theft and computer fraud conspiracy, and faces between two and 50 years in prison.

Stick with us after the break, I will be joined by Maria Varmazis to continue our CyberWire Daily 10th anniversary coverage, where we will speak on public-private partnerships and law enforcement operations over the last decade. And Open AI does the math.

Maria Varmazis and I sit down to continue our CyberWire Daily 10th anniversary coverage, as we will speak on public-private partnerships and law enforcement operations over the last decade. Here’s our conversation.

That was Maria Varmazis and I discussing public-private partnerships and law enforcement operations over the last decade. If you enjoyed this conversation, be sure to check out the full interview on Monday.

Open AI does the math.

OpenAI dropped more than 350 AI-generated mathematical findings in a single day, prompting reactions ranging from “breathtaking” to something closer to professional vertigo. The results span algebra, number theory, topology and other fields, including a proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis that Rutgers mathematician Alex Kontorovich said would merit a Fields Medal if produced by a human.

But mathematics has not simply packed up and gone home. The enormous collection still needs verification, and OpenAI had withdrawn three papers and corrected others by Thursday. Researchers are also wrestling with what industrial-scale AI discovery means for peer review, graduate education and the pleasure of doing mathematics itself.

The consensus seems to be that the machines have climbed some formidable mountains. Mathematicians now get to verify the routes—and contemplate what happens when the climbing equipment starts choosing the peaks.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Wikimedia Says Rogue AI Agents Abused its Platforms
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Rogue AI agents have been caught again doing things they shouldn’t be on the open web, this time on platforms run by Wikimedia.

The non-profit giant, which operates Wikipedia and several other open-knowledge platforms, revealed the news in a blog post published on October 5.

Chief product and technology officer Selena Deckelmann said that her team investigated potential unauthorized agent activity after reading recent reports about this kind of behavior.

The team quickly discovered that OpenAI agents:

Made testing edits to Wikimedia wikis in sandboxed areas of the platform not visible to users, and edits to the configuration of a citation tool. Wikimedia believes the latter “were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services”

Made unsuccessful attempts to compromise Etherpad, a note-taking tool hosted by Wikimedia, in order to fetch data from other websites as a proxy

Made millions of automated requests to Wikimedia’s public APIs, crawled millions of pages and made hundreds of thousands of data queries to the Wikidata Query Service (WQDS), which may have contributed to a partial outage of the service in May

Read more on rogue agents: OpenAI: Hugging Face Incident a “Warning Shot” to the World.

Deckelmann said her team didn’t find any evidence that their systems had data compromised or were used for coordination among agents.

“However, we are concerned about what could have occurred here, the difficulty and effort involved in investigating and attributing this activity, and the growing risks of agentic AI activity on our platforms in general,” she added.

“The open web is a public good. We should not allow this behavior to become the ‘new normal’ for the people or organizations that maintain it.”

Piling Pressure on the Internet

Deckelmann did not pull her punches, arguing that Wikimedia’s findings show how agents can drain resources and crash servers, even when they aren’t compromising data and systems.

“This intense pressure on our infrastructure not only adds costs for servers and humans, but if left unaddressed, can block human visitors by overloading systems and causing outages,” she continued. “We are already paying for costs that come with the increased activity.”

Deckelmann argued that AI companies aren’t doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from possible harm.

“That burden is falling onto everyone else, including smaller organizations,” she said. “At a minimum, their systems should operate in a way that non-profit website owners like us can easily identify and choose how they interact with our services.”

Industry experts agreed. Jamie Beckland, chief product officer at APIContext, argued that Wikimedia’s findings point to a “serious failure of safety controls.”

He added: “Every organization operating public-facing services now needs to be equipped to recognize, manage and, when necessary, block inappropriate agent activity.”

Bri Frost, director of product management at Cloud Range, said that things tend to go wrong when inexperienced users hand agents open-ended tasks.

“Before giving an agent credentials or tools, teams should test it in a realistic environment, including with vague or poorly written prompts,” she added. “Does it stay within its permissions? Does it try to work around restrictions? Does it escalate to a human when a task pulls it outside its lane? If you can't answer those questions, the agent isn't ready for that level of autonomy."

Title: $10 million bounty offered for Chinese Hafnium hacker accused of Microsoft Exchange Server mega-attack
Context: The following the year the pair allegedly exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange Server to steal further information
Full Text:
The US State Department is offering up to US $10 million for information about the whereabouts of Zhang Yu, a 44-year-old Chinese national who is accused of being a key figure in China's state-sponsored hacking group, Hafnium.

Hafnium (also known as Silk Typhoon) is widely believed to be the group thatexploited zero day vulnerabilities to breach Microsoft Exchange Server systems in early 2021,

According to the bounty announcement on the United States Rewards for Justice website, Zhang is a director at Shanghai Firetech Information Science and Technology and works under the direction of the Shanghai State Security Bureau (part of China's Ministry of State Security.)

Zhang is charged alongside 34-year-old Xu Zewei with malicious cyber activity against US computer systems between February 2020 and June 2021.

According to the Rewards for Justice bounty, from early 2020 Zhang and Xu allegedly stole data - including research on COVID-19 vaccines - from the email accounts of immunologists, virologists, and US universities, at the behest of China.

The following the year the pair allegedly exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange Server to steal further information. Once the flaws became public knowledge, other cybercriminal groups and state-sponsored hackers are thought to have also targeted hundreds of thousands of unpatched servers. Victims included the European Banking Authority.

US authorities claim that China uses private companies like Shanghai Firetech and Xu's Shanghai Powerock Network to spy and steal sensitive information, whilst at the same time obscuring the government's involvement in hacking.

Even if somebody provides information about Zhang's location it does not mean that he will be brought to court. Zhang is believed to be in China, which will not extradite its citizens - especially not one who is alleged to have been spying on its behalf on adversaries.

Furthermore, if findings by security firm SentinelOne are to be believed, Zhang's Shanghai Firetech filed multiple software patents about extract data from computers.

That's not to say, of course, that the alleged hackers can breathe easy. Xu, for instance, was arrested at Milan airport in July 2025 and extradited to the United States in April this year.

Xu has pleaded not guilty, saying that he was in Italy on holiday with his wife and that the police have detained the wrong man. China's Foreign Ministry opposed Xu's extradition, accusing the United States of fabricating charges against him.

So, if nothing else, a bounty of up to US $10 million for information about Zhang makes his future foreign travel an increasingly risky proposition, and gives anyone who has knowledge about his future holiday plans a good incentive to talk.
